Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Bill I have the honour of tabling in the House today is to authorize the Governor in Council to instruct the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission, commonly referred to as the CRTC, to harmonize the costs of telephone services within a given socio-economic region.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, the entire matter of longdistance charges is governed by three criteria, namely, commonality of interest, contiguity and distance. These traditional criteria create regional disparity and inequity among citizens in the same region, and the purpose of this Bill is to ensure that within the same socio-economic region, Canadians will not have to pay long-distance charges when they have to make calls within these cities.

Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from a number of constituents who believe that the Government lacks a mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a trade deal with the United States. They believe that the proposed trade deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and undermine our ability as a country to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
There are a number of other points which I will simply bypass in order to get on with the Leaders' speeches. The basic line of the petitioners is that they are asking that Parliament now dissolve to allow the people of Canada the opportunity either to accept or to reject the proposed trade deal during a national general election.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to introduce two petitions from the residents of Spadina and nearby.
The first petition concerns immigration and the promise made several times by the Minister that unmarried sons and
daughters of all ages will be considered as members of the family class of immigrants. As well, it has been promised for two years that the Government would remove the unfair distinction between Canadian citizens and permanent residents of three years or more, the distinction between them in regard to sponsoring their parents of any age. These promises have not yet been fulfilled. Therefore, the undersigned citizens and residents of Canada cal! upon the House to ensure that the Government fulfil these promises now.

Mr. Speaker, this petition from Spadina and nearby is from citizens who are concerned that the Government, without a mandate from the Canadian people, is negotiating and trying to conclude a trade deal with the United States which would compromise Canadian sovereignty and deny Canadians the opportunity to develop our economy on our natural resource base without gaining access to the American market.
Therefore, your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve to allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement in a national general election.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present two petitions on the same subject. I am pleased the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is in the House today. These petitions are from people in Port Alberni, Delta, Mission and Vancouver, British Columbia. Again, it concerns the high incidents of crime, including murder, robbery and sexual assault, committed with knives. This is on the increase in all major cities across Canada.
Whereas the federal Criminal Code and court decisions allow citizens to carry knives for self-defence, and the carrying of knives is directly responsible for knives being used in a variety of crimes, the petitioners ask Parliament to amend the federal Criminal Code to prohibit the carrying of knives by citizens in public places. The only exceptions would be those whose use of a knife is integral to legitimate work or those carrying a knife for religious reasons, such as is in the case of Sikhs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Continuing debate. The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, one year ago the First Ministers of Canada signed the Meech Lake Accord. It was a rare and memorable occasion in the history of our country. For the first time in living memory there was unanimous agreement on a major constitutional amendment. For the first time in a generation there was an answer to that troubling and difficult question; What does Quebec want? For the first time in a decade, we were able to see the way ahead to the next stage of our constitutional evolution as a people.
No one who was there in the old railway station that day will ever forget that day, the great sense of joy, the great sense of pride in our country.

As it happened, Mr. Speaker, the sentiment of June 3, 1987 was summed up by the next day's banner headline in Le Devoir, and I quote;
Le Canada dit oui au Quebec.
Hear, hear!

The Accord reflects our history in that it recognizes the linguistic duality of Canada, and Quebec's distinctiveness within Canada, within the federation-those are key words in the document-while affirming the equality of the provinces. It reflects the aspirations of our people in the recognition that indeed in our judgment there is room enough for all of our citizens to affirm their identity as Canadians. It reflects the reality of our country, this vast, magnificent land stretching thousands of miles from Newfoundland and Labrador to British Columbia, a federation in which the diversity of our regions very much contributes-not damages-very much contributes to our national interest. There are some of the realities about Meech Lake; a sense of history, a sense of country, and a sense of reality.
I am the first to acknowledge that the Meech Lake Accord is not perfect, but we will leave to others the theories of constitutional perfection. We had to deal with the Canada that was left to us with Canada as it is, and that is a Canada that, in 1982, achieved the patriation of its Constitution and the entrenchment of its Charter of Rights and Freedoms without the assent of Quebec, principal home of one of our two official
June 14, 1988
language communities which gave rise to Canada, the existence of our country at the very beginning. As a result, the 1982 Constitution Act, which I have no hesitation in acknowledging had been intended as an instrument of unity, had become the opposite even before the ink was dry. This was a deep and a lasting wound on the body politic of our country.
In fact, by deciding to proceed without Quebec, and this was a value judgment that was made, the federal Government of that day ensured, first of all, that any attempt to reintegrate Quebec would take place in isolation in the future, any Prime Minister or any Parliament called upon to deal with this festering problem would have to do so in isolation, thereby depriving the federal Government of the flexibility inherent in a comprehensive negotiation. Because of this isolation, any formula to bring Quebec into the Constitution could be portrayed as giving in to Quebec or giving up too much for Quebec.
Not only was Quebec isolated in 1982, but the prospects of future constitution reform were also effectively blocked. That was the situation we inherited at Meech Lake and that, Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to say was the situation that we remedied at Meech Lake on behalf of a united Canada.
Hear, hear!

Now the hurt of 1981 will be healed at last and the country whole again will be able to move on to the constitutional, social, and economic challenges of a new decade and a new century.
Much has been said and written about the Meech Lake Accord in the year since the First Ministers signed the document. Hearings have been held, speeches have been made and reports have been published, but nothing that I have heard or read persuades me that the Accord should be reopened. We said, in fact, that we would reopen the Accord if an egregious error were found in it. None has been found.

I am more persuaded than ever that the Meech Lake Accord is a valuable instrument of healing for Canada. And I am quite persuaded of the urgency for all Hon. Members of moving ahead with the immediate ratification process.
I will not have it said of this House and this generation of Canadians that we allowed this opportunity for national reconciliation to pass. Quebec has said yes to Canada twice, in the referendum of 1980, and in adopting the Meech Lake Accord in the National Assembly in 1987. But once before, in 1981, Quebec was left isolated and alone; we must not allow that to happen again in 1988. It is time, once and for all, for the rest of Canada to say yes to Quebec. And the way to do so is to proceed with ratification of the Meech Lake Accord.
Mr. Speaker, I urge this House and remaining legislatures to do so. Then we can at last turn this page in our history, and get on to the next chapter in our constitutional development. Our constitution is indeed a document for the ages, but it is
June 14, 1988

not cast in stone. Our nation's constitutional development did not end with the British North America Act of 1867. It did not end with the Statute of Westminster in 1931. It did not end with the Constitution Act of 1982. And it will not end with the Meech Lake Accord of 1987. At every stage of our constitutional history, as we have settled the agenda of one generation, we have gained the freedom to move onto the next.

And so it was, Mr. Speaker, after the BNA of 1867 which settled the powers of the federal Government and the provinces and established the goal of "peace, order and good government" in the management of our national affairs; and so it was after the statute of Westminster of 1931 which saw our nation achieve autonomy in the conduct of foreign affairs; and so it was after the Constitution Act of 1982 which saw patriation of our Constitution and the entrenchment of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms; and in the next round which will take place, Mr. Speaker, just as surely as summer follows spring in Canada, we will deal with the outstanding issues of Senate reform, aboriginal rights, and enhancing the role of linguistic and cultural minorities in Canada.
Are we as a Parliament, as a people, to hold Quebec's constitutional reintegration hostage to the pursuit of perfection in these other areas? Let us not make the perfect the enemy of the good. Surely, we have a much better chance to improve our Constitution with Quebec as a full participant at the constitutional table. Surely, no Government in its right senses would try to proceed to these other issues without the participation of Quebec.
The Meech Lake Accord is entirely consistent with our constitutional character as a nation. It affirms the federal nature of Canada. Since Confederation there has been a constitutional division of powers and responsibilities and obligations in Canada. And the discussions that led to the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord culminate over 20 years of constitutional debate. The Accord builds on the constitutional discussions of 1968 to 1971. It builds on the constitutional exercise of 1975 and 1976, and on Bill C-60 in 1978. It builds on the negotiations that followed the referendum in 1980, as well as the patriation exercise in 1980 and 1981.
[DOT] (U30)
We have gained much in the Meech Lake Accord in the national interest and for the benefit of all Canadians. We have gained the signature of Quebec on our Constitution, ending its divisive and potentially dangerous estrangement from our constitutional family. In the process, we have strengthened the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms because, for the first time, Quebec has accepted its moral significance and political legitimacy. That means that all the laws of Quebec will be subjected to the Charter, and the Charter will be interpreted in light of Quebec's distinctiveness, as it is now interpreted in light of Canada's multicultural and aboriginal heritage. We have broken out of the constitutional strait-
Constitution Amendment, 1987
jacket, the dead-end, and gained the ability to move on to the next stage of constitutional reform.
Since 1982, constitutional reform has been effectively blocked. By way of illustration four difficult and challenging and important conferences on aboriginal rights ended in failure in some considerable measure because Quebec declined to participate actively. With the return of Quebec we have increased the chances of success very greatly at a future conference dealing with the outstanding issue of aboriginal self-rule. Surely, if there is one group of Canadians which needs and deserves that degree of justice and equality of opportunity it is our aboriginal peoples. The Meech Lake Accord makes justice much more possible for each and every member of our aboriginal communities across Canada.
Hear, hear!

As for our official language minorities, English-speaking in Quebec and French-speaking in the rest of Canada, we have affirmed not only their vital presence but the role of the provinces to preserve their rights. This is in addition to minority rights entrenched in the Charter. These are first-class Canadian citizens with full Canadian citizenship wherever they live. The role of the federal Parliament and the Government of Canada to protect minority rights at all times wherever those minorities live remains a moral and a legal obligation of the Government of Canada.
When we say that the provinces have a role in preserving minority language rights, we will work for that in the broad, generous sense of that word.

We in the Federal Government will continue to "promote" as well as preserve the rights of official languages minorities, through instuments such as Bill C-72, the amendments to update and strengthen the Official Languages Act.
Mr. Speaker, this morning we concluded an agreement with the Governmnet of Saskatchewan, providing assistance to improve the situation of the 25,000 Francophones who live in that province. That is a tangible sign of our duty and our obligation with respect to linguistic minorities throughout Canada.
In some circles, Mr. Speaker, Meech Lake has been extraneously and erroneously linked with recent events in Saskatchewan. Indeed, that has often been tried with the Meech Lake Accord.
Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake accord was not in effect in 1886. It was not in effect in 1905. It is not yet in effect in 1988. For our linguistic minorities, the Accord means that their rights have been afforded an added measure of constitutional recognition-a "major step in the right direction" in the words of Canada's Commissioner of Official Languages.

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987

The Accord for the first time affirmed the authority of the Parliament of Canada to launch programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. We have affirmed the federal character of the Supreme Court of Canada which is, in my judgment, entirely consistent with its ultimate role as the final arbiter of Confederation. Even more so, with its expanded role in interpreting the Charter it is entirely appropriate that the provinces play a role in submitting nominations for Supreme Court justices. It is entirely in accordance with reality.
Mr. Speaker, if you were to compare short lists of the federal Government with the provinces and the bar for this position you would no doubt find in almost every circumstance almost entirely the same names. But the national Government decides in all circumstances and therefore has the absolute and final say.
With respect to the Senate, pending effective reform, we have struck an interim agreement that also reflects the federal character of the upper Chamber in this federation. Vacancies will be filled by Ottawa from lists of competent people submitted by the provinces.
With respect to immigration, which promises to be a central public policy issue for many years to come, both in terms of economic development and social justice, we have also reaffirmed the federal nature of this issue.
Finally, we have institutionalized and constitutionalized the annual First Ministers Conference on the economy which we began in Regina in 1985. This annual meeting on the economy has proven to be an invaluable instrument of policy planning and co-ordination between Ottawa and the provinces and has introduced new discipline into the budgetary planning process.

Mr. Speaker, this is not a unitary state. Regardless of what some people claim, Ottawa is not the omniscient, omnipotent source of wisdom and power in this land. There are those who say that too much has been given to obtain Quebec's signature. And there are those in Quebec who say that we have not conceded enough. On the one hand, you have those who regard themselves as being in sole possession of the truth, who have always treated Quebec's legitimate aspirations with ill-concealed contempt. On the other hand, you have those who have always rebuffed sincere efforts at reconciling Quebec's legitimate needs with the national interest, whose only interest in constitutional discussions is to sever links with the rest of Canada. And somewhere in between, Mr. Speaker, you have the vast majority of people who regard Quebec as their home, but Canada as their country.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, you have the vast majority of Englishspeaking Canadians in other provinces who want Quebecers to feel at home in Canada.

The Meech Lake Accord reflects that idea and that reality of Canada. Opponents of the Meech Lake Accord would have Canadians believe that it somehow represents a decentralizing thrust when in fact it is a pragmatic representation of the reality of our country.
Compromises were made at Meech Lake, honourable compromises to improve as well as reflect the situation we inherited. But nowhere at Meech Lake have we made compromises as significant as those that were made in 1982.
In 1982, Canada achieved patriation and an entrenched Charter of Rights but only at the price, the tremendous price, of a notwithstanding clause. So while the most fundamental rights of Canadians were guaranteed in 1982, the federal Government agreed that Parliament or provincial legislatures could override these fundamental rights by invoking the notwithstanding clause.
Nowhere in the Meech Lake Accord is there a compromise or a concession of the magnitude agreed to by the federal Government in 1982.
There is still a notwithstanding clause.
Hear, hear!

Rather than criticize and live in the past, we tried to build on the good, and there was much good about the process in 1982. We accepted the advances that came from 1982 and moved on as a nation to the challenge of some day together, all Parties and all Leaders, completing the work of Confederation, which brought us to Meech Lake.
[ Translation]
We have affirmed the linguistic duality of our nation, and the distinctiveness Quebec brings to our country. This constitutional arrangement simply reflects reality. Not that Quebec is special, just that it is different and, distinct within Canada. Language and culture in particular give rise to this fact.
We do not close our eyes to Quebec's distinctiveness within Canada, rather we embrace it, for it enriches our national culture, and strengthens our national identity as Canadians on the northern half of this continent.
The Meech Lake Accord acknowledges the distinctive character of Quebec, while upholding the principle of equality of all the provinces. The other arrangements contemplated by Meech Lake are equally consistent with the constitutional evolution and the practical reality of Canada.

On spending power, for example, while affirming the federal prerogative, we provided for opting out with compensation for provinces which meet national objectives in programs of their own. However, opting out with compensation is not a new idea.
June 14, 1988

It was not dreamed up at Meech Lake. Prime Minister Pearson first introduced the possibility of opting out of shared cost programs through the Established Programs Act of 1965. This applied to matters such as hospital insurance, old age assistance, the welfare portion of unemployment insurance, and vocational training. This is nothing new. Under these conditions social programs have been established in the past, they are being established in the present, and they will continue to be developed for the national good in the future.
With regard to the role of provinces in the appointment of Senators, Members will recall the federal Government's Bill C-60 in 1978, 10 years ago, which envisaged that half of the Senate appointments would be made by the provinces acting alone. Under the Meech Lake Accord the provinces can appoint none. They simply have the right to submit lists of competent candidates with the decisions in all cases being made by the federal Government. That is a far cry from the concession made by a federal Government 10 years ago.
As for the Supreme Court, and this interests every Member of Parliament very much, Members will recall that at the Victoria Conference in 1971 the federal Government proposed a provincial role in nominations. The federal Government would not have retained the final say over who was appointed. This is part of what transpired. This is not something that we dreamed up at Meech Lake. This is calling back on parts of our history.
The immigration provisions of Meech Lake entrench the essential features of the Cullen-Couture agreement of 1977 entered into by the Government of Canada. Let me quote an analysis not of a Member of this House, not of a political supporter, but a very distinguished jurist who exercises his power in another jurisdiction, the Attorney General of Ontario, the Hon. Ian Scott. He analysed the last 10 or 15 years, and this was his assessment:
Most of these proposals, including those advanced by the federal Government prior to 1981, would have established a far greater role for provincial
Governments than is provided for in the Meech Lake Accord itself.
I think the analysis of Attorney General Scott is one that all Members of Parliament from all Parties in every jurisdiction should read very, very carefully.

Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake Accord, like all previous constitutional amendments, is not without its imperfections. Our Constitution is being improved with Meech Lake, and it can be improved in the future. I believe we can all be assured of that. The Meech Lake Accord incorporates improvements to the Constitution Act of 1982, just as the 1982 law brought improvements to the BNA Act. At each stage of our constitutional development, we have improved our constitutional structure. All Members of all Parties in this House can properly feel proud of this achievement. With Meech Lake, we have achieved the best possible arrangement under the circumstances. We are correcting the grave historical error of Quebec's absent signature, and we have obtained it on terms
Constitution Amendment, 1987
that are consistent with our history and our constitutional evolution. As Prime Minister of Canada, as Leader of my political Party, I am proud of the Lake Meech Accord.

Canada is one of the world's youngest nations but one of the world's oldest democracies. It is a country with an Atlantic heritage and a Pacific perspective. It truly is a land for tomorrow, perhaps the most bountiful and blessed country on the face of the earth. In this beloved country, which has been enriched by wave after wave of immigrants coming from around the world to build a tolerant and splendid new society on the northern half of this continent, the Meech Lake Accord brings us together as a people. That is our point of departure with Meech Lake, building one Canada, united and strong.
What is it that we all have in common? The answer is simple. All Members of this House, of whatever Party, whatever region, whatever background or whatever religion, are all Canadians and we all very much love our country.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always with a sense of pride and responsibility that I take part in a debate on the fundamental law of our country. Like the Fathers of Confederation and those Canadians who succeeded them in this chamber, we must meet the challenge of having our collective identity and values reflected in our Constitution. We are at an important stage in the constitutional evolution of our country. I am Canadian. I am proud to be Canadian. That is why I have dedicated a large part of my life to serve my country as an elected representative. I do so because I want to build a Canada that is stonger, a Canada that is more just, a Canada that is more equitable, a Canada that is more united. I do so because I want to continue the Liberal tradition, but more importantly, because we must shape the future of Canada. In this regard, I have always been concerned with Constitutional issues and the unity of our contry.
I admit that I am not the first or the only one to promote excellence, harmony and Canadian unity. The fondamental law of this country, the Constitution, flows from and reflects the perpetual evolution of our nation. Constitutional evolution proceeds as a result of initiatives that flow from the needs and aspirations of our society. Each time, we search for excellence. Each time, we make progress. But each time we undertake such an exercise we are bluntly reminded that perfection is out of our reach. But I believe firmly that we must always persist. We should never be discouraged. The constitutional initiative we are looking at today is unrelated to the ones that have come before, nor is it different.
The objective of this initiative, to return Quebec to the Great Canadian constitutional family, is not only noble, it is absolutely essential. That is why I support it energetically. That is also why I am working energetically to improve it.

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
The whole history of our country is one of meeting great challenge and reaching historic compromise. In founding a parliamentary democracy the Fathers of Confederation recognized that a federal state, with powers shared between the provinces and the central Government, would best respect regional distinctiveness and yet ensure a strong national identity. There has been a perpetual ebb and flow in the powers of the provinces and the federal Government. The British North America Act of 1867, which defined that relationship was amended and refined many times to reflect the evolving priorities of our country.
There are two views of Canada which compete for dominance whenever we discuss the constitutional reform. One is the sense of a very centralized country, one Canada. The other is a concept of a very loose Confederation, such as a community of communities or the idea of deux nations. I see the Constitution differently. These two polarized and conflicting views do not reflect the whole debate, nor do they represent the sum total of constitutional discussion in this country. I have always believed in a balanced federalism, a federalism which is in equilibrium, a Canadian federalism. That has always meant to me a strong federal Government and strong provincial Governments operating in their own jurisdictions. Canada has one flag, but it does not fly only over Ottawa. Neither is it a patchwork of provincial emblems.
Hear, hear!

I have always believed, Mr. Speaker, that the test which must be met by any proposal to alter our Constitution is not "does it serve this or that level of government?" There is a higher test. The questions that must be asked are: "Does it respect the principles upon which this nation was founded? Does it enhance national unity? Will it work?"
Canada is a great tapestry. Through its intricate weave there are many competing strands, but there are five strands that are essential to the whole. The first is our sense of Canadianism, our love of country, deeply rooted in our history, our geography and our unique environment. The second is our linguistic duality and Quebec's place as the primary, though not the exclusive, source of the French language in Canada. The third is our aboriginal heritage. The fourth is the multicultural nature of Canadian society. The fifth is the paramountcy of individual rights over the powers we have given to Governments. I believe we must constantly review and renew each of these strands; our sense of belonging to this vast land; the essential role of our two founding languages, the special place of our first peoples; the rich and diverse legacy of those who have freely chosen to become Canadian; and the primacy of the individual in Canadian society.
In amending our Constitution, we must always be aware that the Canadian identity can only be preserved by strengthening and not weakening these continuing strands.
The genius of Confederation in 1867 was that it gave us a living document which could evolve to respond to the changing expectations of our people. The British North America Act in 1867 was not a perfect document. It was a compromise. It had several flaws, most notably the flaw that it could not be amended by Canadians in Canada.
Our constitutional evolution began almost immediately. Our country grew and expanded. It moved west and north. We created new provinces out of existing territories. We built an infrastructure quite deliberately to hold this vast and extraordinary nation as one. We built a railway. We established a postal service. We built a national highway. We created a great national public broadcasting system. We created a national airline. We put in place a national unemployment insurance scheme, a national pension plan and a national medicare plan. We heightened the dream of a fair, independent and sovereign Canada.
For nearly 50 years following Confederation there was a strong pull to decentralize this country. Many of the constitutional decisions of the judicial committee of the Privy Council in Great Britain strengthened provincial rights, but when we were faced with national emergencies in the Depression and the two great wars, it became clear that only with a strong national Government could we respond to those challenges. Then, of course, the courts began to reflect that understanding.

[ Translation]
Canada did not achieve full independent nationhood in 1867. It was only with the Statute of Westminster in 1931 that we achieved control over our own foreign policy. It was only in 1949, that our Supreme Court became the final court of appeal in all legal matters, replacing the judicial committee of the Privy Council of Great Britain.
But the goal of complete independence from Britain was still to be achieved. We were still obliged to seek the approval of the Parliament of Westminster for any amendment to our Constitution.
This question was resolved when our Constitution was patriated in 1982. However, this enormous step forward was made without the participation of Quebec. Quebec is a full-fledged partner in our Confederation and must be a full-fledged participant in our evolution as a country.
The question of Quebec's place in the Canadian federation lies at the very heart of our existence as a nation. All too often the aspirations of French-speaking Canadians were met by a wall of indifference. The Riel crisis, the Manitoba school question, Regulation 17 in Ontario and conscription were the source of many French-English tensions. The Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism set up by Prime Minister
June 14, 1988

Pearson in the 1960's sounded the alarm: the country would face serious difficulties if there was no fundamental reform.
In Victoria in 1971, the Liberal government, of which I was Minister of Justice, tabled a proposal which I believe remains a model of political consensus. All ten provinces agreed to an arrangement which recognized the linguistic duality of this country and provided an amending formula which gave a veto right to Quebec and to each of this country's other regions. But the Victoria agreement collapsed almost immediately. Quebec withdrew its support in response to mounting pressure from within that province. It was already clear that the feelings provoked by the constitutional debate were running so high that they could no longer be ignored.
The election of a Parti Quebecois government a few years later crystalized the debate on the future of Quebec in Confederation. A polarization of ideas rapidly developed. That division culminated in the Referendum Debates. The debate was difficult for Quebecers and for many Canadians as well. It pitted family against family, and friend against friend.
At an important point in the debate, Prime Minister Trudeau delivered an historic speech at the Paul Sauve arena. He told thousands of Quebecers that if they rejected the seduction of independence and opted for Canada there would be a renewed federalism. His message was very clear. And it was clearly understood. On the day of the vote, a majority of Quebecers, and a majority of French Quebecers, said a resounding "Yes" to Canada.
Long after referendum day the wounds and the scars were still evident. Friendships had been broken. Dreams had been shattered. But the promise of a renewed federalism remained well alive in the hearts of Quebecers.
After a long and difficult round of negotiations the constitutional agreement of 1982 was proclaimed. It was both historic and essential. We, as Canadians, finally patriated our constitution with our own amending formula and our own Charter of Rights. Since then Canada can amend its own Constitution without reference to the British Parliament. But the Quebec government did not accept the terms of the agreement. They refused to sign it. A majority of the members of the National Assembly, representing all political parties confirmed the decision of the Quebec government.

Although Quebec, constitutionally and legally, was bound by the Constitution, was bound by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Quebec was an unwilling partner. The elected representatives of Quebec rejected the constitutional arrangement in 1982 because, among other things, it failed to recognize the distinctive character of Quebec.
One only has to travel to Quebec to realize that it is a province unlike any other. It is the only province where a majority of our citizens speak French. It has its own civil code, it has a special culture, a distinctive flavour. The distinct character of Quebec is a reality which enriches our country.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Because Quebec was not a full partner from 1982 onward, thousands of Quebecers felt a sense of betrayal and a sense of exclusion. That situation could not be allowed to continue. I am proud to lead a Party which took the initiative to end that impasse. In early 1986, on behalf of our Party, I presented new constitutional proposals to do just that. I acknowledged that Quebec did have a distinctive character. I responded constructively to the five proposals presented by the newly elected federalist Government in Quebec. Our response received widespread support in Quebec.
Premier Bourassa characterized our proposals and those responses as constructive, precise and concise. Quebecers generally considered them to be progressive. At St. Hyacinthe, Quebec Liberals embraced my proposals. At our convention in November of 1986, 3,000 Liberal delegates from all across Canada resoundedly endorsed a confirming resolution.
This was a Liberal initiative, it is true, but partisan politics have no place in the process of making it possible for Quebec to join our Constitution, and that is why we depoliticized this debate.
Hear, hear!

We have always considered it to be a matter transcending differences between political Parties and a subject that challenged each one of us to find a Canadian solution.
The history of recent years has clearly demonstrated that Quebec's absence from the table, even temporarily, impedes any future constitutional development and weakens our country. Indeed, no future constitutional change or reform is possible without the participation of Quebec. Those who oppose Meech Lake as an imperfect document fail to take that into account.
I do not believe that the Meech Lake Accord is the strait-jacket that its detractors paint it to be. It does not extend the unanimity rule to the entire range of constitutional changes, including the division of powers. The distribution of powers can still be changed under the 50 per cent, seven-provinces rule. The unanimity rule in the Meech Lake Accord extends to federal institutions but will not extend much further than it did before. I say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), however, that constitutional reform should not be a casual affair carried out in haste in the early hours of the morning. It should be a well conceived, well thought out, well executed, deliberate effort to reinforce Canadian unity. We deeply regret that the Prime Minister missed that opportunity to present Canadians with a more complete set of amendments to the Constitution.
Quebec must be a full partner in the Canadian family, politically, emotionally, and psychologically. It is for this reason that I support the Meech Lake Accord despite its flaws. We do not look to this Accord to solve all the unfinished

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
business of Confederation. That being said, we still believe that it could have been a better document.

Mr. Speaker, when the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the 1987 Constitutional Accord presented its conclusions, our party submitted a minority report. In it we proposed changes which would considerably improve and enlarge the Meech Lake Accord. These changes reflect the goals and aspirations of all Canadians. We believe that the aboriginal peoples should not be excluded. Most important, they should not be made to feel less important than other Canadians, because this is not the case. We cannot always be proud of the way we have treated our aboriginal peoples. We have ignored and forgotten them too often. Aboriginal peoples should be recognized as constituting a distinctive and fundamental characteristic of the Canadian society. Aboriginal rights should be a priority in constitutional discussions. That is why our amendments propose that the issue of self-government for aboriginal peoples be put on the agenda of the next round of Constitutional discussions.
Mr. Speaker, since the earliest colonization of North America, our country has welcomed people from around the world. Millions of people from every part of the globe continue to join us. They bring with them a set of values and cultures that enrich Canada and make it a better nation. Our Constitution should therefore recognize the contribution of our multicultural communities. We are proud of the multicultural nature of Canada.
The Charter of Rights and Freedoms stands as one of the greatest achievements of our constitutional development, and it must be paramount. The basic rights and freedoms of Canadian men and women must never be diminished. In particular, we must safeguard the equality rights of women as they are enshrined in the Charter. While we believe that the possibility of discrimination is very remote, we want to ensure that our fundamental rights cannot be threatened by imprecise language.

You know, Mr. Speaker, that we believe in an elected Senate. We want to reach this goal in the foreseeable future. I advanced this course in a debate with the Minister of Justice three years ago in this House of Commons when we debated Senate reform. We propose to eliminate the rigid unanimity rule for Senate reform and return to the formula of seven provinces and 50 per cent of our population.
Hear, hear!

I believe that our current amendment reflects the demographic and territorial facts of our country. Our proposal would accelerate the move from an appointed to an elected upper House. We would have Senators elected now, when vacancies occur rather than appointing them from provincial lists. I believe that the democratic rights
of all Canadians would be strengthened by giving them the power to elect all their national representatives.
Canadians living north of the 60th parallel have been deprived by this Accord of the chance of any future representation in or appointment to the Senate. We propose that the citizens of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories have the right, as do all other Canadians, to senatorial representation. We also suggest that the eventual provincehood of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories be resolved, as it has been in the past, solely by the federal Government and the potential province in question.
We believe that the clauses in the Accord dealing with the appointment of Supreme Court justices could lead to an impasse between the federal and provincial governments. Parenthetically, I believe that the Prime Minister was wrong in his analysis of the 1971 Victoria Charter as it related to Supreme Court appointments.
We have, therefore, suggested a solution which would ensure that the Supreme Court has a full complement of judges at all times in the event of an impasse. It would also protect the basic rights of northern Canadians by granting their governments the same rights as the provinces have under the Accord to nominate candidates to the court.
Another area of the Accord which I have studied very carefully is the provision on shared cost programs. It is my view, certainly shared by the Attorney General of Ontario, that the Accord does not basically change the division of powers as they reside in the federal and provincial governments. In so far as it relates to the federal spending power it probably strengthens its power because it explicitly recognizes for the first time that that power can operate within areas of provincial jurisdiction.
The Meech Lake Accord specifies that national shared cost programs are to be established by the Government of Canada and that if a province carries on a program or initiative that is compatible with the national objectives it is entitled to reasonable compensation.
We believe that this clause should be clarified to ensure that Parliament sets those national objectives and ensures that there are minimum national standards. We would ensure that the minimum standards are met by the provinces in order to qualify for compensation. I do not believe, however, that allowing provinces to opt out of some federal-provincial programs, as has occurred-and the Prime Minister recited this-in the past, will damage our unity.
We also believe that to put the issue of fisheries on the agenda every year would create unnecessary instability in the fishing industry. Three of the four provincial Governments in the Atlantic region have expressed their deep concern that any transfer of this jurisdiction to the provinces would result in anarchy in the fishing industry in the Atlantic. For that reason we propose that the issue be dealt with once and for all at the
June 14, 1988

first constitutional conference called for within the terms of this Accord.
One of the major thrusts of the Meech Lake Accord was the obligation on the part of provincial governments to preserve minority language rights. This strengthening of bilingualism in itself is a step forward for official language groups and ought to be noted. We in this Party, however, want to offer even more protection to official language minorities by ensuring that Parliament is responsible, not only for preserving, but for promoting the status of official languages.
Hear, hear!

For this purpose we have introduced an amendment which would allow any province to adhere to this requirement should it choose to do so. All political leaders in this country have an obligation to ensure that the spirit of the Accord is upheld.
The Prime Minister mentioned Saskatchewan. I am deeply disappointed that the Government of Saskatchewan introduced a language law which the Prime Minister admitted to me here in the House of Commons contravened in spirit and in letter the constitutional Accord. This legislative action was taken by a Premier who sat and negotiated at the table. It was introduced into a legislature which ratified the Accord. Yet our Prime Minister praises that Premier. On his visit to Saskatchewan he should have told that Premier to withdraw the Bill.
Hear, hear!

There are other changes to the Constitution which we have not proposed in our amendments. The reason we have not proposed them in the amendments before Your Honour is that the rules of the House do not permit amendments to parts of the Constitution that are not touched by the Meech Lake Accord. However, these further amendments are part of our constitutional agenda, as are the amendments introduced in the Senate and in the House of Commons in identical language. We would ensure that Section 33 of the Constitution Act, 1982 is repealed. That is to say, the notwithstanding clause which allows both levels of Government to enact legislation exempt from some of the most important sections of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Prime Minister characterized this erroneously, I believe, as a compromise which made 1982 possible. But in any event, the fact that he failed to obtain provincial approval to omit this clause when he had an opportunity to do so underlines his lack of personal commitment to the Charter.
In future constitutional discussions we propose to eliminate the phrase "where numbers warrant" in the clause relating to the administration of minority rights in education. We would rely on the general interpretation clause in the Constitution,
Constitution Amendment, 1987
which would allow schools to be set up in a minority language where that was reasonable.
These are my Party's proposals for constitutional reform. They are the focus of our vision of Canada. They reflect the central realities of our history. They mirror the great tapestry which is our country.
I believe in a federalism in equilibrium. I believe in a balanced federalism. A balanced federalism is the Meech Lake Accord plus the amendments we have submitted to the House. That is the formula for our future. That is the prescription for national unity. That is the formula that responds to the difficulties that have been found in this Accord across the country.
I renew my undertaking to argue for this balanced view here in the House of Commons, across the country, as part of our platform during the next election, and as part of our program when we form a government.
Hear, hear!

I understand that there can be disagreement, but I am going to continue my efforts to persuade those who do not share the vision I have tried to describe of a balanced federalism.
I urge all Members of the House, indeed I urge all Canadians, to accept the fact that constitutional reform is an evolutionary process. The Meech Lake Accord is not ideal. That is true. But it does have the overwhelming advantage to national unity of bringing Quebec to the table and bringing Quebec back to the Canadian family. We have to build on that unity before we move on to any other constitutional reform.
Let us not lose sight of the goal or turn away from the challenge before the House. Let us move forward with purpose toward realizing our dream of building a stronger, more confident, more united Canada. The greatest enterprise we have ever undertaken is this country itself. It is an enterprise which every generation must enhance. It is an ideal for which every generation must strive. It is a dream which every generation must rekindle. I am proud to be a Canadian. I am proud to share that dream. I am proud to stand for a Canada that is sovereign and that is just and, above all, that is united.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, today's debate will have major historic consequences for this country. That is clear. In fact, in the twenty years I have been a Member of this House, few debates have been as important as this one.
In the sixties, Mr. Speaker, Canadians all over the country were asking: What does Quebec want? That was the question in Jonquiere, in Vancouver, in Toronto and in the Prairies. All Canadians were asking the same question. Since then, our history has known some difficulty and I would even say

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
tumultuous times: the October crisis and the federal Government's excessive reaction which lead to the totally unjustified imposition of the War Measures Act; the election in Quebec of a government dedicated to Quebec's independence from the rest of Canada; the referendum in which the majority of Quebecers said yes to Canada; the patriation of the Constitution which gave Canada its own Constitution and its Charter of Rights, but unfortunately isolated Quebec from the rest of Canada; the negotiations that started after the meeting of First Ministers in 1986 in Edmonton, where it was decided that the next constitutional priority would be to include Quebec in the constitutional process, which led to the Meech Lake and Langevin meetings in May and June 1987, which produced the Accord.
Mr. Speaker, what does this Accord give us? Quite simply, it gives us Quebec's answer to the question: What does Quebec want? And the answer is: Quebec wants to take its place proudly within Confederation as a member of the Canadian community, fully participating in our tradition of co-operative federalism. Quebec wants the rest of Canada to reaffirm our history and incorporate, in our Constitution, that which has been unique and distinct since the inception of this country.
That is the very essence of this debate. Mr. Speaker, Quebec has said a clear and decisive yes to Canada, while reminding us of what we really are as a country, and ten provincial Premiers and three federal Parties answered a decisive yes to the concept of a great country with a distinct society.
Like other federal leaders and Members of both sides of the House, I have travelled recently in the Province of Quebec.

It is a fact that the vast majority of Quebecers are very positive about the Meech Lake Accord. It is not just the journalists and politicians in the Province of Quebec. We hear it in the streets of Quebec and in the hearts of the men and women of this province. They are positive about this Accord because they realize that Quebec is not a province like the others, and they like the idea that, at last, the rest of Canada has agreed to include this concept in the Canadian Constitution.

Today, however, I want primarily to direct my comments to Canadians outside the Province of Quebec. I want to explain to them why I believe this Accord is not only good and desirable, but why it is so very important at this precise moment in the history of our country. We have heard a great deal about the terms of this constitutional Accord, and I speak frankly when I say we have heard a lot of nonsense from many parts of our land and from people who, in my judgment, ought to know better or ought to have made an effort to actually read the document before they spoke out. As a consequence, there are
many legitimately perceived misconceptions about this deal, but they are, nonetheless, misconceptions.
There are issues, particularly outside of the Province of Quebec, which have to be addressed and addressed frankly so that the people of Canada will understand that this deal was negotiated in good faith by Premiers who put it on their agenda, and it is accepted in every corner of the Province of Quebec. The people of Canada have to understand that it is good not only for Quebec, but it is good for Newfoundland, Ontario, the Prairies, it is good for all of Canada. We have to understand that.
Many people have said that this Accord drastically changes Canada, that too much has been given away by the federal Government and that the Accord is badly flawed. I want to respond to these arguments because I believe they are fundamentally wrong, and this Accord is fundamentally good. There are those who say that the Accord with its distinct society provision supersedes the Charter. How often have we heard that? How often have otherwise reputable newspapers published, and I speak frankly again, such nonsense? The reality is that courts in Quebec, before this Accord was even written, have referred to the distinct nature of Quebec society in their interpretation of our Charter, and in these judgments, the Charter provisions prevail. They were not abandoned. They prevail in those decisions in Quebec courts, and I say they will prevail in the future. The Charter is not threatened by this Accord.
Professor Peter Hogg of the Osgoode Law School, one of Canada's truly distinguished constitutional scholars, stated quite categorically in his commentary on the Accord:
The new Section 2 does not override the Charter... A law passed to preserve linguistic duality or to promote the distinct identity of Quebec would, like any other law, have to comply with the Charter. If the law was contrary to the Charter ... then the law would be invalid.
My Party supported and fought for the Charter in 1980 and 1981. We would not have supported this Accord had we believed the Charter was endangered or diminished. I say that with great conviction. There are those who say that the federal spending power will be diminished or significantly altered as a result of this Accord. As a Leader of a Party which in the past has pioneered medicare in Canada, which led the fight for pensions, social housing and other programs, and which is now involved, along with others, in asserting the need for a national child care program, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this argument, if it turned out to be true, would have been of great consequence for members of my Party. But again, what do we see? In the Accord, we see for the first time the federal Government's right to create shared cost programs in areas that have hitherto been exclusively reserved to the provinces in the written Constitution, which is now to be enshrined in the letter of the law in the Constitution of Canada. That, if anything, is an expansion of the federal authority, not its reduction.
No longer will it be necessary for the federal Government to obtain legitimacy for such action either from past precedent by
June 14, 1988

courts or from the highly contentious use of its spending authority. It will now be written in the Constitution. The federal Government will still have the right to decide where and how and on what terms it spends. It will have the right to attach strings to such a program. It will be the Parliament of Canada that will decide here in this debating Chamber, with all Parties representing all regions of Canada, what the national objectives of such a spending program ought to be.
In so doing, in order to be effective in a federal state, we would have to obtain the co-operation of the Provinces. I repeat once again, we are spending within provincial jurisdictional authority in this kind of activity, and any Government which is sensitive to the legitimate role of the provinces, which does not see the provinces simply as some unfortunate encumbrance around the neck of the central Government, any central Government knows this. Indeed, that is the way we got national programs in the past. It was absolutely essential to obtain crucial provincial support, and that is the kind of approach the New Democratic Party believes ought to be taken. In other words, it will ultimately be a matter of public pressure and political will in deciding whether new social programs are created, just as it was political pressure and political will in the past that led one of my predecessors, Tommy Douglas, and his colleague, Woodrow Lloyd, into action that first brought hospitalization and medicare to the Province of Saskatchewan and, subsequently, because of political pressure, persuasion and argument, we had national programs established in this field.
My Party would not have supported the Accord had we believed that federal Governments would not be able to continue their right of showing this kind of imaginative leadership in the future, whether on child care or some other important aspect of social policy.
There are those who say we are going to create a chequer-board Canada with a variety of social programs. That is another argument that has been trotted out again and again. The Attorney General of Ontario addressed the Ontario Legislative Committee on this subject. I agree with the Prime Minister and would urge every Canadian who is sensitive to the importance of this debate to the future of our country to read the fascinating submission and argumentation on the subject by the Attorney General of Ontario. It is a first rate argument and a first rate scholarship on the history of our Constitution. He said in his address that those who argue against a chequer-board Canada in this sense are more interested in proposing a radical agenda for change in the future of Canada than they are in terms of accurately describing the past reality or the present circumstances.
The truth is that there are already variations in the design and delivery of programs for Canadians in various parts of the country. That is what a federal Constitution, in part, is all about. It is this very flexibility that allowed Quebec, for example, to create the Quebec Pension Plan, which has been regarded not only as a model in this country but as a model in many other countries. Such variations on a theme, if I can put
Constitution Amendment, 1987
it that way, are a reflection of the difference in public pressure and political will of Governments. Residents of Manitoba, under a succession of New Democratic Party Governments, pay no hospitalization premiums, while Canadians living under different political Parties in the Province of Ontario do.
The point I want to make is that it is not the Constitution that requires one thing to be done in one region and a different in another. What is crucial here is the political decisionmaking of the people in any given province. All they have to do, if they do not like the present circumstances in terms of this kind of program, is to vote for a different Party and make sure that their political will is expressed in the legislature of that province.
Meech Lake will not change this. However, neither will it reduce the ability of a federal Government with the will to act boldly and decisively on behalf of all Canadians.
There are those who say that the federal Government lost too much with this Accord. We have heard this argument very often from the same people who, in 1982, said that that Constitution Act was a veritable grab by the federal Government in the provincial domain.
Yet if we look at the situation with care and get beyond the rhetoric, the Accord does not change the division of powers one iota as they are outlined in Sections 91 and 92 of the Constitution Act. In fact, the distinct society and linguistic duality section of the Accord state quite clearly that it does not affect the division of powers between Ottawa and the provinces.
As John A. Macdonald noted in 1867, under our Constitution the federal Government retains, in his words, "all the great subjects of legislation". The federal Government retains the power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, including the provinces. It retains the residual power which gives it the power to make laws in areas not clearly delegated to the provinces. It retains the extreme power to disallow provincial legislation which, fortunately, has not been used in decades.
It has jurisdiction over, just to name some areas, the military and defence, the money supply, the financial system, the public purse and borrowing, the criminal law and corrections system, trade, commerce and navigation. It retains by virtue of the 1947 Letters Patent the exclusive right to make international treaties. It retains by virtue of the constitutional doctrine of paramountcy the guarantee that in the event that a provincial law is inconsistent with federal law the federal law shall prevail. It retains concurrent powers with the provinces over immigration, agriculture, old age pensions and resource exports. In short, the federal authority to provide leadership in great national issues in the country remains as strong today and will remain as strong after Meech Lake as all Canadians desire it to be.

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
What then did the federal Government give up, if I can put it that way? None of these many powers, for sure, which I have just listed. However, provinces will now have the right to nominate appointees to the Supreme Court bench and to the Senate. With respect to the Senate, I dare say Canadians are no more enthusiastic about patronage appointees coming from the provinces than they have been about those coming exclusively from the federal Government.
Hear, hear!

On a more important matter, what is wrong in the federal strategy with the provinces having a right to participate in the selection of Supreme Court judges? Surely that change as well as many others was long overdue in our federal Constitution. It is one that we strongly support.
The arrangement arrived at in the Accord is a completely reasonable one. It is an example of the kind of co-operative federalism that my Party has always supported. It is one that we think is desirable in the future.
While giving the provinces a say in a very limited range of federal institutions, it retains for the federal Government the great subjects of legislation that John A. Macdonald wanted and that subsequent federal Governments have used to build railroads, the Trans-Canada Highway, the St. Lawrence Seaway, and to create a vast public transportation system. It retains the power the federal Government used to help create a system of social services that is among the very best in the world.

Finally, Madam Speaker, there are those who say the Accord makes matters worse for minority language communities, this as a result of the unfortunate plan of action adopted by the Premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Devine, in response to the Supreme Court's decision on the rights of Francophone minorities.
In fact, Madam Speaker, he has opted for diminishing the rights of Francophone minorities in his province, rights which had been conferred on them by the former Northwest Territories Act. Madam Speaker, no one in Canada could in good faith support this kind of action. However, I wish to point out that the Act was adopted before the Meech Lake Accord became law. The Government of Saskatchewan can for the time being proceed, on the basis of this Act, because it contains no constitutional guarantees for language minorities. But there are such guarantees in the Meech Lake Accord.
Under the Meech Lake Accord, the Government of Saskatchewan and the other provincial governments will be required to preserve linguistic minorities. Given the pressures of the media, culture and assimilation that threaten them, preservation of these minorities requires more than the passive support of the provinces.
One might expect the Supreme Court to interpret this commitment to mean that action is required of all provinces,
although the Constitution in its present form does not require them to take any action.

The Accord does not undermine the division of powers. It does not supersede the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It does not diminish federal spending power. It does not create a chequer-board Canada. It does not give control over the Supreme Court to the provinces. It does not diminish the rights of linguistic minorities.
What it does is complete the job with patriation that was started in 1982 by allowing Quebec to come fully and proudly into the constitutional fold. It allows and, indeed, encourages Quebec to become a full member of the Canadian family.
Hear, hear!

It does that, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and I have all argued today, in a manner that is completely consistent with the best traditions of our country.
It allows us to recognize Quebec's contribution to Canada's history. It recognizes what is already implicit in our law, whether we consider the Royal Proclamation of 1763, the Quebec Act of 1774, the 1867 Constitution Act, Quebec's unique civil traditions, or successive judgments by the Supreme Court of Canada, which all provide historical evidence that Quebec is not a province like the others and is now, and has always been, a distinct society within the Canadian family.

The Accord recognizes a specific historical fact: That Quebec is a distinct society within Canada, with its own language, its own culture, its own history and its own customs, of which it is proud. The Accord recognizes that francophones are the majority in Quebec, but it must be remembered that they are a minority in the other regions of Canada and in North America.
The Accord also recognizes that, while they are proud of being Quebecers, they are also proud of belonging to Canada.
A growing majority of Quebecers believes that the best possible future for Quebec is within Canada. They see this Accord as an integral part of the history of change, social progress and impressive gains of Quebec society expressed in this tradition; Quebec society has developed rapidly since the cultural revolution of the 1960s.
Further, there are many Quebecers, and I wish to underline this today particularly for Canadians living outside the Province of Quebec, for instance, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard), who feels so strongly that this Accord could represent a last chance of rapprochement between Canada and
June 14, 1988

Quebec that he and others have indicated they would leave public life should it fail to be ratified. Should that happen, Madam Speaker, should we allow this opportunity to slip through our fingers, should we fail to grasp the historic significance of this moment, I believe that future generations of Canadians will live to regret it.
As I see Quebec in my travels, I see Canadians who are nationalists in the tradition of my Party as social democrats, like Robert Cliche; I see nationalists in the Province of Quebec like Robert Bourassa in the tradition of his Party in the Province of Quebec; and I see nationalists in the Conservative nationalist tradition like the Minister of Transport himself. They are uniquely Quebec, yes, and they are strong nationalists-
[ Translation]
... the pride of the Province of Quebec is its culture and language.

-but there are also links with the common philosophical ideology of the rest of Canada.
Therefore, we have an obligation in this country to be aware of the consequences of what we might lose if we do not act. We see in the Province of Quebec men and women of good faith, pride in their province deeply embedded, and particularly I speak today of francophone Quebecers, many of whom were on the "oui" side of the referendum, if we are frank as well, who have said, whether they are Conservatives, Social Democrats, or Liberals, that they want to give Canada a chance because in their hearts they are Canadians and good Quebecers. I say to the rest of Canada that we must listen with care. We must respond with a clear mind and an open heart. We must respond by saying "oui" to the Province of Quebec.
Hear, hear!

In short, we must accept this challenge. We must accept this Accord.
Having said that, Madam Speaker, I wish to turn to the amendments my Party has supported and will continue to support. As we stated the last time that the Accord was before the House, and as I have made clear in a letter that I sent out in September, 1987, to the First Ministers and to the Prime Minister we believe that the amendments that we have proposed are fully within the spirit of the Accord, and that they could be adopted without unravelling or upsetting the Accord in any way.
We want fairness for native Canadians, the first peoples in this part of the planet. We want it in the form of guarantees of future conferences on aboriginal self-government. Surely, it ought to have been in the Accord.
We also want fairness for northern Canadians who have lost the right of appointment to federal institutions that Canadians in other parts of our country enjoy. We also want their right to possible provincial status not to be encumbered by the unanimity rule that we find in the Accord.
After having fought long and hard for constitutional recognition of sexual equality in Section 28 of the Charter a few years ago, a number of Canadian women are now concerned that this right might be undermined. By simply adding section 28 to section 16 of the Accord, out of an abundance of caution as we have said, we could provide a reassurance of fairness for Canadian women.
We have every intention of voting for these amendments, and we will continue to press for them after. But if they should fail, we will be strongly supporting the Meech Lake Accord.

With this Accord, Madam Speaker, the future of our country is at stake. On the one hand, we can take this accord and a united country and try to go forward together, to dialogue and discuss together in order to develop a common approach to our country's problems. We can take this Accord and work together to achieve self-determination for native people, a constitutional agreement on the fundamental role of ethnic and cultural minorities, an improved constitutional decision-making process to include guarantees of public participation. And we can talk about removing Section 33. On the other hand, Madam Speaker, we can continue to have the deadlock of years of bad will, a constitutional impasse that existed without the full willing participation of all Canadians, men and women. That is the choice facing us. For my part, I am proud to stand up and be counted among those who say yes to a united Canada. I am proud to say yes to Quebec. I am proud to say yes to a real future as a country.
Madam Speaker, the conquest is past. In our generation, it is time to finally walk together as equals.

subsubtopic: ISOLATED AREAS TAX DEDUCTION PROGRAM-APPLICATION IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the Conservative Government introduced a northern and isolated areas tax deduction program for areas below the 55th Parallel. In doing so, many communities became eligible but still many others were not despite the fact they are quite isolated.
The criteria for an area to be designated isolated are out of touch with reality. For example, the Town of Canso is eligible for the deduction despite the fact that a hospital, museum, library, drugstore, school, et cetera, are to be found there. Meanwhile, areas of the province such as Loch Lomond, where a resident has to travel 30 to 50 kilometres even to find one of those services, are not designated as isolated.
The federal Conservative Government must review the manner in which it designates isolated areas so that equity and fairness are delivered to all rural Canadians.

subtopic: DOCTOR'S LETTER ON TELEVISING ABORTION PROCEDURE
DOCTOR'S LETTER ON TELEVISING ABORTION PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a letter sent to Pierre Juneau, President of the CBC, by Dr. Dennis Culver of Elmwood, Ontario. I totally concur with the letter which says:
Dear Mr. Juneau:
On Saturday, May 28th, 1988, I watched The National news together with my children. I noted scenes from a commentary on an abortion symposium being held in Toronto this week. I am of the opinion that the scene of an abortion procedure being actually performed under local anaesthesia was carrying things just a bit too far.
This sleazy kind of reporting has no place in the living rooms of our household. I and a number of other physicians feel that life at all its stages is to be protected, particularly the unborn child, who represents Canadians of today who are most vulnerable.
This promotional film clip from Henry Morgentaler's clinic I find quite distasteful, and I would like some assurances that your reporters will show some responsibility in the future.
It would be most appreciated if the CBC would show some sensitivity to the position that many Canadians are quite appalled by the deliberate destruction of 60,000 unborn Canadians within the presumed safety of their mothers' wombs each year. This is a disgrace.

subtopic: ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES- VANCOUVER CITY COUNCIL RESOLUTION
ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES- VANCOUVER CITY COUNCIL RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the big issues before this Parliament is whether the Government should spend $8 billion on nuclear submarines. The Government and Parliament want to hear from Canadians on how they feel about this issue.
I have here a resolution passed by the Vancouver City Council on May 31, 1988:
THAT the Vancouver Members of Parliament, as well as the Minister of National Defence, be advised that council is opposed to the Federal Government spending $8 billion on nuclear submarines when there are so many other pressing needs in our communities, and that there are much greater direct benefits to be realized, including employment creation, from a similar expenditure on a municipal infrastructure program;
The Clerk of the City wrote to me saying that the proposal was rejected because the federal Government had rejected a proposed S14 billion joint federal-provincial-municipal fund for improving municipal infrastructure. It was generally agreed there would be a far greater gains realized by this country from the expenditure of this money on municipal infrastructure rather than on the nuclear submarine program.
This is not a left-of-centre City Council. This is a right-of-centre City Council. They are against spending $8 billion on nuclear submarines, and I think the country is against it as well.
