subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF FIRST MASS DEPORTATIONS FROM ESTONIA, LATVIA, AND LITHUANIA
ANNIVERSARY OF FIRST MASS DEPORTATIONS FROM ESTONIA, LATVIA, AND LITHUANIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 14, 1941, the Soviet Union began its first mass deportation of the Baltic people from the Republics of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
In one night, 60,000 men, women and children were torn from their families and homes and deported to Siberia, loaded like cattle into boxcars. Many died during the long journey. Those who survived were sent to forced labour camps where conditions were primitive, harsh and inhumane. Larger deportations were to follow.
These deportations were but one step in the long process of "Russification" of Soviet occupied countries. Earlier, in 1932 and 1933, millions of Ukrainians were starved to death by a Soviet imposed famine in their own homeland.
On the anniversary of these deliberate acts of genocide the Latvian, Estonian, Lithuanian and Ukrainian communities in Canada and all over the world join together to commemorate the tragedies their people endured and as a reminder of the need for vigilance in the defence of freedom, democracy, and fundamental human rights.

subtopic: CRITICISM OF PROPOSED PURCHASE OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
CRITICISM OF PROPOSED PURCHASE OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night on The Journal, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) stated that the goal of the Conservative Government's defence policy was to ensure increased Canadian responsibility for the defence of Canada. In this respect, Conservatives and New Democrats would appear to be in agreement. Canada does need to assume greater control over its own defence. Unfortunately, the Government's proposal to buy nuclear powered submarines will have the opposite effect.
Nuclear technology or, for that matter, any technology, is not the way to responsible or independent action for global survival. Only policy can do that and, unfortunately, instead of adopting a non-provocative defence posture designed to ensure Canadian security without threatening the security of our superpower neighbours, the Government's proposal will tie Canada even closer to the war-fighting strategies of the United States and to the insecurity for the human race that such thinking involves.
The Minister has rejected policies designed to reduce superpower rivalry. Instead his proposal to purchase nuclear powered submarines will increase our ultimate military and policy reliance on the destabilizing and globally dangerous policies of the United States. That, Mr. Speaker, is not Canadianization as the Minister so fatuously called his policy. It is a Conservative high-tech version of the Liberals' deference to the United States' perception of the world that has strait-jacketed Canadian defence policy since the 1950s.

subtopic: LOCATION IN NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION ADVOCATED
LOCATION IN NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the Ottawa-Carleton Board of Trade tabled its 1988 annual policy statement entitled "Clearing the Way for Progress". One of its principal recommendations is that the space agency be located in the National Capital Region.
I fully endorse this recommendation. I have spoken to this effect many times in this House, in Ottawa-Carleton, and

June 14, 1988
across the nation. When you fully understand the role of the space agency, the importance of the space program in the national agenda, and the merits of where the agency can best fulfil its responsibilities, Mr. Speaker, you can only conclude that it has to be located in the National Capital area.
I have and will continue to direct my energies to persuade the front benches of the Government and, indeed, all Members of this House, that this important national agency be located where it can be most effective, in the National Capital area.

subtopic: CANADIAN ASSOCIATION OF RE-REFINERS-PLEA FOR ASSISTANCE
CANADIAN ASSOCIATION OF RE-REFINERS-PLEA FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has a habit of preaching one way and acting in another. In adopting this practice the most recent Minister to join the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse).
In a letter, rich with environmental prose and addressed to Pollution Probe members, dated May 30, 1988, he writes:
We want to work closely with industry and the provinces to enhance
environmental quality.
Yet the same Minister is unwilling to support the Canadian Association of Re-refiners, the people who recycle oil thus practising energy efficiency and sustainable development. In actual fact, re-refiners in Canada are in trouble. Their urgent pleas for assistance from the Ministers of Environment and Energy have fallen on deaf ears.
If the Minister of Energy (Mr. Masse) believes the words he writes, he should act and act quickly in support of this industry before it is too late. Words and letters of self-praise are not enough.

subtopic: CALL FOR PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE ON OPTIONS
CALL FOR PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE ON OPTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the January 28 Supreme Court of Canada decision in the Morgentaler case, we now have no abortion law. The consequences of this can be readily seen.
Abortions at Dr. Morgentaler's Toronto clinic are up 33 per cent. Abortions at Dr. Robert Scott's Toronto clinic are up 200 per cent. The Ontario Liberal Government is proposing to use
public moneys to pay for abortions at women's health clinics. Therefore, we should anticipate that the number of abortions will increase dramatically.
Recognizing that abortion is a fundamental issue and that each Member of Parliament has both the privilege and the responsibility of taking a position on such issues, the Government sought the unanimous consent of the House to have a free vote on several different options to give the Government direction in preparing new legislation. Regrettably, the Opposition played petty politics with the lives of the unborn and said "no".
I would urge all my colleagues in the House to treat this issue with the urgency it demands and put the resolutions to debate and a vote as soon as possible.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-TREATMENT OF THE SHARPEVILLE SIX
SOUTH AFRICA-TREATMENT OF THE SHARPEVILLE SIX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of South Africa has now been defined as terrorist. How else to describe a Government that would bring to trial and condemn to hang the six black citizens of Sharpeville who are thus held accountable for the actions of a mob?
In most countries people are not held accountable for actions they have not been proven to have caused, but not if you are a black in South Africa.
In most civilized countries the courts do not allow the testimony of confessed liars to bring the innocent to the death chamber, but it is possible if you are black and innocent in South Africa.
Most countries are concerned about being considered a part of the world of nations characterized by humanity, respect for human rights, equality and civilized behaviour. Most such countries would respond to the pleas for clemency of the Sharpeville Six from the leaders of civilized nations of the world, but not South Africa.
In most countries, and this is the greatest error of the six, it is not a capital offence to demand freedom and equality.
As South Africa sinks into the inevitable and violent consequences of the terrorist actions of the regime that rules it, many of the world leaders who plead for the lives of the Sharpeville Six will be burdened by the guilt that they themselves must bear for ignoring the pleas of the 23 million who have asked for action against this terrorist regime commensurate with their actions against other regimes they have defined as terrorist.



June 14, 1988

subtopic: CLOSURE OF FIRESTONE PLANT IN HAMILTON
CLOSURE OF FIRESTONE PLANT IN HAMILTON
speechtext:

funded machinery which is now being used in the United States, operated by Canadian workers. What an insult to Canada, what an insult to the Canadian workers.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-GOVERNMENT URGED TO TAKE STAND AT TORONTO SUMMIT
SOUTH AFRICA-GOVERNMENT URGED TO TAKE STAND AT TORONTO SUMMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my dissatisfaction with the Government's halfhearted approach to the question of apartheid in South Africa.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in 1985 that "if there are no fundamental changes in South Africa we are

June 14, 1988
Oral Questions
prepared to invoke total sanctions against that country and its repressive regime".
We can see that the Government is reneging on that commitment. Last week the South African Government renewed the state of emergency. We know that it continues to occupy Namibia illegally. subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES- REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF DECISION

Mr. Speaker, more and more strategic military experts believe that the Prime Minister's plan to purchase nuclear powered submarines is absolutely wrong, and the Cabinet is obviously split on the issue. Will the Prime Minister address the House in response to this question and advise us whether he is now willing, upon reflection, to cancel his Government's decision to purchase nuclear powered submarines?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES- REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course the answer is no. My right hon. friend will be aware of the White Paper brought in by the Government of Canada pursuant to, I think he will acknowledge, many years of neglect of the Armed Forces of Canada by predecessor governments.
Political decisions have been made or are in the process of being made with a number of important objectives in mind: the sovereignty of Canada, the defence of Canada, and the respect of our alliances.
It is a very important proposition that this be done while supplying the men and women who serve Canada in the military with first-class equipment at all times. We have a first-class military which was not always treated in the manner

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the statistics in percentage of Gross National Product which the previous Trudeau administration dedicated to defence are at least as high as those dedicated by this Government. I think that should be pointed out.

We are going to make sure Canada's men and women serving in the Armed Forces go first class and that this country is given first-class equipment at all times.
Hear, hear!
If the Prime Minister and his other Ministers had the good sense and judgment of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, we would be far less concerned about the way his Government is being run.

Hear, hear!

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn, and the amendments of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra, (p. 15617), Mr. Broadbent, (p. 15618), Mr. Caccia (p. 15618), Mr. Johnston (p. 15618) and Mr. Roman, (p. 15620).

Mr. Speaker, this morning, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke in favour of the Meech Lake Accord. Following him, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) rose to speak in favour of the Meech Lake Accord. Following him, the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) rose to speak in favour of the Meech Lake Accord.
I hear people in my constituency of Etobicoke-Lakeshore and elsewhere around the country criticizing the Meech Lake Accord as a document that somehow diminishes the role of the Government of Canada. It struck me, as I listened to the Leaders this morning, that the very best thing I could do would be to reproduce those three speeches by those three Party Leaders and send copies of them to those people.
When the national Leaders of our three main Parties are speaking in favour of the Meech Lake Accord, that most surely represents a deliberate and clear conclusion that this is not an instrument for weakening the Government of Canada or the central purposes of our country but rather for maintaining and strengthening them. Each of the three Party Leaders represents the collective wisdom, advice and counsel that each would have received from those experts in matters of constitutional law, Canadian history and indeed partisan considerations, and in all cases they came forward to speak in favour of the Meech Lake Accord. That is not the position that would be taken, I submit, by national Leaders of any Party if in fact the Meech Lake Accord were, as its critics allege, somehow weakening and undermining the Government of Canada and its positive role in Canadian federalism.
Let us not make perfection the enemy of the good. That statement was made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister this morning, and I was so happy to hear him succinctly express something that in other forums I too have been trying to express. For example, in connection with disabled Canadians, I have recently been saying that part of the difficulty in Canada is this image of perfection that is held out. As soon as we begin to recognize that the image of imperfection is more accurately
reflective of human condition and human society, the closer we will be to realism and in turn to a more gentle and caring society. If it applies there, it is no less true in application to matters of constitutional law.
Perfection in a Constitution perhaps could be achieved by each of us individually, sitting in the splendid isolation of our libraries or some other quiet place, putting pen to paper and writing down what according to our own personal lights might be the perfect Constitution for Canada. The beauty of a democracy, however, is that there is never any one person who has all the answers, and that what we achieve is truly a blending through political debate and through political compromise of various points of view.
Certainly, I agree with all of those who spoke, the Prime Minister and the two opposition Leaders, who said that we do not have in the Meech Lake Accord perfection. There are points in the Accord with which I do not agree. My own view with respect to the Senate, for example, is that the only way to reform the Senate is to abolish it.
I am a native of the Province of Ontario where there was an elected Upper House under our Constitution from 1841 to 1867, as for instance so did the Province of Prince Edward Island at one stage in its history have an elected Upper House. We went through that experience and found it was unnecessary. We found that indeed, in a democratic country like ours, with all the different levels of Government, we have more than enough elected representatives to speak for and to represent the Canadian people.
I have deeply held views on the importance of ending the existence of the Canadian Senate as an institution that has long since outlived its historical role in this country. Yet, there is in the Meech Lake Accord provision for getting on in the next phase with discussions to see how the Senate can be reformed. Each of us, I submit, must look at the Meech Lake Accord, and although there are parts in it that may rankle and may not accord with our own views, we have to see that there is something greater here.
I have listened to a lot of debate and discussion. I see in the House the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston). He and I were debating this issue recently, not in the Chamber but in fact in a television studio. There were many people who came forward from the audience and expressed their concerns and points of view. What struck me as I heard some of these criticisms was that there seems to be a propensity in Canada for loading on to whatever vehicle is passing all the freight that it can carry. I do not know if this comes from something in our pioneer background. People were scattered across a fairly empty land. Someone who was stranded in the North was happy to see the bush pilot arrive, and those on a homestead were happy to see the wagon finally come by. They wanted to get everyone on the aircraft or on the wagon at once. Our approach intrinsically seems to be that whatever is going by, we want to load all of the traffic onto it.
June 14, 1988

I see the same thing happening with the free trade debate. We are dealing with a treaty that governs the trading arrangement between two countries, and on the one hand some Canadians are saying that that document is the panacea that will solve all of our problems. At the other extreme, people are saying that with this approach, in 25 years the country will be gone. They are putting onto the free trade debate all kinds of issues relating to cultural sovereignty and the like. No matter how many times they read the document and see that those issues are not touched, no matter how many times Ministers of the Crown rise in the Chamber to give assurances of that, there are still people who want to load all of this extra traffic onto the vehicle of the free trade debate. The same is happening with Meech Lake.
I am hearing the argument, for example, that the position of native Canadians, the position of women, the position of disabled people and the position of so many other groups in society will be adversely affected by the Meech Lake Accord. I would like to speak to that for a moment or two. There is one historic moment here that we must recognize. This is not the one and only time, the now or never chance, that we will have to deal with all of these issues of aboriginal rights, the position of women and the position of Canadians with disabilities, but it is the one and only time, the now or never chance, to say yes to Quebec.
In 1980, Quebec said yes to Canada and Quebec is still waiting. That was the verdict of Quebec in 1980 when the people of that province held a referendum to make a choice between thinly disguised separatism and a renewed federalism. As someone who believes profoundly in the importance of referenda and plebiscites in our system, I watched closely what happened in the Province of Quebec. I saw the people of that province at organizational levels, levels of families and parishes, and everywhere possible meeting and debating. It was a cathartic experience for Quebecers to be put to that choice. They made the choice and in the majority they said yes to Canada, yes to renewed federalism.
There was another chance after Quebec was sidelined in the 1982 approach to amending the Constitution and entrenching the Charter. The result of that in 1982 was Quebec's isolation which, as J. W. Pickersgill has said, was to leave a grievance and a wound open in Canadian political society.
The 1987 constitutional accord has again held out to Quebec the promise of a renewed federalism. This is the second chance and the second time that Quebec has said yes. This time it was not the people in a referendum, it was the men and women who are the democratically elected representatives of the people of Quebec voting in the Quebec Legislative Assembly who voted in favour of the Meech Lake Accord.
As in baseball, whether you are playing for the Toronto Blue Jays or the Montreal Expos, the rule is three strikes and you're out. So it is in constitutional law and what is happening in this
Constitution Amendment, 1987
country in terms of the position of Quebec in relation to the rest of the country. Quebec has said yes twice and it must not have to say that again. Quebec has now made its position clear.
All the years when I was growing up in Ontario, living in the West, and living in Quebec, I heard other Canadians ask, "What does Quebec want?". The answer came in five very specific questions, very specific answers and proposals by Premier Robert Bourassa. It was to those five specific proposals that a response has been made and embodied in the Meech Lake Accord.
We have voted in this House on this question before and we voted affirmatively. Now, months later, we are being asked to do it again because the other place has succumbed to the smaller view of Canada, the Lilliputians who tied down with a thousand small threads the great giant who otherwise could stand and walk proudly and freely.
Let us transcend the legitimate but smaller points of debate. In the symbolism of politics I believe that some statements and some acts can transcend and transform. There is now an opportunity to transcend, to go beyond the legal minimum of what national unity requires and into a patriotic sharing of the full promise of Canadianism.
I will vote again in favour of the Meech Lake Accord because I believe that we in the Parliament of Canada must say yes to Quebec and to renewed federalism which meets Quebec's needs to preserve and promote its distinct society within Canada yet safeguards the federal Government's role as the voice of all Canadians and respects the equality of all provinces. Not to do so would cast doubts about our commitment here in the 33rd Parliament to a renewed federalism which, I repeat, acknowledges the reality of Quebec as a distinct society within Canada.
I believe we are long past the point where the Accord can be reopened or renegotiated. I believe there has been no demonstrated need to reopen it or to renegotiate it. Take for example the submissions made by some of the women's groups in Canada which say that somehow the Meech Lake Accord is going to undermine the position of women in Canada.
I have here the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Section 15 says that every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination including discrimination on the basis of sex. Has Section 15 of the Charter been repealed? No, it is still a vigorous and entrenched part of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms which, by virtue of the Meech Lake Accord, is now going to apply to all Canadians including Canadian women who live in Quebec.
This not an undermining of the position of Canadian women but an enhancement of it by the very fact that years after the Charter was included in our Constitution the Government of the Province of Quebec has signed its agreement, indicating that in laws enacted in that province, it will be subject to Section 15 and all other provisions of the Charter.

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
There are other provisions in the Charter. There is Section 28. Again, I mention this in the context of some of the lamentations which are being made by women's groups. Section 28 says:
Notwithstanding anything in this Charter, the rights and freedoms referred
to in it are guaranteed equally to male and female persons.
Has Section 28 of the Charter been ripped up? No, it has not. It is still in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It has not been repealed, it is there. It is guaranteeing the protection, the equal rights, and the equal freedoms of women with men in Canadian society.
Therefore, why in this debate in our country are groups trying to undermine the effort to, at long last, bring Quebec fully into a renewed federalism by trotting out arguments that the Meech Lake Accord is somehow detrimental to the position of Canadian women? It is a snare and a delusion to argue that way. I must say that those who so argue are doing a tremendous disservice to the great possibilities and prospects which are currently and have historically been before us for a renewed federalism along the lines set out in the Meech Lake Accord.
When the joint Senate and House committee heard testimony on this point there were many who spoke to this very issue. For example, on the issue of sexual equality-and I am not leaving this point because I believe it is fundamentally important and the one that raised perhaps the most concern before the committee-William Lederman, the dean of Canadian constitutional scholars, to name but one, told the legislators on that committee that the Charter "speaks loudly and clearly and it rides right through".
The Meech Lake Accord does not change the Charter. The Charter is there with Section 15 and Section 28. That is why even, for example, the Federation des femmes du Quebec and Quebec's Conseil du statut de la femme told the committee that women's rights are not threatened by the distinct society clause.
The distinct society clause is an interpretive provision in the Constitution, as is the section that talks about our Charter being interpreted according to the multicultural traditions of Canada, and as are the other interpretive provisions to be found therein. There is clear need to think back to that referendum and to what the people of Quebec said with eloquence which speaks so loudly when, in a deliberate act of casting a ballot, men and women indicated a conscious choice which they had made.
There was moving testimony given before the joint committee by Yolande Chaput-Rolland, an ardent partisan of federalism, a renewed federalism, in all she said and fought for during that referendum campaign in 1980. This is what she told the committee:

For me it is really the first time that I have felt I won that referendum.

"For me it was really the first time that I had felt, yes, I won that referendum". Let us answer Madam Chaput-Rolland and every other Canadian who is prepared to go beyond the points of difference, the legitimate but smaller issues, and see an historic opportunity to move Canada to a new plateau in its evolution.
This is the unfinished business that was begun by a former Prime Minister in his effort to entrench the Charter of Rights, to have an amending formula that would allow Canadians to see our own Constitution amended here in our own country. That process was begun but it has yet to be completed. We are now in the process of completing it.
I stand as the representative for the men and women of Etobicoke-Lakeshore, an Ontario constituency, and say with deepest conviction as a Canadian that I will stand in this House and vote in favour of the Meech Lake Accord.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments? Debate.

Madam Speaker, one year after the Meech Lake Accord was born, a date historians will not remember as a great day for Canada, a strong case can be made for rejecting it. Canadians would be badly served by this Constitutional Accord. It was arrived at without public consultation, driven by the notion that a yes vote for Canada in the 1980 Quebec plebiscite requires reciprocation. It makes only one province responsible for the promotion of linguistic rights. It is based on an outdated vision of a Canada mortgaged by the distinct society concept which could lead to the two-nation idea, a view of Canada pursued by the Progressive Conservative Party in the 1960s. It would jeopardize the equal opportunities provided to all Canadians in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This is where I disagree fully with the Hon. Member who just spoke.
The process also must be severely criticized. The way the Accord was arrived at can only be described by one word: awful. The process pre-empted any reasonable thoughtful input by any interested citizens, who were left out in the cold by 11 omniscient politicians playing kings. Interested Canadians were politely listened to by the joint parliamentary committee but their concerns were ignored. Indeed, the process did not produce a single amendment. What a disgraceful performance, so much in contrast with our fine democratic traditions and practices.
As many have noted, the Accord reveals a severe imbalance. While each of the proposed changes transfers powers to the provinces, there is no transfer of power to the federal state. If the Accord is approved, the national Government will emerge
June 14, 1988

weaker. At a time when social programs, education, environment, international issues require new and creative federal roles, Ottawa strips itself of powers needed to tackle the future. What a vision of Canada this Progressive Conservative Government reveals.
Fortunately, Canadians have realized the dangers of the Accord. Public support has rapidly been declining. Provincial premiers who signed the Accord are gradually being knocked off by their electors. Witness New Brunswick and Manitoba. Some of those in power have admitted there are flaws. Time will take care of these short-sighted self appointed constitutional wizards, unperturbed by the absence of public input, inebriated by power, blissfully applying the "trust me" school of decision-making. If you have ever searched for a classical example of pornography of power, there is one here.
The disturbing fact about this Accord is that while technically it has not yet and may never come into force, its spirit is already being applied in the shaping of laws presently going through Parliament. The Environmental Protection Bill presently in the Senate is a case in point. There is the pathetic scene of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) first trumpeting this Bill as the strongest ever federal legislation in Canada that will remove and prevent all polluting evils from the face of the nation. He emphasizes that the federal Government will proceed on its own in enforcing its legislation. However, one day he appears before the legislative committee sheepishly requesting amendments to his own Bill. Why? Because Ottawa must consult first with the provinces before making federal environmental regulations.
The federal Government yields again when it decides not to apply federal environmental protection standards if a province comes up with provisions considered to be equivalent, whatever that word means. What has happened? There is no political will. The Government has given up on its federal mandate. It will not establish national standards of environmental protection for all Canadians.
The Meech Lake virus has infected the thought process of the Government and weakened Canadian federalism. The Coalition on the Constitution, which is comprised of the Canadian Environmental Law Association, the Citizens Network on Waste Management, Energy Probe, Pollution Probe, in a letter to the joint committee dated December 10, 1987, made two significant points regarding the Accord and the environment. First, commenting on the environment Bill, they said that this is a step backward from existing federal law. Second, commenting on Section 9 of the Meech Lake Accord which allows provinces to opt out from national programs, they said that this provision could apply to national environmental programs, undermining the ability of the federal Government to provide national standards of environmental protection.
The same can be said, alas, for national social programs because they too will be affected.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Another upsetting aspect of the Accord is how Canada and Canadian society are described, something that you could call the heart and soul of the Accord. A constitution should make the citizen say with a certain degree of pride: "Yes, I recognize myself in that definition of Canada". That is what a good constitution is all about. Instead, we see a definition which excludes millions of Canadians. If you are an aboriginal, you have been left out. If you do not speak English or French, and many good solid decent citizens do not speak English or French, you have been left out.
In other words, the Accord fails to describe all the people of this country: the new Canada that has emerged in recent decades and first Canadians.
The description of the Canadian society in the Accord is not the Canada of today, it is the myopic view of tired politicians who failed to recognize the society they were supposed to understand and represent. What did the 11 wizards do in the middle of the night while the nation was sleeping? They provided, if indeed the courts will accept at all the distinct society notion, a springboard for special status to one province, thus laying the foundation of a duality which could lead to the creation of a two nation Canada. That is what they did. What a prospect. This is certainly not the Canada Canadians want for themselves, for their children or for their grandchildren. The evidence produced in the Senate, and the contributions made by Senators, is sufficient to convince any reasonable person that the Accord should not be supported. The evidence contained in Issue No. 6 of the proceedings of the Senate submissions group, most ably chaired by Senator Molgat, says it all. I would like to quote from the report which deals with the comments of 43 groups and individuals on the Accord.
Many Canadians fear that the rights accorded to them by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms will be diminished by the linguistic duality and distinct identity clause. Women's groups, French speaking Canadians living outside Quebec, English speaking Canadians living in that province, to name but a few groups, want the Accord amended to ensure that their charter rights will not be diminished by the "linguistic duality-distinct society" clause.
And I quote again:
Aboriginal organizations stated that they are left out of the description of Canada ... Aboriginal people asked to be recognized as distinct societies.
Some witnesses say the Accord does very little to promote multiculturalism. They request that it also be recognized as a fundamental characteristic of Canada, and so on.
One has to conclude so far that the only parliamentary institution which has really defended the views of people, the rights of Canadians, and made a really powerful contribution to this debate, is the Senate. The Senate held hearings that were meaningful. It moved amendments and certainly did not vote for the Accord. The House of Commons hardly had a debate a year ago on this matter. One would think, then, in light of the evidence brought out in the Senate, in the wake of the language dispute in Saskatchewan, in light of the defeat of Premier Hatfield and Premier Pawley, in light of the tensions

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
caused every day by Bill C-101 and the pending Supreme Court decision, in light of the substantial decline in public support for the Accord, that the present Government would stop and think instead of having the Prime Minister engage in threats against those who do not agree with the Accord.
Would it not, I ask, be in the public interest to find out what "distinct society" really means in constitutional terms, what the consequences would be to national unity if such a term were to have legal meaning? After all, a reference to the Supreme Court is not novel. In 1981, former Prime Minister Trudeau referred the constitution proposal of that time to the Supreme Court. "Oh, but listen", some say at this point, "you don't need to worry too much now. If amendments are needed, there will be a chance to make amendments on a second round. Approve the Accord now. We can improve it later". I submit, this is utter nonsense. These people who are not accepting changes now will not accept changes in a second round. If they are serious about changes, why not make the changes now? Why go ahead with constitutional changes when almost everyone agrees it is bad for Canada?
The amendment the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) and I are proposing tries to define Canada and Canadians. It is a description of the Canadian people in contemporary terms, the very people for whom this Constitution is written. We wrote this motion with three thoughts in mind, first, to offer a mirror of contemporary Canadian society, second, to strengthen the notion of one Canada with two official languages and, third, to highlight an historical fact and evolution over time. In our amendment, aboriginal Canadians are included. Canadians who do not speak either English or French are included, and the distribution of English and French speaking Canadians across the nation is described. This amendment describes today's Canadian scene, the new Canada to which present and future generations belong. If, in reading this amendment, each Canadian recognizes himself or herself, then we will have succeeded in our effort. I invite the House to examine it and support it. Our amendment reads:
That the motion be amended in paragraph 1 of the Schedule
(a)	by deleting Section 2(1) and substituting the following therefor:
"2(1) The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the recognition that Canada consists of aboriginal and multicultural societies, with English and French as the official languages of Canada, French-speaking Canadians being centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada and English-speaking Canadians concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec",
(b)	by deleting Section 2(3).
In so doing, we bring together a concept, a mirror of Canada, which we think is contemporary, one that does not leave out one Canadian citizen, because one would be too many. We recognize in this motion the linguistic duality of this country and the spread of the population from coast to coast according to the language they speak. When we hear someone in this House say: "Let us not make perfection an enemy of the good", we believe that kind of approach is a signal for settling
for less than mediocrity. We do not want to have a Constitution that is less than mediocrity. We have had the time and we have the skills and ability to produce a Constitution that corresponds with the composition of the society of today, not only that, but a Constitution that will not lay the foundation for division in future times. The Conservative Government vision of Canada is the wrong vision. It must be rejected.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I am reminded that he was the former Minister of the Environment, a portfolio in which precious little was accomplished. Yet day after day we hear him comment and criticize the great work our Government has done on the environment. We hear again today some relatively hollow remarks from the Hon. Member with respect to the Meech Lake Accord.
I am not sure if the Member was in the House this morning when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke, but I disagree strongly with the Hon. Member for Davenport when he says the Accord should be a perfect document. We are not saying it is mediocre. We are saying it is a good document. One of the telling points the Prime Minister made, I thought, was that Quebec should participate in the final completion or other phases of the document to deal with the aboriginal people or if there are some issues surrounding women as well. Why would the Hon. Member deny the people of Quebec the right and obligation to participate in future improvements to that important document?

Mr. Speaker, I am certain the majority of people in Quebec would want to have the best possible constitutional agreement that can be arrived at, and that the majority of Quebecers do not really wish to be singled out and given a special status. That is what the issue is all about. Quebec's vision of its own role in Canada is one that encompasses this nation from coast to coast. It wants to be in a Canadian federalist state in which no one is given special privileges. I am sure that Quebecers are the last ones who would want to be given special privileges.
What I am saying in my intervention is that we have here a document which was arrived at without public consultation. That in itself is a poor process. In a way it is a signal to members of the public that politicians know better than they, the people for whom the Constitution was written. I am saying that this proposal which we have before us today makes only one province responsible for the promotion of linguistic rights. That is not the approach that Quebecers or anyone who speaks French in Canada would want to have. We want to have this responsibility across the nation, as it should be because in law and linguistically we are a society which speaks two languages.
We are saying that the concept of a distinct society could lead one day to a two-nation Canada which is a concept that the Party of the Hon. Member fondly developed in the 1960s and one which it has flirted with on more than one occasion.
June 14, 1988

That in itself is reason enough for speaking against the Meech Lake Accord. Who wants to lay the foundation with this document for future generations of politicians to say: "Well, there is a distinct society clause in the Accord which allows, gives us the premise, the jumping board to claim one day that actually one province should become a separate nation"? That is not what the majority of Quebecers want. The Hon. Member has it all wrong.
If one looks at the totality of the document before us and the impact that it has and adds to that the description of Canadian society in Section 2(1), which is so outdated, one cannot help but say that this exercise, this drafting has to be sent back to the drawing-board to be started all over again. In the long term it is not a real definition of Canada. It is not a good document in the long term for Canadian unity.

Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member is talking about the idea of perfection, and I gather he is, then I think he is being misleading. I do not know what he did before he was a politician, whether he was a teacher, a businessman or something else. In any endeavour I think one works toward the greatest degree of success along with a number of men and women attacking the problem. However, there comes a point in time when a decision has to be made and we must move on. One cannot keep striving for that perfection. Maybe that is what he was trying to do in the environment portfolio when he was Minister. Is that the reason he accomplished nothing?

Mr. Speaker, I would be the last one to boast about my record as Minister of the Environment. I would seriously question the Hon. Member's concept of a healthy democracy when constitutional amendments are made and the people who will be affected by them are not consulted and when no amendment will be accepted in the process. That is not a definition of perfection. That is simply a definition of healthy democracy which we apply in our country in every walk of life. We seem to have forgotten that in the evolution of this most important and central document, the Constitution of Canada. What is wrong with healthy consultation with the public?

-I want to question the statement that the Hon. Member made about public consultation on the Constitution and on the Meech Lake Accord. The Constitution has been the subject of consultation with the provinces and with people from all walks of life for many, many years.
Back in 1980 and 1981 when the former Prime Minister and most of the First Ministers reached an agreement on the Constitution, it was done with a great deal of negotiation and bargaining in the back rooms. We all remember the Hon. Roy McMurtry, the Hon. Jean Chretien and the Hon. Roy Romanow and the deals they were cutting in the back kitchen to bring the Constitution together for the First Ministers of the

land. We remember at the time the joy there was because a decision had been made, although it was not perfect. We also remember that at the time one province was left out. The Meech Lake Accord has a great deal to do with bringing that province in.
Since that time there has been public consultation among people in all walks of life. The Hon. Member knows that full well. If the Hon. Member had paid any attention to the election campaign of 1984 and the speech that the Prime Minister gave in the Province of Quebec on the constitutional Accord and bringing Quebec into our Confederation under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Constitution, he would know full well that there has been a great deal of public consultation going on since that period of time. For the Hon. Member to stand up and tell the Canadian people that there was no public consultation is completely erroneous. Mr. Speaker, I would always defend the right of the Parliamentary Secretary to disagree with me. Nevertheless, that does not take away from the fact that his knowledge of historical facts is totally incorrect.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to elicit a comment from the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) by way of a question. The Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) referred to the Hon. Member's remarks as being somewhat hollow. I would ask the Members of the House not to impute motives or try to castigate Members who hold legitimate opinions. One can have one's opinion about this agreement. One can be for it or one can be against it.
I say to the Hon. Member for Davenport in support of his remarks that there are two competing visions of this country. One is a vision of Canada wherein Canadians owe their attachment to the country as a whole, a Canada greater than the sum of its parts. The other vision is that one owes one's loyalties to the particular province or region from which one comes.
The former Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, in his remarks to the Senate on March 30 really made that point when he was referring to Henri Bourassa who said that many generations of Quebec politicians will have fought for the establishment of the French fact in Canada, not in Quebec. He saw this as a retreat from that way of viewing the country.
Does the Hon. Member care to make any additional comments about what I feel, and what I beg all Hon. Members to understand, is a very legitimate view of what Canada is all about?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of my hon. friend. I do seek the indulgence of Members if I run slightly over the time, but I do not expect to be much in excess.
The 1987 Constitutional Accord, which like others I refer to as Meech Lake, has been with us now for almost one year. Despite the conspiracy of silence, one might call it, established among our so-called political leaders and some of our aspiring political leaders, Canadians are slowly becoming aware of what is truly at stake in Meech Lake. The result of that awareness was predictable. The more Meech Lake is understood, the more it is being rejected by Canadians. Some Canadians see it only as a problem for themselves, and that is understandable. For example, the native peoples, women, representatives of the Yukon and the Territories, and so on, have pleaded their cases eloquently at every opportunity.

The proposed constitutional amendment is invasive in that it affects every aspect of our economic and social fabric, even our political geography. When we talk about Meech Lake, we are talking about the future of Canada, the Canada we have known for 121 years, the Canada we love and the Canada where we have prospered.
Mr. Speaker, my concerns about Meech Lake aren't restricted to a single issue: whether we are talking about the future of Anglophones in Quebec; whether we are discussing the sad plight of our Native people, the weakening of sexual equality, the restrictions that would apply to federal spending powers, the absurd suggestion regarding appointments to the Senate or the dangerous proposal for appointments to the
Supreme Court, my concerns rise from the proposed amendment as a whole.

Thanks to Meech Lake Canada is to be partitioned into two distinct societies based on language and territory: Quebec will be French, the rest of Canada English, albeit with each agreeing to preserve the existence of those whose tongue is alien to the particular society in which they find themselves.
Linguistic genocide, therefore, is not proposed, but neither is a bilingual nation where public services would be available in French or English from coast to coast.
Quebec will have a special status, authority to promote its distinct identity at home and abroad, with additional powers not available to other provinces. What authority remains to the federal Government to deal with the social and economic challenges of Canadians is also being removed.
Canada is to become an association of provincial fiefdoms with semi-annual meetings between First Ministers to coordinate national objectives and policies, and strip Ottawa of whatever other authority the provinces might cherish. Meech Lake is very clearly the beginning of that process.
At Ottawa's expense, the provinces acquire powers in immigration, social and economic areas, appointments to the Senate and the Supreme Court, and a veto for each over all major changes, including the creation of new provinces. To make those gains secure, there is an amending formula that puts Canada's evolution on a one-way street to more and more decentralization and the potential break up of the federation.
You might ask, Mr. Speaker: Why do so many accept Meech Lake? Well, most accept it looking through rose-coloured glasses, hoping that the various scenarios implicit in Meech Lake do not unfold. Having listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Leaders of both opposition Parties here today, I believe that they are wearing the rosiest glasses of all. They rationalize away what concerns they may have on the ground that Quebec's moral adherence to the Constitution is worth the price. They hope the price is not too high, but they do not know. Some, even our Prime Minister as a matter of fact, admit that they do not know what the price is. What is the meaning of the distinct society clause? "Some day the Supreme Court of Canada will tell us", he says. Yes, indeed, the courts will one day tell us what we have done to Canada through Meech Lake, should it move forward. If we do not like it at that time, too bad. It will be too late to change directions.
Others, of course, embrace Meech Lake because they covet a further reduction of federal authority. If a form of sovereignty association with a unilingual French Quebec is necessary to achieve that reduction, well so be it. Quebec nationalists want it because they will finally have created the long dreamed of deux nations, and the extreme nationalists in Quebec see Meech Lake as a solid stepping-stone to Quebec's independence.
June 14, 1988

When the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the NDP Party (Mr. Broadbent), say: "We now know the answer to the question: 'What does Quebec want?'" I would say we have a vague idea of what the current Quebec Government wants. The two are very different. We have heard all leaders, and we just heard the Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) say that Quebec has said "Yes" to Canada and now Canada must say "Yes" to Quebec. In fact, the Prime Minister said very specifically Quebec-

"Quebec said yes twice". That is not true, Mr. Speaker. The people of Quebec said yes in 1980, but the Parti Quebecois Government said no to Canada.
The two are not the same. What the population said and what the Government said are two entirely different things.

In 1980 the Quebec Government said "No" to Canada, and we are not hearing from the Quebec people except through the Quebec Government which replaced the Pequiste Government of Mr. Levesque.
What does this adherence mean? We hear that it will allow Canada to move forward with constitutional evolution, that Quebec will now come to the negotiating table on a regular basis, that this is the Quebec round that has been finished. We have heard all of this, Mr. Speaker. Where do we see any of this in Meech Lake? As a matter of fact, when I look at Mr. Bourassa's comments in the National Assembly, I hear him say, or I read that he has said that Quebec has not lost anything through Meech Lake, that there has been no step backward.

In fact, the Liberal Party, and I quote: "recognizes Quebec's right to determine its internal constitution and to express freely its desire to either maintain or terminate its membership in the Canadian federation". That was a resolution passed by the Liberal Party in 1980, and it has in no way been changed or affected by Meech Lake.

I am not so sure that the attributes of this adherence that are being given to Quebec's signature by Members in the House, and by the Leaders of the Parties, are really those that Mr. Bourassa gives. I see no guarantee that the Quebec Government in future will come to the table, if it does not suit its purpose.
Where are the defenders of Canada in this debate? [Translation]
Today, Mr. Speaker, I am here as one of Canada's elected representatives, and I am ashamed, because our elected politicians have done a disservice to the 25 million Canadians they are supposed to represent. Mr. Speaker, this is a sad moment in our history. It is a sad time for our political system,
Constitution Amendment, 1987
and I think it is even sadder for those in whom their constituents have placed their trust.
Mr. Speaker, this constitutional debate, the most important one of our time, and its effects that will determine the very nature of our federation, of our national, political and economic institutions, and even the future of our country, this debate will go down in history without any expression of dissent from the Opposition parties in this House.
What have some of our political Leaders said about the Meech Lake Accord? In recent weeks, and I will come to some of the comments made today, I heard Premier Bourassa ask: "Who has found a serious flaw in Meech Lake?" The answer to that is: "Who has not?" We can begin with 80 per cent of the lawyers polled by the Canadian Bar Association who responded with various degrees of concern about Meech Lake. The list of flaws and critics is virtually inexhaustible. Only our so-called political Leaders have chosen to duck the issue.
The Prime Minister stood in this House again this morning claiming that no one had found an egregious error. That is simply nonsense and the Canadian people know it. Mr. Lucien Bouchard, who supported the separatist aspirations of Rene Levesque and the Parti Quebecois, is now an unelected Minister of the Government. He is reported in the May 18 edition of Le Devoir as saying:
[ Translation]
"What we must tell English Canada is that Quebec's aspirations can no longer be kept out. There is a very simple solution-the Meech Lake Accord."
What aspirations is he talking about? Something like the sovereignty-association that he fought for in 1980. It is quite obvious, as my colleague from Davenport (Mr. Caccia) has just said, that the Accord could provide a way to attain it. And like the Meech Lake Accord, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Bouchard divides the country into two language groups, French Canada in Quebec and English Canada elsewhere.
And my colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), who is in the House this afternoon, talks in the same way. In an interview in La Presse on May 18, he accuses us, that is Jean Chretien, Pierre Trudeau and myself, whom he considers the old guard, of completely misunderstanding the Meech Lake Accord:
"I said that I was going to Ottawa to defend Quebec's interests, not to defend Ottawa's interests in Quebec."

My friend from Laval-des-Rapides also seems to divide Canada into two territorial linguistic communities. Here we find a fundamentally different view of Canada and even of the role of Members of Parliament. Mr. Bouchard and my friend from Laval-des-Rapides are no doubt sincere in their belief

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
that they are here to defend the interests of Quebec. However, by that they clearly mean the interests of the Quebec Government. Clearly they have no better mandate to speak on behalf of the people of Quebec than I do. Or, would they say an Anglophone MP cannot speak for people of Quebec? If so, would they say that the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), a Francophone, cannot speak for people of Ontario? Or, the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay), also a Francophone, cannot speak for Manitobans? I do not think they mean that. Therefore, when my friend from Laval-des-Rapides refers to Quebec, I believe he refers to the provincial Government of Quebec and sees this House as a kind of brokerage house for provincial interests which he believes he has a mandate to defend.
I say to you and to him that if we in this House adopt that attitude, who in this Chamber is going to speak for Canada? Who is going to defend the national vision? I would add that I have enormous respect for my friend from Laval-des-Rapides, whose sincerity, dedication and integrity are beyond reproach. That is a healthy and welcome contrast to what I sometimes see elsewhere in this Chamber.
I did not come to Ottawa to defend the interests of the Quebec Government. Premier Bourassa does a good job of that. We here are elected to a national Parliament and we must never forget it. Our duty is to defend the national interest. In doing so, we must be accountable to those who elected us but not to provincial Governments. While we defend and promote the interests of our communities and our regions, we must do so within a national context.
Meech Lake is very much in keeping with the other view, namely that the federal Government and this Parliament are simply delegates of the provinces, like the manager of a condominium project with the responsibility delegated by the owners to take care of the common property, cut the grass, remove the snow, and clean the lobby and hallways. That is not my vision of Canada. It was not the vision of the vieille garde and all those who preceded them, from Sir John A. Macdonald to Pierre Elliott Trudeau. I want to say, judging by the volume of mail I have received and the reception I have received across this country on many speaking engagements, that this vision of the old guard is strong, healthy and growing every day.
During the past year I have addressed the subject of Meech Lake on many occasions in all the provinces of Canada with the exception, regrettably, of Newfoundland. That experience tells me that Canadians believe in one nation, one society, and when informed they overwhelmingly reject Meech Lake.
I respect the fact that some sincerely believe that the federal Government should be, as it were, a condominium manager and Canada should be divided into two nations, one French speaking and one English speaking. I profoundly disagree and I will fight to defend my vision of the country. I do respect those views, but I do not respect those, and we heard from the three Leaders in this House today, who would have us believe
that Meech Lake is not changing the nature of our federation. Some even pretended, for goodness' sake, that it promotes national bilingualism even in the Province of Quebec. I refer to the earlier speeches of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnaty-shyn), my friend from York Centre, and the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), and the speeches again given today by the Prime Minister and the Leaders of both opposition Parties. If I may say so, those speeches are replete with naivety, inaccuracies, and even legal stupidities.
How conceited can you get?

I am glad to see my friend from New Westminster-Coquitlam here today. She said:
If Meech Lake were already in effect, it is our firm belief that that limiting
action of the Saskatchewan Government would have been declared contrary to
the Constitution as amended by Meech Lake.
Right on.
Really? That seems to be the view supported by the Leaders today.
We think it is the right view.

As far as Saskatchewan is concerned, Meech Lake was in effect morally, it being the second province following Quebec to accept it. However, if one reads Meech Lake, which most people apparently have not, it clearly states that provincial legislatures have a role to "preserve the existence of French-speaking Canadians elsewhere in Canada". There is nothing in there referring to the preservation of rights, notwithstanding the fact that the Prime Minister said that today and the Leaders of both opposition Parties said the same thing. One final nail in the coffin of that argument is that Section 2(4) of Meech Lake is absolutely clear: No power with respect to language that belonged to a legislature prior to Meech Lake is affected by Meech Lake.
The Supreme Court of Canada told Saskatchewan it had the power to do what it did, but it would seem the Prime Minister and the spokespersons for the opposition Parties are offering us legal opinions that even a layman would reject reading the text of the Meech Lake Accord itself.
Finally, I ask them this question. If Meech Lake is intended to protect existing rights, then French-speaking Canadians elsewhere in Canada would have more rights in Saskatchewan or in Ontario than they would in British Columbia. Mr. Vander Zalm presumably feels that he would be discharging his role to "preserve the existence of French-speaking Canadians" without adding any rights to his statute books. Why should not Mr. Peterson and Mr. Devine be entitled to discharge their roles at the same level as Mr. Vander Zalm? Some day the courts will answer these questions, but please do not then turn and say that we were not warned about the disastrous consequences of Meech Lake on the linguistic rights of Canadians from coast to coast.
June 14, 1988

Finally I turn to some of the remarkable comments of the Minister of Justice speaking on behalf of the Government, Mr. Speaker. He assures us that the territorial division of Canada into a distinct society of Quebec on the one hand and the other distinct society in the rest of Canada is not to be feared by minorities in Quebec. He said:
When we say that Quebec constitutes a distinct society within Canada, it is
understood that all residents of Quebec are an integral part of that society ...
Those Quebecers from a multicultural community are part of it. Quebec's
English-speaking community is an integral part of the Quebec's distinct
society.
That is an interesting comment. Is that what Premier Bourassa meant when he said in the National Assembly:

For the first time in 120 years of history, the Constitution will recognize Quebec as a distinct society. The Constitution will provide Quebec with the means to preserve and promote its distinct identity and will give a constitutional basis for the French fact in Quebec.

Is the Minister of Justice really telling us that the Quebec Government sees itself as having a role to preserve and promote the English presence in Quebec? If so, how does he view the current policies which forbid the use of English on commercial signs, which limit access to English schooling, which insist on French dubbed films before general film distribution and so on? Does he see all this as changing after Meech Lake when Quebec will set about to promote all elements of its distinct society including the English component? If he does, then the Minister of Justice-

Constitution Amendment, 1987

I thank you and my hon. colleagues for the courtesy, Mr. Speaker.
I was pointing out what had taken place in the Province of Quebec and that the Minister of Justice seems to believe that there is an obligation to promote the English component of Quebec society. In light of what we have seen, if he believes that, I would add that he must still believe in Santa Claus and the tooth fairy.
Professor Lederman in the Financial Post on August 31, 1987, an authority quoted with approval in this House by the Government, had it right when he wrote of "the distinct society of French-speaking Canadians in Quebec". That is what Meech Lake is all about. It is about a French Quebec in an English Canada. There are 800,000 English-speaking people in Quebec who are not part of that distinct society. Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker. Meech Lake is opting for the Belgian solution, which our Commissioner of Official Languages in his recent report has described as a recipe for national suicide. Only days ago as we know Mr. Remillard made the Quebec Government's view absolutely clear. Meech Lake is to support a French Quebec not a bilingual Quebec. For once I found myself in entire agreement with Mr. Remillard because that is what Meech Lake is telling us.
The message is coming through to Canadians despite efforts to suppress debate even in this House. What is that message Canadians are receiving? If you believe in one Canada, you must reject Meech Lake. That is part of the message.

And if you believe that this country should keep a national vision that is greater than the sum of the provincial visions, that is, that Canada is greater than the sum of its provincial parts, you must reject the Meech Lake Accord.

If you believe that the individual minority rights of Canadians, be they linguistic rights or sexual equality rights, should be protected against the collective rights of a distinct society, then you must reject Meech Lake. If you believe that Canada requires national programs meeting national standards or criteria in research, education, training, income maintenance and health and that the federal spending power should be used for such purposes in the future, I should say as it has so successfully done in the past
You are totally off.
You are totally off.

-then you must reject Meech Lake. If you believe the Constitution of this country should be a flexible instrument reflecting changing economic and social conditions as our country evolves with a constitutional amending formula to allow that to take place, then you must reject Meech Lake.

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987

And if you believe, Mr. Speaker, that the 11 First Ministers should not have the power to change behind closed doors our fundamental law, namely the Constitution, you must reject the Meech Lake Accord. And if you believe that the judges of the Supreme Court should not be appointed from among candidates submitted by the provincial governments, you must reject the Meech Lake Accord.

If you believe that the Senate should be reformed to reflect the original intentions of the Fathers of Confederation, namely, to protect the regions against an overbearing central authority, you must reject Meech Lake.
If you believe in that, in a federation like ours the provinces should exercise the same powers and that no one province should have a special legal status which entitles it to exercise important powers not available to other provinces, you must reject Meech Lake.

So, Mr. Speaker, if you see our country as one with two official languages and bilingual institutions in every province, in every region, with sufficient protection for linguistic minorities, you must reject the Meech Lake Accord.

For those who look at this Accord and see where it can take the country, I say to those who voted no in the Quebec Referendum in 1980 that you must also reject Meech Lake.
So, Mr. Speaker, I have tabled amendments, which are found in the Order Paper, seconded by the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger), which are designed to satisfy the Quebec Government's five demands for moral adherence to the Canadian Constitution. They are virtually identical to those adopted by the Liberal Party at its 1986 November policy convention and were supported overwhelmingly by Liberals from all regions of this country. I say to my fellow Liberal Members in this House and the caucus, regrettably of which I am no longer a member, that if they do not support the amendments brought forward which reflect the mandate given to us by the Liberal Party of Canada, they are turning their backs on the Liberal Party and rejecting not only the Liberal vision of this country of Canada, which we have held through most of the century, but the specific mandate given by the Party at the November 1986 policy convention.
In order to save time, and I appreciate the generosity that Members have extended to me, I will not go through all of these amendments but I hope Members will look at them because they incorporate the Victoria formula, for example for the appointment of Supreme Court Justices. They invoke the Victoria formula suggested by the Liberal Party for constitutional amendments. They put in a preamble which recognizes the distinctive character of Quebec as the principal but not the exclusive source of French language and culture in Canada.
They cover all of those points that were subject to the Liberal resolution of November, 1986.
In conclusion, let me say that these amendments are important because the Meech Lake Accord is not acceptable to Canadians in its present form. Those in this Chamber who think this will pass through all the provincial legislatures, I say that they are dreaming in colour. The answer is not simply to reject what we have, it is to come forward with something that will be acceptable to the Province of Quebec and which will be acceptable to Liberals from coast to coast.
I say to those in this House who argue as they have time and time again that it is necessary to proceed with Meech Lake despite its obvious flaws and that it is necessary to adopt it without amendment, remember the wisdom of William Pitt who said in the British House of Commons nearly 200 years ago:
Necessity is the plea for every infringement of human freedom; it is the
argument of tyrants, it is the creed of slaves.
Canadians are not slaves, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) for his excellent speech. I think that he has shown the House that his vision of Canada is shared by many Quebecers and most Canadians.

I would like to ask the Hon. Member a somewhat precise question about the distinct society clause. How does he feel about the distinct society clause not being in the preamble but in an operational clause, therefore giving clear instructions to the courts that they should interpret every other part of the Constitution relative to that clause? It would be interesting to know if the distinct society clause overrides the Charter or overrides anything that is in the Constitution so that that may be interpreted in favour of a distinct society for Quebec. I wonder if we should refer that clause to the Supreme Court of Canada for interpretation before we vote on this important issue.
Second, I wonder if the unanimity clause prevents amendments to the Constitution as far as the Senate is concerned. As the Hon. Member well knows, western Canadians believe that we should have an equal, effective and elected Senate. Will having the unanimity clause in the Accord prevent us from changing the second House in this Parliament?
We have seen what can happen. Last year we were called back to deal with emergency legislation on refugees. The Senate has been holding back that legislation for the last year. Those who are not elected, not responsible to constituents, are holding back our legislation. Will the Meech Lake unanimity clause prevent us from changing the Senate? These are some of the concerns I have, and I am also concerned as to whether
June 14, 1988

or not the distinct society clause overrides the Charter of Rights.

Mr. Speaker, I have been asked a legal question and I have my own legal opinions, but I do agree that it would be very useful to refer the distinct society clause and a number of other clauses to the Supreme Court of Canada for determination so that Members of the House would vote with the full knowledge of what may be involved. In June of 1987,1 in fact wrote to the Prime Minister suggesting specifically that, and I wrote as well to all of the premiers because the provinces also have the right to refer matters to their respective courts of appeal for interpretation, as in fact the provinces did back in 1981 during the patriation exercise. I think there is a very serious question as to what the implication of the distinct society clause is, not only on the Charter but also on power transfers.
We have heard Members of the House say that there is a non-derogation clause, we cannot change Section 91 and Section 92. However, some of the most important powers in our Constitution, their distribution and application, including communications and much of trade and commerce and the application of the peace, order and good Government clause, have been brought about through the interpretation of the Constitution. As Professor Beaudouin, a proponent of this particular Accord, said-

"It is an interpretation rule that has changed the Canadian federation."

This interpretation clause then is very significant.
With respect to the Senate, that is not a legal question, that is a question of political dynamics. I ask Members of this House who are practising politicians if they know any politician who would voluntarily give up the right to appoint 24 Senators to the Senate of Canada in return for an equal, effective and elected Senate in order to satisfy the concerns of western Canadians. I might say that in the amendments I have put forward, that kind of Senate is put right on the agenda of the First Ministers. The Triple E Senate should be addressed by the First Ministers as soon as possible. In the meantime, no change should be made because if the change which is provided for in Meech Lake is made, then I do not think, and I think the Hon. Member from Calgary shares my view, that we will ever see Senate reform in our lifetimes.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a short comment on the Hon. Member's speech and on some of the points of view he put forward. First, I would observe that we have had in Canada a long history of the implementation of the kind of philosophy he advocates, namely that of an extremely strong central Government, the heavy hand of Ottawa coming down on the provinces. We have to ask where that got us, and that is only in recent history.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
If this philosophy is the one that keeps our country together, how is it that in 1980 at the time of the referendum, 40 per cent of the people of Quebec and almost 50 per cent of the French-speaking people of Quebec voted to leave confederation as we know it? If that is the philosophy of success as far as keeping our country together goes, how is it that in 1980, we faced a major constitutional crisis, perhaps the most significant crisis in this century?
The Hon. Member spoke of constitutional documents, their perfections and their imperfections. How can a Member speak with such criticism of Meech Lake when in 1982 there was a constitutional agreement reached which left out the Province of Quebec? The National Assembly of Quebec rejected the document. The Government of Quebec was not a signatory to the 1982 constitutional Accord, notwithstanding the fact that the change which was reflected in that document was the change which was promised to the people of Quebec in 1980, change which was an effort to respond to the legitimate aspirations of the people of Quebec.
In the 1987 Meech Lake Accord, there is a series of constitutional changes that date well back into the history of the Liberal Government which was ruling this country in 1968. Changes to the Supreme Court of Canada, the Senate, the shared-cost programs, references to distinct society, the duality provisions and the role of the provinces, all of these have a history that predates this Government. What was new in 1987 was that for the first time, these elements were brought together and an Accord was reached. That is what eluded Canada before this.
The question for us all to consider is not who will speak for Canada, because there is a far more basic question than that, and that is, will there be a Canada. In my view, there will be a stronger, more prosperous Canada because Meech Lake is the glue that will keep us together.

Madam Speaker, I think it is quite appropriate to have a debate in this country on centralization or decentralization or whether we should have two nations in order to keep the country together. I have no problem with having that kind of debate, but let us have that debate, because that is what we are talking about. I do not happen to share that view, but let us not pretend that Meech Lake is anything other than a stepping stone to deux nations and to a highly decentralized federation with an amending formula which does not permit the flexibility that we have known historically.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) asks what has this done for us. It has brought us to being one of the seventh largest industrialized countries in the world with one of the highest standards of living known to man. I think Canada has been a great success, though certainly there could be improvements.
The Hon. Member referred to the 1982 patriation exercise. It was former Prime Minister Trudeau who pointed out in the Senate that in fact, of elected Members from Quebec, whether

June 14, 1988
Message from the Senate
in the National Assembly or in this House, comparing the two of them, 109 voted in favour and only 74 against it. The entire Parti Quebecois and only four others in Quebec voted against it. We remember that in this House overwhelming support was given to the patriation exercise in the Charter by Members who represented every single region of Quebec, just as the Hon. Member represents Cape Breton Highlands-Canso.
It is simply pure folklore to say that there were not elected Members from Quebec speaking in favour of the patriation exercise. Did anyone really expect a pequiste Premier of Quebec, Rene Levesque, whose life was dedicated to taking Quebec out of Canada, to sign a constitutional document which would basically bind Quebec to Canada? I think that is somewhat unrealistic.
