Madam Speaker, I really quite doubt that I am going to have an opportunity to finish what I would like to say with respect to this debate on Meech Lake. I understand that we have perhaps two or three more minutes before this portion of the debate ends.
I quite agree with those who say that Meech Lake has its imperfections. It may very well be, as one Member has indicated, that those who believe that it will ultimately be ratified by the provinces are dreaming in Technicolor. However, let me make myself clear. While it is possible to have alternative visions of Canada, it is not possible to have a vision of Canada which disregards the history of Canada. If Quebec is recognized as a distinct society, that is not established by Meech Lake but by the history of this country.
As one whose family has been in this country for 150 years, the debate, in my view, is not on the issue of whether or not Quebec should be a distinct society, but whether one-third of the population will be considered a part of this society.
I grew up in a nation which, according to all that I experienced, seemed to consist of only two peoples, those who were French and those who were English. For too long this country has failed to recognize that one-third of the population of the country, which proportion is increasing, has been disregarded all too completely. It is true that we have provision for multiculturalism. However, insofar as I am concerned as a representative of that one-third of the population which is not derived from either of the founding peoples, the Meech Lake Accord has one single most notable flaw, that is, its total irrelevancy to me.
If it was important, if it was critical to have Quebec a willing partner in Confederation; it if was important, if it was essential to have Quebec as a part of Canada, it is equally essential to have those who are of neither French nor English origin equally a part. That is just as essential, just as critical. Meech Lake failed one-third of the country. We were not included at the time of Meech Lake.
There has been some question raised about the significance of ascribing to Quebec the status of a distinct society. There is no question about the result which leaves unchanged the situation of the one-third when one looks at the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and reads Section 15 which is of
June 14, 1988

fundamental importance to those of us who are neither French nor English. It reads:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
That sounds as though it were a ringing clarion call for equality and equal participation of all citizens in this nation. However, there was a bit of work undone and that was the fatal flaw for one-third of us in the 1982 Constitutional Act. That resides in Section 33 which reads:
Parliament or the legislature of a province may expressly declare in an Act of Parliament or of the legislature, as the case may be, that the Act or a provision thereof shall operate notwithstanding a provision included in section 2 or sections 7 to 15 of this Charter.
In other words, the rights of one-third of us can be overruled by a decision of any legislature and as long as that is so Meech Lake is irrelevant to one-third of the population of Canada. While Meech Lake may solve the problems which have been historically rooted in this country, a new problem is created when one-third of us consider Meech Lake inevitable. Until that is changed, until the override is eliminated with respect to equality, Meech Lake is an indication of the incompleteness of Canada rather than its completeness.

Madam Speaker, I was interested in the comments of the Hon. Member with respect to the override provisions of the Charter of Rights in Section 33. The Hon. Member indicated that Section 33 was aimed only at one-third of Canadians, those Canadians who are not of French or British origin. He implied by his comments that Section 33, the notwithstanding provisions of the Charter, was aimed only at all other Canadians, those Canadians who are normally described as the multicultural community and come from various backgrounds other than French or British.
I am sure the Hon. Member does not want to leave the impression with this House and the public that Section 33 applies specifically only to all other Canadians, that third of Canadians who are not of French or British origin. In fact, as the Hon. Member knows, that provision, which I am sure offends everyone in this House, applies, unfortunately, to all Canadians, whether they be of British origin, French origin, or any of the other many origins which make up this country.
I am sure the Hon. Member would want to correct the record and ensure that he in no way, whether deliberately or non-deliberately, or just by confusing the issue, leaves the impression that that is the case and that Section 33 applies only to one-third of Canadians when, in fact, it unfortunately applies to all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I do not know whether that question is based on an erudite understanding of those articles of the Charter to which the notwithstanding clause applies or whether it is based on gross insensitivity to the realities of this country. It is true that the override clause applies to Articles 2
Constitution Amendment, 1987
and 7 to 15. It applies to a number of articles that have nothing to do with non discrimination or equality.
If the Hon. Member does not understand it, I know of no situation in this country where the English have been subjected to unequal treatment. I know of no situation in which the English were denied the ability to be pilots in the Royal Canadian Air Force. I know of no situation in which English were not employed or had no access to apartments. I know of no situation of that sort.
The situation of the French in this country was historically much more comparable to that one-third of the population who were denied so many rights. When we look at Section 15 as a guarantee that everyone in this country will be treated equally, we understand that it applies to everyone but that it applies with greater significance to those of us in this country who have been denied the very equality that it refers to, who have been objects of the discrimination to which it refers. That includes Ukrainians, Poles, aboriginal people and members of minority groups.
This is significant because it states that one does not have to be of either French or English derivation in this country to be treated on equal terms. Therefore, Article 33, the override with particular respect to Article 15, is fundamental to the nature of Canada as I understand it. Progress is made in developing a nation of many peoples, all of whom are equal citizens, with preferences to none.

Madam Speaker, I have enjoyed debating the Hon. Member and working with him in committees. I know that he is a distinguished Member, a passionate speaker, and a career scientist. I do not think he has a legal background.
I have the benefit of having had a bit of a legal background and I want to suggest to him that while I understand his concern about Section 33, and find it equally abhorrent, before we had a Charter of Rights we had ways of defending the rights of all Canadians under our Constitution. I will not get into the whole discussion of the implied Bill of Rights or a constitution similar in principle to that in the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom does not have a charter and rights are not violated with impunity there because of the fact that there is not a charter.
While I find Section 33 abhorrent and agree that it should be removed from the Charter, I cannot conceive of any Government invoking that clause with impunity in respect of the kind of concerns he has expressed here today. There was a government in Quebec that did it as a political tool, but any government that would do this would suffer from the weight of public opinion.
Even with the notwithstanding clause, the Charter was a great step forward. It was a step forward in the progress that Canadians have sought for 120 years to make our rights more formal, more explicit and provided for in constitutional provisions or human rights legislation. Would he not agree that the Charter should be seen in that light, as a step

June 14, 1988
Royal Assent
forward? Even with the notwithstanding clause, the trend was upward and forward to greater protection for rights and more rights for Canadians.
With Meech Lake, however, for the first time we are stepping back from that trend. Now the trend is down. Therefore, I deplore the fact that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was negotiating this agreement he did not use the opportunity to get rid of that notwithstanding clause. That is where his ire should be directed.

Madam Speaker, I do not know whether my legal training is at all relevant since my hon. colleague, whom I respect equally as he respects me, ended up with the same conclusion as I, that Meech Lake is flawed from the point of view of one-third of Canadian citizens.
When we were dealing with the problem emanating from the failure to recognize Quebec's distinctiveness, we failed to take that opportunity to correct that flaw in the Charter. More than anything else, it is the symbolic value of the Charter that is important, and the importance of recognizing our status within this country. I admit that the Charter was the most significant provision in the 1982 Constitution Act to me and many others.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HOUSING METRO TORONTO HOUSING SHORTAGE
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HOUSING METRO TORONTO HOUSING SHORTAGE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should make the solution
of the developing housing shortage crisis in Metro Toronto a matter of top
priority in forming housing and financial policies for 1988.
He said: Madam Speaker, I ask you why this House should recommend that the Government give priority to the housing crisis of Metro Toronto. The answer is very simple, for the same reason the Government gives priority to crises in other regions, be they drought on the Prairies or fishing rights in the Atlantic. This motion is not just about a city, it is about a region, what sociologists call "a conurbation," an urban region that is home to more than four million Canadians. They are people who are just as much a part of this country as if they lived in the East, the West or the North. As such, they make a claim on us in this House and in this debate because they are facing a crisis. It is a crisis in meeting a basic human need, a basic human right.
I do not exaggerate when I refer to the housing crisis of Metro Toronto in those terms. There has to be a crisis for most people when the price of an average house in this region has risen since last February from $200,000 to $233,000, and when the rent of an average apartment is over $800 a month, if one can find an apartment. That average is based on the rents for rent control departments as well as those in the so-called free markets.
The social implication of this crisis demands the recognition of this House of Commons. A basic cause of poverty in Metro Toronto is now housing. Where 30 per cent of a person's income was once enough for accommodation, it is now 40 per cent or much more. This vast conurbation stretching from Oshawa, or even Bowmanville, to the east, right around the "horseshoe" to Niagara Falls, a spur going up from Hamilton to Cambridge and Kitchener, is close to 100 miles long and embraces four million or more people.
We have in that area a tragic paradox of full employment and "food banks". That is why we have a new social category called "the working poor". But this crisis afflicts not only low-income people, not only those at the very bottom of the scale. It threatens others who are just above the level of low income. It threatens people who hitherto had enough to provide for themselves and perhaps had a little more to help provide for others. But the escalation of the housing crisis in this kind of conurbation threatens to erode the middle class. Part of its essence has been its ability to provide for itself. The soaring cost of housing now makes many ask if they can do for themselves what their parents did for them. For so long in Canada we have assumed, generation by generation, that each new generation would try to do better than the one before it. Each generation of parents hoped their children would go
June 14, 1988

further than they were able to take them. We are now finding the possibility of a reversal of that. We find young people wondering if they can achieve what their parents achieved, when the sorry cost of housing makes them wonder if their dream of owning their own home is going to be nothing more than that, a dream.
I speak of this as a small cloud on our social horizon. But it is a warning cloud that should alert us to a sinister social change, that is, the erosion of the middle class. I call upon the House to give attention to all who are anxious about housing, the destitute homeless, the working poor, the threatened middle class, none of whom aspire to the so-called "executive homes" that are advertised in the Saturday editions of our newspapers or that some municipal councils favour. I am referring to people who seek what no Canadian should be denied, a place that he or she can call home.
Let us look at some questions that might be raised in this debate. For instance, why do these people not go where housing is cheaper? That is a good question, since housing is dramatically cheaper in some parts of the country. Last February a $200,000 house in Metro Toronto would have gone for $120,000 in Winnipeg, or $84,000 in Fredericton.
Moving is no solution. Metro is where the work is. That is why there may be pouring into this region 100,000 a year. One reason for increased housing prices in Metro is this ingress of people from all parts of Canada as well as from beyond. That is why it is not simply a municipal problem, not simply a regional problem. It is a problem that should concern us all in this House because it is generated by the needs of people from all parts of Canada who are concentrating in one region.
All the efforts of government to decentralize the industry of Canada, to spread jobs around, so that they are more plentiful in other areas has not had the effect to which these sincere desires have aspired. Metro remains the Mecca for job seekers. People will not leave in order to find the blessing of a cheap house and the curse of no job.
Let us look at another question. Why should Parliament care about a problem in Metro Toronto? Why not let the people fend for themselves? A former Mayor of Toronto once said Toronto provides the most unifying effort in the whole of Canada because it gives everybody else in Canada something to hate. So we might ask why Parliament should care about a problem in Metro. I hope that none of us here forget that when money was needed to assist grain farmers Metro Members stood with rural Members to provide what was needed, and stood rightly.
That is what I ask today. My motion focuses on Metro because I speak as a Metro area Member of Parliament. That is where the housing crisis is most acute. However, if any Member of the House wants to amend the wording of the motion to embrace a larger area, I would support any initiative
Housing
that would bear on meeting human need anywhere in the country.
Let us look at another question. What can the Government do? The tone in which the question is normally raised assumes from the outset that there is no possibility. A partial answer would be that the Government should stop exacerbating the problem.
Here is an example of how three levels of government in the Metro area have been guilty. First, many municipalities impose approval processes that are so long and so expensive that they add immeasurably to the cost of every dwelling unit. The Province of Ontario has maintained a rental control system that has often helped the people who have needed it least and left unprotected those who have needed help the most. This is a system that has exacerbated the critical apartment shortage when the Government should have encouraged rental construction. This is a system that has led to property deterioration that has not been a blessing to people. That is not saying that the system should be abandoned. It is to say that the system could be examined, amended and improved.
Let us remember federally that we are not guiltless. Recently the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation unintentionally but no less effectively drove up the price of land in the north-east Metro region by using a sales method that at one time may have been plausible but in this time of crisis served to add fuel to the fire of speculation. It set a new level of price for the cost of land, a level of pricing that was inflationary in itself.
We might agree that if Governments just stopped making the crisis worse they would certainly help. I believe that Governments can do more. I put before the House a 10 point housing program which I believe should be considered by all three levels of government, points upon which all three can cooperate and which can certainly serve to meet the needs of our people in a way that are not being met now.
First, the Government of Canada should devote a major part of the Armed Forces base at Downsview to affordable housing. This act alone could provide 5,000 affordable homes, if CMHC can rid itself of its bottom-line mentality and made sure that the lots were made available to people within the price range of low and middle-income earners.
Second, let these lots be leased rather than sold, or at least be available for leasing. Let them be leased to people who can buy the house and rent the land until they are in a position to acquire the land as well. This method has already been tried and has been found to be effective. When the Malvern housing project was opened by Canada and Ontario in Scarborough less than 20 years ago that was precisely the method that was used. It worked then and it can work now. All we need is the will.
Third, in several elections the Progressive Conservative Party promised to remove the federal sales tax on building

June 14, 1988
Housing
materials used for houses. That promise was not made in 1984, and this Government is not committed to it. Let us be clear on that. But it is a policy that once committed itself to my Party. If it did so again that move could reduce the price of a new house by several thousand dollars, especially for people who would meet income criteria.
Fourth, to put more money into mortgages let us examine the possibilities of a mortgage exchange which would create a secondary market for mortgages. This proposal has already been approved by the Parliament of Canada, a previous Parliament. It has never been implemented for reasons that have never been made clear to any Parliament. But now that we are freeing up the financial services industry, I say again that this idea, already proposed and approved in a Budget by the Parliament of Canada, should be looked at again with a view to opening up the market and making more money available at competitive rates.
Fifth, let us look at subsidizing the interest rates on mortgages for home buyers who meet income criteria. We do that for organizations. The idea that I am recommending is not radical at all. We are already doing it. This Government has already announced it in terms of serving organizations who sponsor co-ops in that way. What I am asking is for this Parliament, for this Government, to look at the practicality and the possibility of doing that for individuals, to believe in individuals, to believe in families as much as we believe in organizations. Will it work? It has already worked. Between the years 1968 and 1972 that method helped fund the purchase of 400,000 family homes in the United States. So it is certainly worth looking at.
Sixth, we need to examine flexible loan structures with a view to enabling people to buy homes with lower downpayments and longer term mortgages. Lower downpayments and longer term mortgages stretch the payment period out. It means that the person might never acquire the home free and clear. "But so what", many people would ask for their priority is not aspiring to own the house free and clear. Their priority is to get a roof over their heads. Therefore, if they have a monthly payment within their means, they want that home with the equity they would build up, however little, month by month. They want it with the assurance of having security of tenure as long as they can pay their monthly payment. What I am suggesting is being practised in other countries where they provide for lower downpayments and longer mortgage periods than we are accustomed to in Canada.
Seventh, the Government should consider imposing a speculation tax on people who buy housing not to use it but to flip it. This type of speculation only increases the problem. The best way to reduce it is to burn the speculator. The capability of a government doing that was already demonstrated by a Conservative Government in Ontario. In the early 1970s the Davis Government did precisely that and it cooled off the
speculative market within days. I can remember the moaning and the groaning of developers whom I knew in the City of Scarborough, at the thought of what this was going to do to them. They are not the only speculators. There are many individuals who try to take advantage of the speculative market. The Government has within its possibility at either provincial or federal levels, or in concert one with the other, to cool that off and cool it off quickly. Even announcing such a tax could turn the spiral of speculation around.
Eighth, in co-operation with Ontario, let us re-examine the fees charged for insurance, legal services, real estate commissions, and other costs added to the price of a home to ensure that the consumer receives fairness.
Ninth, let us investigate the value of an accommodation or rental allowance as a way of helping low-income persons who are now lined up on waiting lists two years long for social housing in Metropolitan Toronto.
Tenth, I urge the Government to make a study of the economic, social, and psychological implications of social housing which is located in what are rightly called ghettos. Such a study should ask the questions: "Is this the only way people can be served? Is it the best way? Are there options open to us?"
I have put forward those 10 proposals to show that there are initiatives open to governments, including our own, to deal with what is a crisis in Metropolitan Toronto, and in the future could become a crisis in other communities. Each proposal is practical, each has been tried; none is radical, none is living in a dream world. All of them can succeed. I sum them up by saying that together they offer hope.
"Hope" was defined by one French philosopher by the word "possibilities". People have hope when they can see possibilities. Part of the burden of life in our huge conurbations is the hopelessness of seeing or at least feeling that we have no possibilities in front of us, no possibility of gaining a home of one's own, no possibility of owning a piece of Canada, no possibility of providing for ourselves and our families as our parents provided for us. No possibility, but instead frustration, insecurity, and anxiety.
I do not believe that Canada has to be like that. I believe that Parliament can change that and offer the people such as I have described new hope and new possibilities, that we can say to people the simple dream that they have is still possible.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HOUSING METRO TORONTO HOUSING SHORTAGE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to respond in the 10 minutes allocated to each subsequent speaker. First, I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) who spoke very passionately on his Private Member's Motion. I would like to commend him for raising the subject and as a Parliament attempt to deal with a matter that is obviously of concern to Metropolitan Toronto, but also to the major centres across the country.
June 14, 1988

Perhaps the metropolitan area of Toronto defines crystal clear the problem the Member attempted to address. In reference to Toronto, there used to be a saying that everyone's home was their castle. That dream for Metropolitan Toronto is evaporating in the sense, as the Member pointed out in his motion, that there is indeed a housing shortage crisis, yet there is a crisis in affordable housing. Many homes are being built in Metropolitan Toronto and the various suburbs, but they are simply and clearly becoming unaffordable for the average Canadian citizen who resides or wishes to reside in Metropolitan Toronto, and in the major urban centres from one coast to the other.
In Toronto the average young couple is in a dilemma. The dream of owning a first home and then building that nest and moving to the second home is evaporating. For a young married couple in Metropolitan Toronto even the dream of renting is becoming next to impossible. The whole evolutionary process of moving from a starter home to perhaps a larger home to reflect the needs of a family, or perhaps to meet the upward mobility of both parents in terms of their economic livelihood is being stunted, and they are fortunate if they can buy an affordable starter home.
The whole picture of parents aiding their children in the purchase of that first home is also becoming stunted. How can parents who may have three or four children begin to assist one child in purchasing a house, which is now in the neighbourhood of $225,000 or $230,000? How can that parent or parents treat their children equally? It is obviously becoming impossible. In terms of affordable housing, Metropolitan Toronto has, unfortunately, become an exclusive backyard for the well-to-do. This has not happened by any master grand design, but that is clearly the direction in which Metropolitan Toronto is heading.
Without deference to the various municipalities and towns that have sprung up around Toronto, for example, Brantford, Ajax, Newmarket, or Bolton, which are beginning to flourish as they should, but flourishing from individuals who work, shop, and go to Toronto for their various social, cultural, and entertainment opportunities. That should not be the case. The individual ought to have the opportunity of residing and living in that same community without commuting great distances. Those distances are becoming farther. There are people who do the daily trek from Newmarket, Stouffville, Ajax for one hour or an hour and a half into Toronto, they work, and then return because they cannot afford to live in Metropolitan Toronto. Clearly that is wrong.
If we as a Government are to be interested in where and how people live, and why people can live here and not there, and if we have that social conscience as a Parliament and as a Government, and I believe that we can muster that, then we cannot run away from the problem in Metropolitan Toronto, and indeed in the major centres of the country.
In his 10-point agenda the Hon. Member for Scarborough West offered a number of stimulating concepts and ideas that
Housing
we need to address. We need to address those not only as a Government, and as a federal Government, but in partnership with provincial and municipal elected leadership. We also have to bring into that partnership the builders in Metropolitan Toronto, as well as the real estate industry. It goes beyond simply trying to have a program of assistance for that first time home buyer, or perhaps to take the Downsview Airport base and give portions of that land to affordable housing. Those are legitimate programs and proposals that we need to look at.
We also need to look at the speculative real estate market in urban centres like Toronto. The Hon. Member touched on that briefly but we need to delve into it much more seriously. There needs to be some sort of apparatus which would not allow these artificially inflated prices to take root. How many times have we seen in Metropolitan Toronto a real estate market cutthroat competitive to the point where real estate agents, rather than losing a listing, will list a house at an inflated price.
I am not knocking the real estate industry because they have to put food on the table. However, it is clearly wrong to have an agent list a home for $240,000 or $250,000, when it would realistically sell for $175,000 or $180,000, just to satisfy the seller. It is not the individual transaction that is worrisome. It is the collective effect of many real estate agents and companies doing it. Prices will start upward in an artificial spiral and the transactions will legitimize the price of a home at $240,000 or $250,000 rather than a realistic figure of $170,000 or $175,000. Clearly there needs to be a code of ethics in the sense of looking at housing not only as an economic transaction but as the centre-piece of an individual's existence in any major urban centre.
We should also, particularly municipal leaders, look at the question of property taxes. How often do we hear, from our more senior citizen population in particular, that having suffered and sacrificed for 30 years to move from an apartment to a semi-detached to a bungalow or perhaps a split-level, the property tax becomes a problem. The income of a senior citizen in Metropolitan Toronto is so poor that they cannot keep up their homes much less afford the increasing property taxes imposed on them.
It is time to look at that situation because municipalities have to replace their infrastructure and to do so, perhaps they should have a piece of the income tax pie. When you really get down to it, it is unfair, given what we expect from the various city councils and their budgets, to ask them to deliver the necessary services without passing the cost on to individual home owners. It then becomes a vicious circle. The property tax base is becoming archaic and unrealistic. For example, it is time to reform the system so that when people improve their home through an addition, which will be immediately reflected in increased property taxes, we should have perhaps a freeze so that those taxes do not have to be paid except when the house

June 14, 1988
Business of the House
is sold. Otherwise, not only are people not going to be able to afford improvements, we will be discouraging them from making those improvements which keep our city clean and proper.
I hope the House of Commons and the Government take this motion and others very seriously so that we can avoid our major municipalities going the way of New York where apartments rent for $10,000 a month. From that lesson let us learn to be different. Let us learn as an elected body to confront the challenges now for a better tomorrow.

The co-op movement, taking the same view, which in part is shared by the Hon. It also requested something similar to what was promised, namely, 40 per cent of the unit would be for low income people and 20 per cent for people of not quite such low income. There would be cut-off lines. People with modest income, as the Hon. Member for Scarborough West, said often have great difficulty in Metro Toronto. They also ask that administration of co-op housing units be transferred to the co-operative organizations, not each individual co-op, but the 60 service organizations for co-ops that have grown up in the country. They point to the general experience that co-operative housing after five years or so is so efficiently operated that housing charges are lower than



June 14, 1988

comparable housing rents in the districts around them. In other words, co-ops manage their funds efficiently.
In addition to these, Madam Speaker, I would urge several other points. I agree strongly with the Hon. Member for Scarborough West in saying that we should reinstitute a tax on speculation. Perhaps in the direct sense that must be done by a provincial government-and I am not sure-but this Government could very well do it simply by rescinding its ill-advised capital gains exemption of, I believe, $100,000 at present since that is considered to have done a great deal to inflate land prices in places like Metro Toronto.
There is also the question of lands in Metro. There is more than just the Downsview lands. The federal Government owns a good deal of land in different parts of Metro, which it has been selling off to the highest bidder. Metro council is instituting a reform of its own practices with its own Metro lands, namely, to give non-profit housing first refusal on Metro lands to be sold. That would not produce such a high price in all cases, but it would very directly and quickly go to meet the need of which the Hon. Member for Scarborough West has reminded us. This federal Government would not only with the Downsview land but other lands in all parts of Metro follow the same principle of giving housing, that is non-profit and affordable housing, the first chance whether it is leased or lease-to-buy as the Hon. Member suggests to co-ops. There could be a variation or several plans tried.
I would also agree roundly with the Member's suggestion of removing the federal sales tax on building materials. That would cost some money in taxes lost but I will come back to that. There was a suggestion that a mortgage exchange ought to be assisted financially by the Government. Other suggestions the Hon. Member makes would cost the Government money, and I will come now to that point.

Member has pointed out is urgently needed and much more clearly needed than nuclear powered submarines. Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to participate on Motion No. 156 put forward by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse). I commend him for his fine 10-point program. I want to say a few words on the economic situation generally and then speak
Housing
on matters of housing, particularly for our growing elderly population, especially in Metro Toronto and in my riding of Willowdale which is part of Metro.
I believe all Members will agree that a strong and stable economy is a requisite for a vigorous housing industry capable of meeting the needs of Canadians. The actions of the federal Government in managing the national economy well with low interest rates, low inflation rates and the creation of 1.3 million jobs since 1984 had a profound influence on private business and industry. In the field of housing, entrepreneurs and the Government through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation have worked together since the earliest days of the corporation in providing decent housing for Canadians, especially for low income Canadians.
This private public partnership arrangement has been of immense importance. In the early days of CMHC, the private sector developed the land and built the housing according to CMHC standards and designs that were fashioned to make homes available to the majority of Canadians. This partnership philosophy has continued through a variety of government programs, and Canada's housing industry has been a powerful ally in making these programs work effectively. The policies and programs of CMHC as an agency of the federal Government since the end of the war have been designed to encourage home ownership as well as to make housing available to those who cannot afford to buy a home, especially those in the low income groups.
The federal Government and other levels of government have undertaken the responsibility of providing affordable housing to low income Canadians. For Canadians who are able to buy homes, the private sector plays the lead role while the Government's supporting activities set the climate. An area of growing interest is the challenge we face in the coming years of housing our senior citizens, especially in Metro Toronto and in my riding of Willowdale. Before too long, one in four Canadians will be a senior. We must prepare now for that day together with private industry, the provinces and, of course, the municipalities.
It will be necessary for the private and public sectors to continue to work together to meet the challenge. We must determine how the housing for senior citizens will be financed, how regulations can be developed to assist rather than hinder innovation and how appropriate levels of support can be provided within communities. Canadians in general and seniors specifically are well housed. Many of them built their homes in days when NHA mortgages and mortgage insurance helped create 25 per cent of all the homes in Canada. They offered low downpayments on long mortgage terms.
There are about 2.7 million seniors in Canada now and they live in about 1.3 million households. Of that number, 1.1 million own their own homes. This is a group envied by those of us who have not yet graduated to the status of senior, though some of us are getting close. This group is fortunate in that 92 per cent of them own their own homes outright. They

June 14, 1988
Housing
have no mortgage whatsoever, and on average, their homes are worth precisely the same as younger households, $57,000.
Looking at the net wealth of senior-led households versus those who are not there yet, the statistics are remarkable. The total assets minus the total debts of seniors versus non-seniors is again precisely the same, $133,000. The principal difference is that seniors have more liquid assets and little or no mortgage. I do not mean to suggest that turning 65 somehow creates riches. It does not, but planning, good fortune and a wide range of other factors have brought the majority of Canadians to this happy circumstance.
As you and I know, Madam Speaker, there is a group of Canadians who are seniors but do not fit the profile of the fortunate individuals I have just described. That is where Governments have historically played the most important role, in helping those who need it most.
In housing, there is a mix of programs available to ensure that senior citizens remain integrated in the mainstream of society. Through CMHC non-profit housing, co-operatives, rent-supplement assistance and residential rehabilitation, Government helps to provide decent, affordable housing.
In the last three years, more than 15,600 social housing units have been added for seniors, bringing the total number of senior units to more than 184,000. The residential rehabilitation program is a tremendous help for elderly home owners to keep their homes in good repair. In 1986, approximately 10,500 seniors' homes were repaired under this program, using a full 30 per cent of the total budget. A special residential rehabilitation program is now available throughout the country for Canadians who become disabled. All that is required is a call to the local CMHC office.
Seniors have built a country which has created much wealth and they have also encouraged the value of compassion. It is an important legacy which we must carry into the future. There is virtue in this and there is also an imperative. Governments, private industry and concerned groups must lift their eyes to this horizon.
Can we ensure that seniors continue to live independently and in dignity? I believe we can, and this Government is taking leadership in preparing an environment that will allow new financing mechanisms, new types of housing styles and a wide range of housing options for future seniors.
CMHC already has a number of important research programs under way in preparation for this changing population. It is already looking at a wide range of styles of housing and at some very interesting new ways of financing these households. A national demonstration project of garden suites or granny flats is already under way and has met with tremendous response. It may be one option for the future.
Many elderly home owners have equity in their homes but lack the income to pay the taxes and keep them maintained.
The federal Government could assist by having property taxes and repairs deducted from income taxes for seniors, or could give a grant similar to that which the province gives on property taxes. Methods of converting this equity to cash are currently being developed by both the public and the private sectors. Reverse annuity mortgages, for example, could allow home owners to take out a significant portion of home equity and use all or part of it to buy an annuity that provides monthly payments for life.
Another option is a sale-lease-back arrangement in which an investor pays below market value for a house in return for a reduction in the rent paid by the seller. Alternatively, the seller could take back the mortgage, ensuring a steady stream of income from the payments. Arrangements such as these allow the elderly home owner to remain independent in his or her own home with security of tenure and an improved cash flow to meet taxes and maintenance needs.
Another area of investigation is the concept of made-to-convert housing which is designed to make it easy for a portion of a house to be made into an accessory apartment during different periods in the life cycle of a family. It could be an income-producing apartment or accommodation for elderly parents. We should also encourage the provinces to gradually reduce rent controls, of course.
An important step in meeting the challenge of housing for the elderly has already been taken. A major national conference will be held in Halifax this October to discuss the issue and to look for solutions.
An incentive for the housing industry to get involved in the problem is a new affordable housing achievement award. This award has been established by CMHC to give public recognition for excellence to those who bring adequate and affordable housing to Canadians.
The Government could lower the tax on building materials for affordable housing, as my friend from Scarborough West suggested. When industries move out, we could use that land for residential and commercial purposes rather than for the present commercial use only. The Government could make available leased federal surplus lands in Downsview and Vaughn, as the Hon. Member for Scarborough West has said, for various types of housing in one community, or could make mortgage deductability available for first time home owners and institute a land speculation tax to cool the market.
Housing the young and the elderly requires urgent and long term planning now. I am pleased to know that once again the private sector is working with the public sector to plan for the future.
