speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we on this side of the House also much appreciate the services provided by our pages, both ladies and gentlemen, during the past session.

Hear, hear.
However, Madam Speaker, this afternoon I was exposed to the, I must say appalling, experience of listening to the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) who gave us a picture of Canada that is completely outdated.
If we rise above the melee around Meech Lake and ignore the purely linguistic and legal considerations, we get a very clear impression of what this country is, what it should be, and what Canadians want it to be.
The Accord is the expression of a desire to reaffirm and reinforce the federal nature of our country. This is particularly necessary since for many years, the federal Government did so much to make Canadians forget the federal nature of their country. This attitude, unfortunately, led to divisions, the like of which Canada had never seen before. That is now over and done with, as Professor Kenneth McRoberts of York University said, and I quote:
The Accord will at least have the effect of establishing once and for all that
Canada is a federal State.
Professor Pierre Fortin of Laval University added:
June 14, 1988

Meech Lake is important because of its form and its substance. It fosters confidence in our efforts to build this country in the future, with eleven governments working together in the national interest, instead of just one.
Madam Speaker, I think that the vision of Canada that we see arising from Meech Lake was described far better than any one has done so far by the Hon. Lowell Murray, when he appeared before the Committee of the Whole in the other place on March 31. Senator Murray said on that occasion:
The Meech Lake Accord will help transform our Constitution [... ] into a more authentically federalist document. In so doing, the accord will not revolutionize our constitutional arrangements. Rather, it reaffirms the view of the federation held by a broad spectrum of Canadians. This view is not based on mistrust, a pugilistic vision of competition between the partners of the federation. Rather, it assumes the interdependence of the federal and provincial governments and provides a better reflection of what Canadians want Canada to be-a generous, tolerant and united society which respects diversity and which believes that governments should work cooperatively within their respective spheres of juridiction. [End of citation]
Madam Speaker, I do not believe that it is necessary to add anything at all. That is what the Accord does and the vision of Canada that it defends.
Unfortunately, not everyone shares this vision of Canada. Many prefer the pugilistic vision that Senator Murray spoke of.
And the Liberal majority in the Senate is full of those people for whom federal-provincial relations must be a no-holds-barred combat. For them, the central power is an empire; they are its gladiators and they are sworn to fight for it in the federal-provincial arena.
For the Liberal Senators, Meech Lake is the end of the empire and its replacement by a true federation.
It is not surprising under these circumstances that they applauded when the emperor visited them to inquire about their loyalty. It is not surprising that these Liberal gladiators in the Senate saluted and answered Ave Caesar, morituri te salutant or rather, if I may be allowed a free translation, " Hail, Pierre, those who would like to kill the Meech Lake Accord salute you."
But although they did everything in their power to make their vision of Canada triumph, the Senate gladiators cannot prevent Canadians from hoping for a new era of greater cooperation and respect between the two levels of government and all Canadians.
Most Canadians wants us to pass the Accord, I think, because it will bring about this vision of a Canada of cooperation and respect, of a stronger, more united Canada.
How? That is just the question I intend to answer today.
The 1987 Constitutional Accord recognizes first of all, as Senator Murray said, the interdependence of the federal and provincial governments and is based on the principle of intergovernmental cooperation.
This principle was sorely tested during the events that led to the repatriation of the Constitution in 1982. Of course, repatriation, the formula to amend the Constitution in Canada, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms are achievements worth mentioning.
Nevertheless, there is an extremely important shortcoming: every time, the decision was made without the consent of Quebecers in the National Assembly of Quebec. Quebecers did not take part in the constitutional banquet of 1982. They were kept out.
How can one help being struck by the irony of Quebec's situation in 1982, considering the history of constitutional reform in Canada over the last two decades?
As Gordon Robertson, chief constitutional advisor to the federal Government from 1975 to 1979, pointed out when he testified before the joint committee examining the Accord, it was Quebec that launched the idea of reform. After years of fruitless constitutional debate, Quebecers said no to sovereignty-association in 1980 and yes to the renewed federalism solemnly promised them by the rest of Canada.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
And instead of renewal, an agreement devised behind its back was imposed on Quebec. The Constitutional Accord helps us turn the page on the worst aspects of the 1982 deal, without compromising the major gains. It helps us reunify Canada. But the Accord does much more than help Quebec return to the Canadian fold, Madam Speaker. It sets up a framework which encourages greater cooperation between the two levels of Government. The Accord reinforces the federal nature of major national institutions such as the Supreme Court and the Senate by offering the provinces an opportunity to suggest candidates. Moreoever, the Accord paves the way to a complete reform of the Senate, and the temporary procedure for the selection of candidates reflects the will of the Government to achieve this reform. It shows that for the Federal Government, the type of Senate as it exists now has become obsolete.
In the case of the Supreme Court, the provinces' participation in the selection of judges will also help reinforce the Federal fabric. After all, it is the Supreme Court which is called upon as a last resort to rule on the interpretation of all Constitutional issues, including conflicts between the Federal and Provincial Governments. It is also the Supreme Court which must rule on the constitutional nature of Federal and Provincial legislation.
As far as the First Minister's conferences are concerned, the Accord eliminates once and for all a traditional source of conflict in Federal-Provincial relations. All of you probably know that until 1985, it was the exclusive privilege of the Prime Minister of Canada to call a First Minister's conference. The Provincial Premiers who, by the way, had been meeting for over 30 years ... even the 10 Premiers could not force the Federal Government to hold a Federal-Provincial conference. The situation was such that, before 1985, they spent more time trying to convince the Prime Minister of Canada of the necessity to call a conference on the economy than of the need to co-operate and co-ordinate the economic policy.
As you know, in 1985 in Regina, the Prime Minister and his Provincial counterparts signed a memorandum of understanding calling for five yearly economic conferences. By entrenching these economic conferences of the First Ministers, the Accord adds an element of stability in the relations between the two levels of Government. Likewise, the Accord makes it possible for the Constitutional reform to proceed in a more orderly fashion, free from the arguments which always surrounded the calling of a conference.
We find the same concern for stability in the provisions of the Accord dealing with immigration. Here, the Accord makes it possible for the various Governments to constitutionalize the Federal-Provincial Agreements to administer this shared responsibility. Free from political interference, the Constitutional Agreements will contribute to a long-term planning of Government action in this area. It is also the Accord which will ensure the stability without overlooking the need to protect national interests efficiently.
Under the Accord, it is the responsibility of the Parliament of Canada to set "national standards and objectives relating to immigration or aliens including any provision that establishes general classes of immigrants or relates to levels of immigration for Canada or that prescribes classes of individuals who are inadmissible into Canada". The Federal supremacy in the area of immigration is therefore secured.
Madam Speaker, there is another factor which contributes to clearing up relations between governments and strengthening the Canadian federation, namely the provisions concerning the power to spend. This power of Parliament will be maintained and, for the first time, explicitly acknowledged in the Constitution. It seems to me that is one of the factors which has been ignored by the critics of the accord.
Sometimes these people would have us believe that the provinces are forced to join shared cost programs set up by the federal Government in fields under exclusive provincial jurisdiction. Of course this idea is akin to the vision some people have of Canada.
Whether you like it or not, the provinces never did have to accept such programs.
The integrity of provincial jurisdiction is acknowledged in the accord, guaranteeing as it does fair compensation for provinces whose programs are tailored to the specific needs of the people and compatible with the national objectives.
According to Queen's University Intergovernmental Relations Institute Director Peter Leslie, this arrangement might prove to be very good for

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Canadians, both as taxpayers and as people on the receiving end of various programs.
He also stressed that the provinces will be in a position to find new solutions to problems which are common to most Canadians, and they will be urged to set up the mechanisms required to reach the national objectives as effectively as possible.
For their part, the joint committee members came to the conclusion that, in fields under exclusive provincial authority, shared-cost national programs can still be negotiated to the benefit of both the federal Government and the provincial Governments, and that basically the proposed change will reaffirm the importance of negotiations. In other words, the accord guarantees that from the outset the federal Government will be inclined to proceed through cooperation and negotiation rather than make unilateral attempts to force the provinces to accept rigid programs. Again this goes to show that after the accord the Constitution will be more respectful of our federal character.
Madam Speaker, this brings me to the conclusion that the constitutional accord strengthens the Canadian federation in two ways.
First it enables Quebec unashamedly to get back to the job of building the Canadian nation.
Second, it ensures that the federal Government and the provinces will make a joint effort in a spirit of co-operation rather than confrontation.
Thanks to the accord we will be united rather than divided in our quest for better ways to respond to the challenges of tomorrow.
Certain critics seem to have quite simply chosen the old approach: seek confrontation and send the country down the warpath.
As I see it, Robert Stanfield aptly summed up the situation when he appeared before the Senate committee and said: "Some people do wonder what the Government and the Canadian Parliament are getting out of the accord. Well, among a few other things, the perspective of leading a united country where people fully respect one another rather than a country slowly moving towards self-destruction."
Madam Speaker, that is a challenging undertaking which all Members can proudly support. I hope they will vote in favour of the resolution.

I wish to congratulate my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary, on her remarks this evening and to tell her that I whole-heartedly agree with them. As she is aware, I am a whole-hearted supporter of the Meech Lake Accord. Inclusive in that is the provisions of the Accord which incorporate the concept of a distinct society. My own personal belief is that the Accord merely puts on paper what has been and has always been a part of Canadian society ever since our country started and, for that matter, for hundreds of years before there was a formal country of Canada.
I know that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is aware of concerns that have been voiced by approximately one-third of Canadians whose origin is neither French nor English but come from a variety of minority cultures and backgrounds that make up our great country. In my own constituency there are over 70 different cultures and ethnic groups. On many occasions they have voiced to me their concerns with respect to the fact that there is no mention in the Meech Lake Accord of these other ethnic and cultural communities and that they are concerned that this, in some way, may take away from their rights.
Earlier today we heard a comment from another Member of the House to the effect that they voiced that concern, in that they feel that perhaps the Meech Lake Accord overrides the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and takes away some of the rights enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
That concern is also reflected in some of the amendments put forward in the House. The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) deals with that concern in one of his amendments. It is also reflected in the amendment put forth by the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Roman), that somehow or other the concept of a distinct society for French Canadians overrides the rights of the multicultural communities of Canada.
As you and the Parliamentary Secretary know, Madam Speaker, Section 27 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides that the Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians. That provision relates to Section 1 which says that the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it.
In my view, in no way is there any amendment to that Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in no way is the concept of a multicultural Canada overridden by the Meech Lake Accord.
I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if she and the Government agree that the rights of various multicultural communities as set out in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms are in no way overridden by the Meech Lake Accord and in fact remain as a solid basis of the rights and freedoms and privileges of all our minority groups as citizens of Canada?
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first like to say that the question asked by my colleague, and especially his preamble, do reveal how much he appreciates the Meech Lake Accord. Concerning minority rights, I think that somewhere in my speech mention was made of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That is a vested right for Canadian society and it's for keeps.
The reference in the Meech Lake Accord to a dictinct society means a situation peculiar to Quebec. The idea is not to curtail the rights and freedoms of others, but to recognize that Quebec lives in a situation all of its own. As far as the government and I are concerned, there was never any question of denying other groups any particular right or freedom. To my mind, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms will prevail for Canada's multicultural groups.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. [Translation]

Madam Speaker, as a Quebecker, I have always considered it essential for the future of our country that Quebec be a major, full fledged partner in

*
June 14, 1988

the Canadian federation and that it have at its disposal the essential tools for development.
In 1980, when the referendum on sovereignty-association took place, a majority of Quebecers said yes to Canada and to constitutional reform. That was the signal which set in motion the process of constitutional reform and renewal.
However, since patriation, we have all deeply felt Quebec's absence and it was imperative to find a respectable way to bring Quebec back into the constitutional fold.
Although I feel that Meech Lake is far from perfect, Madam Speaker, I find it an acceptable compromise to pull Quebec out of constitutional isolation.
It fits our venerable constitution to the realities of the times.
I contend that this debate can be rightfully termed fundamental to the future of Canada. Furthermore, it concerns the Constitution, the uppermost document in our legislative framework.
For some, of course, Quebec should be a province like the others. In their view, any concession to Quebec opens the door to separatism. Their vision of Canada is static and they are neither able to sense the ever evolving reality of our country nor to adapt to it.
Quebec wants certain guarantees with regard to its distinctiveness, to the growth of its population, to its participation in federal institutions, to its full freedom to use the legislative powers granted to Quebec under the Constitutional Act of 1867.
History has shown clearly that there can be no building of Canada without Quebec and that the men and women of Quebec must have their place in life and institutions of this country. In fact, the distinct character of Quebec is a fundamental aspect of Canadian federalism.
The role of the Canadian Government is not a passive one. It has the full right and responsibility to protect and promote the French fact not only here in Canada, but also abroad.
It must constantly define and attune that responsibility in light of changing situations and greater challenges as the country evolves.
Such is the vision that guides us today in this debate on the Meech Lake Agreement.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I was among those who supported the motion the first time and I now reiterate my support today.
As for the distinct society concept, Madam Speaker, Quebec's distinct identity is not new. Quebec is the main wellspring of the Francophone community's linguistic and cultural energy and inspiration and, as Senator Eugene Forsey pointed out, Quebec is the citadel of French in Canada.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
It is a fact that Quebec is different from the other provinces. Its differences lie in its history, language and Civil Code, its origins, feelings and politics.
Madam Speaker, Meech Lake is not unique in recognizing Quebec as a distinct society. The Constitution Act, 1867, created a federal rather than a Unitarian State, in order to respect and protect the distinct society established within the territory of the Province of Quebec.
Madam Speaker, that is a historic fact, even if the Constitution Act, 1867, does not say so specifically. However, many sections of our Constitution recognize the distinctiveness of Quebec. Section 133 of the Constitution Act, 1867, provides guarantees for the use of French and English before federal courts, the courts in Quebec and in the National Assembly. These guarantees are not found among the other founding provinces. Section 94 of the Constitution Act, 1867, provides that the Parliament of Canada may make provision for the uniformity of all and any of the laws relative to property and civil rights. This section applies to only three of the four founding provinces, namely Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
From the outset, the Fathers of Confederation decided that Quebec's Civil Code and Code of Civil Procedure would remain distinct from the Common Law practised in the other provinces. That is, in fact, what happened.
Madam Speaker, although the Constitution recognizes provincial equality, this equality is not a major consideration, because on the other hand, the Constitution provides that on historic and geographic grounds, treatment may differ from province to province. As the Joint Committee pointed out, the principle of provincial equality is an important one, but it should not be allowed to stand in the way of the development of a large part of our country and penalize its population. In 1979, the members of the Pepin-Robarts Commission, in referring to Quebec's distinctiveness, pointed out that in a society in transition, politics take on a new meaning. Because of these aspects, Quebec is a society, it is a province and it is the citadel of the French Canadian people. So there is nothing revolutionary, in this day and age, about the constitutional and exclusive recognition of Quebec as a distinct society.
I don't think Quebec will turn inwards or that the Accord will lead to the two-nation or two-Canadas concept. The existence of a political society does not necessarily lead to the creation of an independent State. Quebecers don't want to live in a ghetto. It is possible to have a pluralistic State. The distinct society concept will not affect bilingualism. On the contrary, the Official Languages Act remains in effect. The protection afforded by the Constitution to official language minorities across the country is in no way diminished, and every province still has the option of declaring itself officially bilingual. Finally, Meech Lake obliges governments to preserve Canada's linguistic duality.

Constitution Amendment, 1987
As far as immigration is concerned, Madam Speaker, Section 95 of the Constitution Act, 1867, provides for concurrent powers, with federal paramountcy should provincial legislation not be compatible with federal statutes.
Sections 95 (a) to 95 (e) in the Meech Lake Accord which deal with immigration are, in fact, a constitutional rendering of the Cullen-Couture Agreement that will provide Quebec with a sound basis for claiming the right to select prospective immigrants. The Accord guarantees that within the annual immigration quota set by the federal Government for all of Canada, Quebec will have a number of immigrants, including refugees, proportional to its share of the population and, for demographic reasons, it can exceed its immigration quota by 5 per cent.
We cannot help but be pleased with this provision. All the provinces may avail themselves of it, but I believe that especially for Quebec, which faces a serious problem due to a low birth rate, this provision will have major beneficial effects because it will help Quebec protect its particular linguistic character.
As regards the Supreme Court, creation of the Supreme Court of Canada does not go back to Confederation. The Judiciary Committee of the Privy Council of Great Britain at that time took the place of a court of appeal for all British colonies and the obligation to apply to it was maintained even after Confederation. The 1867 Constitution Act provided for the creation of an appeal court for Canada.
Section 101 of this Act authorized the federal Parliament to adopt measures to create, maintain and organize a general appeal court for Canada. The court was created by an Act of Parliament in 1878 and therefore Parliament could amend it by a federal law.
In 1949, the federal Parliament abolished the right of appeal to the Privy Council and in 1975, it required appellants to obtain authorization to do so, thus giving the Supreme Court effective control over the cases it would hear.
I am glad that paragraphs 101(a) and 101(e) of the Meech Lake Accord enshrine the Supreme Court in the Constitution.
This is even more important because since the Charter in 1982, the Supreme Court influences the evolution of Canadian society as never before. We need only refer to the latest decision on abortion to see what an effect the Supreme Court can have on the Canadian people.
Such a unique court must be enshrined in the Constitution. Furthermore, reports on the Constitution presented over the years are unanimous on this point.
Quebec's civil law legal system is distinct from the other provinces.
It was necessary to guarantee the civil law component in the Constitution. Quebec judges are trained in civil law and
June 14, 1988
practise in French. Their presence is therefore crucial in civil law cases and those pleaded in French.
As for constitutional conferences, Madam Speaker, the Accord also has a provision requiring that a conference of First Ministers on the Constitution be held at least every year, the first one to be held within 12 months of the proclamation of the present constitutional amendment, not later than the end of 1988. The following items on the agenda are expected to be written into the Constitution: Senate reform, roles and responsibilities in fisheries, as well as any other question on which agreement is reached.
But I am wondering: Why did the Canadian Government include none of the matters of concern to it in the agenda of the First Ministers' Annual Conferences on the Constitution. It should have included among other things a provision to abolish the nothwithstanding clause, i.e. Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, with the aim to provide all Canadians with the most complete protection of their rights and freedoms. Also, it could have proposed an amendment to Section 23 of the 1982 Constitutional Act to provide official language minorities with control and management of their publicly supported educational institutions and also to delete the words "where the number so warrants" in Section 23, while recognizing that Section 1 of the Constitutional Act, 1982 applies to Section 23.
Concerning the spending power, Madam Speaker, it has been there for a good number of years. Mr. Pierre E. Trudeau defined that power as the power of Parliament to pay monies to individuals, organizations or governments for purposes which do not necessarily fall within the legislative power of the Parliament of Canada. That power was not provided for in the 1867 Constitution. It is now entrenched in Clause 106A of the Meech Lake Agreement. But the wording is ambiguous. I am thinking for instance to the terms "shared-cost program" and "national objectives".
As pointed out by Mr. John Whyte, the Dean of Queen's University law school, during the Joint Committee's hearings, the uncertainty as to the eligibility to compensation and its related conditions apparently constitute a very strong disincentive for the Canadian Government to engage into certain expenditures related to social social programs. That uncertainty as to eligibility to compensation is a disincentive because it is impossible to know two things: first, the amount of compensation to be paid, that is compensation for which the Canadian Government will be given no credit and for which it cannot be held responsible either. And second, the attainability of the project objectives because no one can say how many provinces will decide, when a project is announced, to bring their own measures in line with the national objectives.
Will that prevent us from having national programs? Does that mean that from now on it will be impossible to establish a national childcare program? What about the guaranteed annual income and medicare? Would unemployment insurance
June 14, 1988

have been impossible under the Accord agreed to by the First Ministers?
Will the possibility of opting out of programs with compensation undermine the quality and uniformity of services throughout Canada? Who will set national goals?
As for the Senate, the amending formula will require from now on the unanimous consent of the provinces. It is too strict even with regard to federal institutions. Isn't there a danger of eventually being trapped within the Constitution? Will Senate reform come to pass? Will we finally see a Senate elected according to the formula adopted by the Prime Minister and his provincial counterparts? A reform of the Upper House is highly desirable, but the proposed amending formula is a strait jacket. It will make it very difficult.
And now, Madam Speaker, I would like to go somewhat against what my colleague from Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif) said when she seemed to hold the Senate responsible for holding up the ratification of the Lake Meech Accord. As for me, I say that we must live with our institutions and that, as long as they are not changed, we will continue to respect them and each other. It is only by respecting each other that we will be able to make the changes required to get the political instruments we need to go forward and give Canadians the best Government and the best political system in the world.
Madam Speaker, we know from experience how hard it is to amend the Constitution. The Meech lake Accord is more than just an agreement. It is a unanimous agreement which cannot be dismissed out of hand. This unanimity weighs heavily on all Canadians. It means the pride of belonging to a nation which, despite its regional disparities, succeeds in creating harmony from coast to coast. As Mr. Whyte told the Joint Committee: Those who continue to oppose the 1987 Accord, after it has been accepted and approved by Quebec, must realize that they are not only working against conditions for reconciliation, but also attacking an historic document of reconciliation which will clearly have a long term negative impact on Canada. The deficiencies of the Accord would have to be very serious and have highly probable consequences and I don't think it is the case, Madam Speaker.
This time, Canada and Quebec must not miss the boat, although a few riders could be added on later. There will always be time to correct the flaws in the Accord, Madam Speaker. We are at a privileged juncture. Let us say yes to Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin) for his interesting speech and especially for his interest in Quebec. Madam Speaker, I was thrilled with the first part of his speech, but the conclusion of his statement leaves me somewhat confused, because there he begins to quote and list the weaknesses that might be found in the Meech Lake Agreement, which was unanimous, as he rightly mentioned, and
Constitution Amendment, 1987
because we have certain institutions, he must respect their decisions. I have great difficulty understanding the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice, Madam Speaker, because on the one hand, he says that we must absolutely respect the Agreement as it is, in the interests of Quebec, and he is prepared to defend Quebec's interests particularly. On the other hand, he says that we must respect the decision of the other place, a majority of whose members belong to his party, Madam Speaker.
We know very well that the Senate has a Liberal majority. So how come those Senators decided not to accept a decision of the House of Commons, accepted by all three parties and the Canadian people so that Quebec can return to the constitutional family and they decided for all sorts of reasons that it is not necessary, it is not important, because it is not a perfect agreement? We never claimed to have a perfect agreement. How can you amend a text that you don't even have, something that does not even exist? How can the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice accept the decision of his colleagues, of his caucus, of the Liberal Senators, to say no to Quebec once again and at the same time say, "Yes, Madam Speaker, I voted for the Meech Lake Agreement and I intend to continue to do so"? How can they split their decision? How can they divide their interest for Quebec into sentimental and political categories?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Chambly (Mr. Grise) for giving me this opportunity to say that, in this case, respect is a matter of respecting our parliamentary institutions that make decisions on the basis of the texts they receive or the bills submitted to them by the House and which may require improvements or amendments or changes to make these bills acceptable.
If I may make a comparison between the texts we send to the other place and the Government's decision to ask us to sit this summer, we must abide by the decision even if we disagree with the Government's proposal, since we will have to bow to the will of the majority, and the same applies to the amendments proposed by the Senate which will probably be rejected by the Government's majority when the Senate has finished its review.
Madam Speaker, I may also inform the Hon. Member that I always agreed with Meech Lake as a way to bring Quebec back in the Canadian constitutional family, but I am also in favour of adopting certain amendments that were unfortunately rejected by the Government majority. Personally, I believe that the proposals made by the Opposition included amendments that would have been acceptable to Canadians as a whole, especially to Native people and other groups that may feel somewhat frustrated by the Accord as it stands today. I look favourably on Meech Lake because of the prospect of a second round of negotiations that will give us an opportunity to correct the weaknesses of the initial document. That is why I am in favour of Meech Lake and why I pointed out the weaknesses of the present version, and I hope that the second

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
round will give us a chance to remedy those weaknesses and make the Accord responsive to the wishes of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to say a few words in this debate in support of the Meech Lake Accord. I am also very proud to say that all three political Parties are in support of the Meech Lake Accord.

I have been a Member of this House since 1968. In fact, it will be twenty years a little less than two weeks from now, and I remember very clearly when the referendum was held in Quebec eight years ago. At the time, Quebecers said yes to Canada and now it is time for Canada to say yes to Quebec.

In the last 25 or 30 years, this country has spent an awful lot of time and political energy on the constitutional issue. We have talked about this issue month after month, year after year, at various conferences around this country. Now, for the very first time in the last 30 years, we have unanimous agreement on a constitutional Accord for Canada that is signed by all 10 premiers, including the Premier of Quebec.
For me as a Canadian from western Canada, perhaps the most moving moment of the constitutional debate surrounding Meech Lake was when the Premier of the Province of Quebec, Robert Bourassa, sat at that table and put his signature on the Accord with the other Premiers of Canada and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

Madam Speaker, it was in my view an historic moment for all of Canada, for all Canadian men and women, since we have now spent the last 25 or 30 years in constitutional debate.
And I do remember the last 25 or 30 years. At first I was only a young lad in Saskatchewan but I have vivid memories of the quiet revolution in Quebec. I clearly recollect the great quiet revolution headed by Jean Lesage, the former liberal premier of Quebec, and his ministers, Rene Levesque, Gerin-Lajoie and many others who were there at the time of the quiet revolution in Quebec.
Afterwards, there was an evolution with Daniel Johnson as leader of the Union Rationale and I recall very well his campaign slogan or "Egalite ou independance". He won his election campaign on that slogan, on that platform.
Madam Speaker, after that I was elected in 1968 and I was here facing Prime Minister Trudeau and others, before the Victoria Conference, held in 1971. And as I remember very well, an agreement was signed in Victoria, in June I believe, by the Prime Minister of Canada and ten provincial Premiers, including also Premier Bourassa of Quebec.
After a few days however, Mr. Bourassa changed his mind, he was won over by many Quebecers such as Claude Ryan
and others and he came back on his position. That was the end of the Victoria Agreement of 1971.
Madam Speaker, after that, as you well know, there came November 15 1976, the election of the Parti Quebecois, the election of Rene Levesque and his crusade for independence and sovereignty-association and the May 1980 referendum.
After that, there was Meech Lake last year. And that is how the constitutional debate has evolved, not only for Quebecers but for all Canadians.
Quebec has been holding out its hand and saying: "Look, we have signed a document, we are ready to come into the Canadian constitutional family, here is a piece of paper, come and sign it with us and approve it with us". We must accept that gesture. We must not at this time fail to reach out to Quebec. We must seize the historic moment and sign the Meech Lake Accord.
I was one of the Members who sat last summer on the special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons during July and August hearing witness after witness. I want to refer to the words of Madam Chaput-Rolland which were some of the most moving words we heard about the necessity of seizing this historic opportunity and ensuring that we pass a resolution in this House and all across the country in favour of the Meech Lake Accord. The special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons was co-chaired by Senator Tremblay and the Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer). I quote from the report at page 139. Madam Chaput-Rolland said:
I think none outside Quebec knew the reality of the referendum. I travelled throughout Canada, about a few months after. It was all over, eh? Good. It was not exactly all over. Families against families, towns against towns, fathers and mothers not speaking to their children.
During the Referendum we spoke with thousands of Quebecers. Women wanted to leave to their children a country as big as the one they had received from their father. That was mainly the article that reached the heart, because you are right: in this country if we put a little more heart into what we are doing, maybe we would be aware of the hurt we inflict on others.
And then we came home. We went back to the National Assembly, back to our villages, back to our houses, back to the friends that were no more friends; they were on the "yes", we were on the "no". It was not a picnic, it was not a social gathering, it was not a think-tank, it was a battle between brothers, a dangerous, divisive battle, and we still feel it. It was not 100 years ago, it was seven years ago that we lived that referendum.
English Canada could not care less one month after, and it stung me and it stung all of us who fought so hard to remain in Canada and to find ourselves outside of Canada. You know, it was a very dramatic gesture when Mr. Levesque put the flag of Quebec at half mast on the day you were all celebrating here. But our hearts were at half mast too that day, because we were out of a country we had chosen to remain.
So the Accord of Meech Lake brought us something "incroyable" as a gesture of friendship.
It is very important that we all listen to the words of the Madam Chaput-Rolland. She was on the Robarts-Pepin Commission on National Unity and is a very wise and
June 14, 1988

intelligent Quebecer. She goes on to give English speaking Canada a warning. She says:
But surely by now, surely, you all know that if Meech is to fail for whatever reason, there can be no more negotiations, no more justifications. If Quebec is once again to realize that it is more difficult to opt in Canada than to stay out of Canada, then surely, you know that the roads of tomorrow can only lead to another form of independence, but this time not chosen by any political party in Quebec, maybe chosen and imposed on Quebec outside Quebec.
[ Translation]
Madam Speaker, that is what Mrs. Chaput-Rolland said when she testified before our Special Committee on the Constitution last year.

I accept her warning that if we do not seize this opportunity and accept the Meech Lake Accord as it is we may have some extremely divisive and troubled times ahead in terms of keeping this great country of ours unified.
Therefore, my first point is that we must accept this historic opportunity. My second point is that I believe the Meech Lake Accord offers this country a new vision of co-operative federalism, a vision of national conciliation, of reconciliation that recognizes the great diversity of this country; on one hand a strong federal Government and on the other hand provinces that are treated as equals and respected in their own domains of jurisdiction.
That vision of co-operative federalism is not a new vision in this country. I remember very well the 1960s when Mr. Pearson talked a lot about co-operative federalism and negotiated the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan, recognizing that Quebec was different and unique and wanted to handle its own affairs in terms of a pension. Mr. Pearson was moving with the co-operation of both opposition Parties in those days.
Tommy Douglas talked an awful lot in those days of cooperative federalism. In Quebec he had with him Robert Cliche, a tremendous Quebecer who talked about the uniqueness of Quebec and the need for a vision of a co-operative federalist society in Canada. In the Conservative Party in those days there was Robert Stanfield, another great Canadian who recognized the importance and value of diversity in this country and the need for co-operative federalism.
In 1968 Pierre Trudeau was elected. Even though I have tremendous respect for Pierre Trudeau in many areas such as the Official Languages Act, the Charter of Rights, his intelligence, his frankness, and his honesty in terms of conducting public affairs, the one area in which I violently disagree with his philosophy, dream, and vision is in how he saw Canada in terms of federalism.
I think that in that particular area Trudeau set this country back by 20 years. We are now, with the Meech Lake Accord, where Pearson, Douglas, Stanfield, Robert Cliche, and all those other people were in the late 1960s. We had a national consensus then. Since then we have had 20 years of confrontation, 20 years of centralism which was too rigid, and 20 years
Constitution Amendment, 1987
of inflexibility in terms of federalism. Now we are back into an era where this country was 20 years ago. That is another reason why I support the Accord that is before us today.
This afternoon we heard from the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston). Although I respect the gentleman, as an Hon. Member opposite said, it was a voice from the past. He spoke of a Canada of yesterday. It is a Canada of yesterday that all three political Parties in this country reject.
I can say that I am proud to see a Leader of the Liberal Party get up and reject that voice of the past and the philosophy of yesterday when he, along with my Leader and the Prime Minister spoke about a co-operative federalism and a Canada that is flexible and built on diversity, with a strong federal Government and provinces that are created equally.
In addition to the historic opportunity and co-operative federalism that the Meech Lake Accord embraces, there are a number of other reasons why I believe this Accord is positive for all Canadians, regardless of where we live.
The third reason is the distinct society. The clause recognizes Quebec as a distinct society within Canada, and I stress that it is within Canada.

Saskatchewan, where I come from, is not a province with a large French-speaking community since only 5 or 6 per cent of the population speak that language. Nevertheless I think it is important to recognize that Quebec constitutes a society different from the rest of Canada. It is not a province like the others. It must have a different status and, as I said, that fact was recognized long ago by Mr. Pearson and his Liberal Government in the 1960s, by Mr. Stanfield when he was leader of the Progressive Conservative Party and leader of the Opposition here in the House, as well as by Messrs. Tommy Douglas and David Lewis as national NDP leaders and Mr. Robert Cliche as NDP leader in Quebec in the 1960s.
And I remember very well the national consensus among the three political parties on issues relating to Quebec and its reality. Quebec is different from the other provinces. I also support the Meech Lake Accord because it recognizes Quebec's distinct society and that reality is now acknowledged in the Canadian Constitution.

The fourth reason why I support the Accord is the amending formula itself. I come from a small province, with some one million people or about 4 per cent of the population of Canada. We maintain the same amending formula that there was before, in most cases. In order for constitutional amendment, the requirement is that the federal Parliament pass the resolution and seven provinces, representing 50 per cent of the population of Canada, also approve.

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
That recognizes the equality of the provinces in Canada and recognizes that in a federal state, Prince Edward Island is equal to Quebec, is equal to Ontario, that Saskatchewan is equal to Newfoundland. In a federal state, all provinces must be recognized as equal on the one hand, while on the other hand, there must be some recognition of the population difference. Our amending formula states that we need seven provinces, but those seven provinces must represent 50 per cent of the population of Canada.
Every federal state in the world of which I am aware has a similar amending formula and recognition of the equality of states. For example, in the United States there are two senators per state, whether it is Rhode Island, California, Maine or New York. That equality is recognized in this amending formula.
The fifth reason why I support the Accord is the spending power. My friend, the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), already stated that for the first time in Canadian history the Constitution will refer to national objectives, where federal spending power can be used in terms of national objectives. As she pointed out, Mr. Pearson had attempted this many times in the 1960s without success. For the first time, this will be reflected in the Constitution of Canada as a result of Meech Lake.
The sixth reason why I support the Accord is that it recognizes that this country is a federal state through the way Supreme Court Justices will be appointed in this country. Until now, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice or both would unilaterally appoint a justice of the Supreme Court. While a practice had built up whereby provinces were consulted, bar associations were consulted and there was a mechanism for consultation to take place, the federal Government ultimately would unilaterally appoint a justice of the Supreme Court.
According to the Meech Lake agreement, the federal Government can choose from a list that is submitted by the provinces. In other words, there is a co-appointment of the justice of the Supreme Court. I believe that is only proper in a federal state. The Supreme Court is not solely the instrument of the federal court but is in Canada as the highest court of our land which often must mediate between a federal government and a provincial government in disputes. My Party and I wholeheartedly endorse the approach we see in the Meech Lake Accord.
I have stated the reasons why we support the many positive aspects of the Accord. Our Party has suggested for some time that there are some things missing from the Meech Lake Accord. My Leader mentioned today that there is a lack of fairness for northern Canadians, a lack of fairness for women in this country and a lack of fairness for the aboriginal people of Canada.
Last summer, when we were writing this report to present to the Parliament of Canada, our Party, including myself and the Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam,	included
addendum B which is found at page 155 of the special joint report. At that time we suggested that the Prime Minister and the premiers go back to the table to try to reach a consensus and clear up at least three areas that are not fair for many Canadians.
The first area of unfairness is the way the Meech Lake Accord unjustly treats the people of northern Canada. The change in the amending formula requires unanimity for the creation of new provinces. That is not fair. My province came into Confederation in 1905 through negotiation between the province and Ottawa. Newfoundland came in in 1949 in a similar fashion, as did Manitoba, British Columbia and Alberta. Suddenly, unanimity is required for the creation of new provinces. That is unfair to the people of the Yukon and Northwest Territories and I urge First Ministers to go back and renegotiate an Accord to include an element of fairness for the creation of new provinces. I believe that would have the support of all Members of the House.
The same applies for the appointment of Supreme Court justices. The provinces will submit lists, but what about the Northwest Territories and the Yukon? They are not provinces and there is no mention in the Accord about the territories. Both territories are treated as second class citizens.
Section 28 of the Charter of Rights talks about equality rights for women in this country. That should be included in Clause 16 of the Meech Lake Accord so that it is very clear there is no discrimination whatsoever based on gender.
Third, there must be an element of fairness in the Accord for the aboriginal people of Canada. Why not do what Pierre Trudeau did in 1981, when he held a conference with all the premiers to discuss women's rights in this country? They eventually agreed, after much pressure, to insert rights for women of Canada in the constitutional agreement at that time. Why not try the same thing in these three areas? If it fails, so be it, but if not, it will improve the Accord and make it much better for all Canadians.
In conclusion, we also suggest that the Constitution should be expanded in the future to recognize not only the duality of this country as a fundamental characteristic of Canada, but recognize the multicultural and ethnocultural reality as a fundamental characteristic of Canada. There must be Charter review to do something about Section 33 in particular as it pertains to minorities and visible minorities.
Finally, I believe we should democratize the process in the future, as suggested by the committee, so that more Canadians are involved in the process of constitutional change.

Madam Speaker, I would like to refer to a comment made by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). During his remarks he referred to the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) as being a voice from the past. I would like to put to him, as I
June 14, 1988

pointed out earlier in this House, that there are two competing visions of Canada at play here, both equally legitimate. One holds that Canada is greater than the sum of its parts, that there has to be some way for the national interest to find its expression through our federal and national institutions. The other vision is that we owe our allegiance, perhaps, to the provinces or regions from which we come. These are two visions and I think they are equally legitimate. I think it is wrong to refer to the vision I hold as being a vision from the past.
I would also put to the Hon. Member that perhaps there is a curious intergenerational issue at play. I feel many young Canadians and many young Quebecers do not have the same kind of preoccupations held by the Premier of Quebec today. When the Hon. Member talks about voices from the past, I can only tell him that I am happy that the Liberal Party has been the only Party which has focused this debate. The focus on the Meech Lake Agreement has been in the Liberal Party. It had to take place somewhere, and I am glad it has been within our Party. Canadians clearly are concerned. A Gallup Poll in April indicated that support for the agreement had dropped by half in the last year. I am glad there are young Canadians and young Quebecers out there. I could name someone like Timothy Danson, a lawyer in Toronto, the son of a former Cabinet Minister, and John Kaplan, the son of our former Solicitor General. I read in the paper a few weeks ago John Kaplan was travelling throughout the country this summer on a campaign against the Meech Lake Agreement. He says he has agreed to disagree with his father on this particular issue.

1 could speak about Michel Simard, a young Quebecer who shares our vision of this country.

I could speak about a young Canadian of Greek origin. He was born in Canada but his parents came from Greece. His name is Bill Mavridis. He wrote a letter to the editor a couple of weeks ago expressing his concerns and opposition to this agreement. These are all young people probably under 30 years of age. I do not regard them as voices from the past.
All I can say is that the Hon. Member's Party is out of step with the times and his Party will pay for it eventually.

Madam Speaker, the question was one about two competing visions. I do not really think there are two competing visions. I think there is a great national consensus of three Parties. I ask my friend in the Liberal Party to look at his own Leader's speech today and understand and realize how most members of the Liberal Party are going to vote when it comes to the Meech Lake Accord.
He should also look at the history of his own political Party. If I remember its history correctly, there was former Prime Minister Laurier, one of the great leaders of the Liberal Party, who said: "You get unity through diversity". He did not mean
Constitution Amendment, 1987
great centralization and everything being controlled by Ottawa. Lester Pearson in the 1960s was one of the fathers of the whole philosophy of co-operative federalism. It was Mr. Pearson who brought in the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan and who recognized the uniqueness of Quebec and the diversity of this country. It was the Liberal Cabinet of that day that moved in unison along with the country toward recognizing the vision of the country we now have with the Meech Lake Accord.
It was the Opposition of that day, led by people like Bob Stanfield, who also recognized that Quebec was unique and different and that the country was diverse. It recognized that our country was going to grow strong by realizing its diversity and building upon it. It was the New Democratic Party led by Tommy Douglas and great people like David Lewis who also supported that vision in the 1960s. We had a consensus in those days that Quebec was unique, different and distinct as a society. We realized we had to build this country on a foundation of co-operative federalism, that there was diversity and we needed flexibility and harmony, that we would achieve it through this kind of approach.
Then there was Pierre Trudeau, and I suggest rather than having a different vision, Trudeau was an aberration who set back national reconciliation and nation building in terms of the Constitution of this country by 20 years. In 1988, we are back in 1968 in terms of a national consensus. Today, to his credit, the Right Hon. Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner) is back where Pearson, Laurier and the Liberals were in the 1960s. Mr. Turner is there now with a majority of people in his Liberal Party. Sure, there are some voices from the past like the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount but Mr. Turner knows where Canada is in terms of nation building and how he wants to organize this great federal state of ours. He knows because that is where his Party was back in the 1950s and 1960s. That is where the CCF was, that is where the New Democratic Party was, and that is where we are today. I am proud because of those reasons that we once again have this national unity in terms of how we approach this country.
I am also proud to say that after Quebec ratified this Accord in a resolution of the Quebec National Assembly-

If I remember correctly, it was in July that the Quebec legislature ratified the Constitutional Accord.

After that, the first province that did so was the Province of Saskatchewan, with the support of all three Parties in that province, including the Leader of the Liberal Party. I am very pleased to see this kind of opening up toward Quebec and toward a vision of co-operative federalism in western Canada, and indeed, all across this great country of ours. Rather than two visions, I think we have some kind of a throw back to the past with Pierre Trudeau, Marc Lalonde, Jimmy Coutts and Keith Davey. Once we go beyond that circle, we are really scrambling to find a few more names.

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987

As I was saying in my remarks to the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), Madam Speaker, I repeat that the House was presented with two different visions of Canada, both legitimate. One vision...

And that is that Canada is greater than the sum of its parts. [Translation]
You will admit that this is not easy to say in French. The other vision is that our loyalty is first and foremost to the provinces or regions we live in. Personally, I feel that there should be a way for national interests to be expressed in a federation. We must find a way for the national interests to be reflected in our institutions, failing that we might witness the break up of our country not because the men and women sitting here in the Canadian Parliament are wiser, but simply because we have been elected to promote the national interests.
The Provincial Governments and legislatures have a more restricted mandate, which is to promote the wellbeing of their province, something which, you will certainly admit, is sometimes quite different from the wellbeing of the country as a whole.
Over the past six months, we have seen just to what extent the Meech Lake Accord is detrimental to the national interest and to what extent the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has failed to understand where the national interest of Canada really lies.
Let us have a look at the debate on the linguistic rights of Francophones in Saskatchewan. Let us remember the remarks which the Prime Minister made-I do not have the exact quote-when he stated that if the linguistic rights of minorities were not well protected, it is because the minorities had been overlooked in 1981 by the previous Government. The Prime Minister has also stated in the House, and I quote: "The only way to protect the linguistic rights of minorities in Canada is to include guarantees to that effect in the Constitution".
With all due respect, Madam Speaker, I will say that the Prime Minister is trying to rewrite history. We are aware that the Prime Minister had held several positions and now he would like to play the part of an historian. I feel that Canadians will seek elsewhere an assessment of history.
I feel that the history of our country can be defined as a constant effort to ensure equality among all Canadians. The Prime Minister and the Meech Lake Accord have broken with this tradition. Those who want to have a fair assessment of history should refer to the statement made by former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau when he appeared before the Senate on March 30th at which time he reminded us of the efforts of such persons as Henri Bourassa to protect the rights of Francophones in Western Canada: "The purpose was to make sure that Francophone and Anglophone Canadians felt at
home everywhere in Canada". To achieve this, the Constitution of 1867 included such provisions are Section 133 and Section 93.
In the 1960's, the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission described the linguistic guarantees which I have just mentioned and which dated back to 1867 as pre-concepts of equality. The commission was seeking equality and increased rights and mention was made in its recommendations about what had to be done for the Federal Government and even the provinces to consider Francophones and Anglophones as equals. With respect to employment opportunities, the courts and services offered by federal Government agencies like the CBC or Air Canada, there is no need to go over all the details of major advances made as a result of work done by the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission and of the Official Languages Act of 1969.
The 1982 Charter of Rights enshrined a number of these gains in our Constitution, and we went one step further by including minority language educational rights in Section 23 of the Charter of Rights.
As you can see, Madam Speaker, for 120 years or since 1867 we have been trying to widen, more clearly define and guarantee the rights of all Canadians. That was the work of the Fathers of Confederation. That was the goal of Henri Bourassa, that was the objective of Commissioners Lauren-deau and Dunton, and that is what we did in 1982.
Today the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) may very well blame us for not doing more and endorsing the notwithstanding clause. There is always room for improvement, Madam Speaker, but at least we were headed in the right direction.
Such was the history of our country until the day this Prime Minister appeared on the national scene. Before he was elected, the curve of rights was pointing upwards, but now it has shifted and the pattern is just the opposite. So far it has been a trend towards more equality and more rights, the ultimate goal-I mentioned this a moment ago-being to have all Canadians, both anglophone and francophone, feel right at home anywhere in Canada.
The Meech Lake Accord is the first historic constitutional document which takes us one step backwards. With the Meech Lake Accord we are not seeking more rights but a political agreement which ignores rights, which creates an ambiguity that ought to be dispelled by the Supreme Court, of course, but still which leaves a cloud of uncertainty over the maintenance of historic rights.
When the Prime Minister never misses an opportunity to blame somebody and say that the rights of minorities are badly protected, when he claims that the only way to protect rights is to include them in the Constitution, he is guilty of shameful hypocrisy, Madam Speaker. If minority rights ought to have been better protected under the Constitution, why did he fail to do just that at Meech Lake? That is the question I would like to ask him today.

June 14, 1988
Perhaps the Prime Minister does not understand the logic of his approach. It has always been in the national interest to recognize the French fact and the English fact everywhere in Canada. It is in the national interest that Canada as a whole feels obliged to promote the two languages. With the Meech Lake Accord, we revert to a less generous vision, where provincial interests are paramount. We said the same thing a year ago, six months ago, during the debate which occurred here in September, in October, but now, recent events have confirmed our position.
With the Meech Lake Accord, we are heading towards a French Quebec and an English Canada. Instead of recognizing that linguistic minorities are an integral part of this nation's fabric, we barely accommodate them. We acknowledge their existence, but without conviction.
One would have to be deaf not to have heard the concerns about the Meech Lake agreement expressed by linguistic minorities during the course of the past year. I invite any Member of the House to read the papers or to obtain a tape of the Peter Gzowski show from two months ago on which he talked about the state of bilingualism in Canada today. He interviewed Anglophones in Quebec and Francophones outside Quebec. Hon. Members will see what they had to say about this agreement and how they expressed their concerns.
Yesterday I had an 11-year old boy who is in grade five, an English-speaking Quebecer, come to interview me. He asked me a number of questions about my political career and about the upcoming election. One question which he asked me toward the end of his interview was as follows. He said: "What is the future of the English in Quebec?" I had hoped that that question had been laid to rest over the course of the past 15 or 20 years. I thought it would be unnecessary for an 11-year old English-speaking Quebecer to ask such a question.
The same thing applies to Francophones outside Quebec. I would have hoped that they would not have to ask questions about their future, that their future would be guaranteed. They would be getting a pat on the back, an extra dose of generosity, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has referred to in his speeches, but which we find absent in the Meech Lake agreement. Why? Because, as I have tried to explain, that is the essence of what this country is all about. Obviously there has been concern with Meech Lake. One does not hear that very often in the House today. Obviously there has been concern because of the actions of certain provincial Governments.

Indeed, Madam Speaker, at the first opportunity following the signing of the Meech Lake Accord when a government had the choice of maintaining or abolishing the rights of its
Constitution Amendment, 1987
linguistic minority, it chose to abolish them. I am referring, of course, to Saskatchewan, the first province to ratify the Meech Lake Agreement and one of its staunchest supporters. Premier Devine of Saskatchewan, said that from now it would be up to his government to decide when and if provincial acts will be translated in French.
Therefore, the rights of the Francophone minority of that province are at the mercy of the majority. Mr. Bourassa did not want to intervene when he went to Saskatchewan because he did not want other provinces to meddle in the affairs of Quebec later on. And here is what Mr. Bourassa said before going to Saskatchewan, in Victoria, on April 12 last, and I quote:

"Mr. Getty ... ", and he is referring here to the Premier of Alberta, " ... was expressing an obvious fact with which I am in agreement. I take care of language questions in Quebec, and he takes care of language questions in Alberta. That is a selfevident fact". He goes on to say: "I don't think I would be justified in interfering in the powers of other provincial jurisdictions, just as I hope that in Quebec we can take care of our own problems on our own".
Again, I think that most Canadians can see that that is a satisfactory statement coming from the mouth of a provincial premier, but it is not the type of vision of this country that we want to entrench in our Constitution.

So, the Saskatchewan matter is a good lesson. It shows the consequence of forgetting the national interest and giving precedence to provincial interests.
I am not blaming provinces, Madam Speaker. They are not required to act in the national interest. Such is not their mandate-it is the national Government's mandate, the mandate of Members here in this Canadian Parliament.
Six months ago, we were told the Prime Minister was relinquishing another aspect of national interest in the area of federal spending power. As we know, under the Meech Lake Accord, provinces can opt out of shared cost programs, with compensation, provided their provincial program is compatible with national objectives.
My concern and that of many others was that it would be impossible to set up new social programs with such a provision. Six months ago our points were rather academic, but today we have an example of new funding programs for childcare services that are satisfactory to no one, including the Quebec womens' groups that oppose the programs. Indeed this is a childcare program in name only, because there is nothing to deal with workers' health, safety, security and qualifications, training requirements, the number of children under the care of each worker, and so on.
This Conservative Government is proposing a program devoid of basic criteria because it fears such criteria would

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
cause provinces to opt out, thus vindicating the Meech Lake's opponents.
I am not asking for uniformity, Madam Speaker, nor that the Canadian Government should dictate how provinces should manage their programs. What I am looking for is a compromise that would come out of negotiations between both levels of government. That is what federalism is all about. Each level puts forward its own vision.
This leads to healthy competition that benefits all Canadians. Indeed, it is the only way to consider new social programs or an overall reform of our existing social programs, because with the huge cost of that reform and that of new programs, neither provincial nor federal Governments can proceed alone. But under the Meech Lake Accord the dice are loaded. The federal Government, as we have seen with childcare, cannot afford to put forward its own concept because it fears provinces would opt out. So what we are left with is a hollow program where the Canadian Government is limited to keeping the books, supplying money to provinces and saying nothing as to program contents. Under those terms, Madam Speaker, there will be no future social program. The federal level will refuse to take up the odium of taxing in order to transfer moneys to provinces without saying anything about program contents.
Many other examples of how the Prime Minister sacrificed the national interest come to mind, but I cannot mention them in a 20-minute speech. We know very well that Quebec asked for a veto for historical reasons. The Prime Minister gave all provinces a veto for a series of issues, like the future of the Senate.
A few weeks ago, a Minister in the Alberta Government said that his province would object to any constitutional reform unless it obtained an elected Senate with equal representation for all provinces. The veto that Alberta has obtained on several aspects of the Constitution will enable it to do so and block the constitutional development of the whole country.
So I ask you, Madam Speaker, is this the way to encourage the healthy development of the country? I am sure that many Quebecers and many Canadians will say no.
Madam Speaker, in the statements by the leaders earlier today, I detected a note of unreality, because they took the Meech Lake Accord as a fait accompli. But it is becoming increasingly obvious that the Meech Lake Accord will not be adopted in its present form. Indeed, more and more Canadians are asking questions about the Meech Lake Accord and wondering whether it is really the best way to ensure the country's future.
If you allow me to conclude, Madam Speaker, the amendments proposed by the Liberal Party are a step in the right direction because we will have to find a way out, some way to go beyond the Meech Lake Accord, since, as I was just saying, it will not pass in its present form. As I said, the amendments proposed by the Liberal Party are a step in the right direction
but the amendments drawn up by the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) and myself better reflect the philosophy and traditions of our Party.
Madam Speaker, perhaps on a point of order, I could make a few comments . ..
I rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker.
