The debate is proceeding in an orderly fashion. It is time to make comments. I shall ask the Hon. Member whether he has further comments to make. It could be taken on his 10 minutes. Then, there would be no problem, because the debate is proceeding in an orderly fashion.
It is a personal comment which I wanted to make. We will thus keep the order in the House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Then, we have reached the period of questions and comments following the intervention of the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger). Evidently, he could answer a question put by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme). In concluding, I want to say that I understand the enthusiasm with which the signing of the Meech Lake Accord was received. When I say enthusiasm, I am referring to the enthusiasm of Quebecers, because Quebec got what it asked, and more. There is a lot in the Accord that is far removed from the initial positions. However, Quebecers are Canadians too. That is the point I am trying to make today. It is important for us to know what impact this Accord will have on Canada. We should consider the national as well as the provincial perspective, and realize that if Canada is weakened by the Accord, Quebec is the loser.
I want to ask Quebecers and my colleagues here in the House to reflect on the significance of the political achievements of Trudeau, Marchand, Pelletier, Sauve and so many others. These French Canadians imposed their way of seeing things on the entire country. Our economic, social and cultural policies in this country were shaped and influenced by their philosophy. They showed by their actions what French Canadians can aspire to in this country. They can aspire to leadership roles, to positions in which they can influence the direction in which this country is going. We can and must ensure that our national institutions reflect the values, needs and aspirations of French Canadians. They were convinced, and I share their view, that the best way to guarantee the future of French in this country is to involve the entire country in promoting its existence. It is a role that is as appropriate for the Parliament of Canada as for the provincial legislatures and the Quebec National Assembly, and I am referring to the promotion of the French fact. It is a modern vision that recognizes the fact we are living in a global society and that
June 14, 1988

Quebecers should not limit their aspirations to a single province.
As Quebecers and Canadians, we must realize that we do ourselves a disservice if we ignore the national interest and if we undermine the ability of the federal Government to act in the best interests of all Canadians.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Madam
Speaker, as I rise to speak in this historic debate, I want to say to the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) that when he says Ottawa has had a role in promoting the French fact, it is fitting that he comes from the riding of Laurier. I think those are almost exactly the words Sir Wilfrid Laurier expressed as his philosophy of the role of French Canadians in Canada.
I am from western Canada and western Canadians in the past, and I think in the present as well, when they really think about it, have looked upon the federal Government to promote their interests and to help them when they were in need of help. The federal Government represents the larger entity that can sometimes deal with problems, both external and internal, which the provinces cannot. Of course that is the flaw in Meech Lake. In my view it creates not one distinctive Government but eleven distinctive Governments. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made this deal to get Quebec to accept the proposals in the 1982 agreement, he gave a lot of other powers to the provinces. In doing that he fundamentally weakened the federal Government.
Some of my colleagues disagree. I respect them, and I do not have a monopoly on wisdom. They may be right in the long run and I hope they are. However, my position is quite clear. I spoke in the House on October 22, 1987, as shown in Hansard at page 10287. I expressed my opposition to the constitutional Accord at that time.
To summarize, I said that I thought it was important to get Quebec's signature on the Canadian Constitution but it was not a priority such that nothing else mattered. The real priority was a good and sound Constitution. I felt the problem with Meech Lake was that it went beyond bringing Quebec into the Constitution. Under Meech Lake I believe the Senate would become a provincially controlled body endowed with enormous powers within 12 years, which would lead to a decline in the House of Commons. I think the Supreme Court will in effect be appointed by the provinces and, instead of a national institution, I see it becoming a protector of narrow provincial interests. I hope that I am wrong.
I see power as shifting away from Parliament, the provincial legislatures, and the people, to a constitutionally entrenched First Ministers' Conference which I see as a new level of super government, therefore weakening our power here in Parliament. By giving the provinces veto power in some key areas we
Constitution Amendment, 1987
make the amending formula too rigid and in certain key areas it will be impossible to change in the future.
If there ever was an egregious error it is in the treatment of northern Canada. Northern Canadians will not get a voice in the Supreme Court. Surely that is an egregious error. They cannot appoint Senators and cannot form new provinces without the unanimous permission of other provinces.
I said at the time that present and future spending programs like medicare and child care could be compromised because the provinces can opt out. Commentators differ on that, but some respected commentators say that it will be difficult to get the kind of national programs which progressive people in this country want.
There are people who say that women's equality rights, so hard fought for in 1982, could be put in danger by this Accord. There is dispute over that. The recognition of duality in Canada in the wording of the Accord neglects the original inhabitants and ignores the present reality of a multicultural Canada. Provincial power over immigration could result in a chequer-board of immigration policies across Canada with the possible restriction on people's freedom of movement from one province to another. I hope that does not happen. To some extent we will have to look to the future and trust that these things do not happen, but I see it as possible because of the Accord.
In my remarks tonight I do not want to repeat those arguments but to deal, instead, with some of the things the Prime Minister said today. I listened carefully to his speech and I share his desire to have Quebec sign the agreement. I share the obvious joy he expressed in being a Canadian. I shared his joy in seeing and experiencing this great country, yet I was disappointed by his speech. I did not think that it was very statesmanlike.
There was no mention-and I do not know that any of the Leaders mentioned this-that Meech Lake was in trouble. The fact is that Manitoba has said that it will probably not deal with it. Sharon Carstairs, who has the balance of power as Leader of the Opposition, says that it is dead.
No, you have the balance of power.

She said that. The Premier of New Brunswick said that he would not pass the Meech Lake Accord without amendments. However, the Accord must pass all the provinces, not just this House.
Yet I got the feeling, when I was listening to him, that it was sufficient for him to get this thing through the House now and deal with the by-election next week or the general election in the fall or the spring. The Meech Lake Accord and those people who believe in it in good faith will have to deal with the fact that it has to get through the provincial legislatures. I ask the people speaking in this debate why they and the Prime Minister did not talk about how it is going to get through. This

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
debate is as though we are debating in a vacuum. The Prime Minister also said in his speech: "We would open the agreement if there were egregious errors and we have not found any".
Surely the provisions dealing with northern Canada, for example, as one of the provisions, are egregious errors and worth changing. Some of us were here in 1981-82 during that historic time when we debated the Constitution not only here in the House of Commons but in the country at large. The Trudeau Government said at first, it could not make any changes. Gradually the Liberals needed the New Democrats' support in western Canada, and they gradually started to listen about making changes. I cite two areas: native rights and women's rights. These are areas where Prime Minister Trudeau came around. The Premiers said that they were not going to make any changes. They threw out native rights and women's rights, but Canadians forced the Premiers to make the changes. When Governments and even Prime Ministers say "we can't make any changes", I say: "You have done it in the past and you can do it again". I think those changes made a better Constitution. I am very proud to have voted for the 1982 Constitution in this House of Commons. I am very sad that I cannot vote for this Meech Lake constitutional amendment.
The Prime Minister said in his speech today that Meech Lake is consistent with the federal nature of Canada. I do not think so. I think it is quite different from the federal nature of Canada. This Meech Lake Accord gets the provinces into federal institutions for the first time. I have heard people say in this debate that those of us who are against Meech Lake do not understand it, have not read it properly, or are missing something, but let me quote Tom Berger, former Leader of the provincial NDP in British Columbia and former Judge of the Supreme Court of British Columbia. In The Globe and Mail recently we find that he said the following:
But the provisions of Meech Lake relating to the North and to the Supreme Court of Canada also are of great concern; they may seem peripheral, but they go to the heart of the accord. Their impact is clear: they undermine the legitimacy of federal institutions.
That is a real concern. That is why I think it is different. It changes the federal nature of Canada by putting the balance too much on the side of the provinces. The Prime Minister said in his speech today that this builds on the previous constitutional accord. I kept thinking when he said that about our debate and our own Party, in I believe 1981, in Vancouver at our national conference in which the pros and cons in a very democratic and open debate were voiced on the 1981 proposals. It seems to me that in 1981 and 1982 those who spoke against the Constitution in that debate are now on the side of supporting the Meech Lake Accord. It was the decentralizers and that type of argument which lost the day in 1981 at our convention, and I think lost the day in this House in the vote on the debate, who are now for Meech Lake, with some exceptions.
I felt that the Prime Minister took the low road in his speech today. Let me give two instances. First, he said with respect to
the native people that with the return of Quebec into this deal it help aboriginal people. We have had three years of constitutional talks and no agreement with aboriginal people. Then we had one evening when the Premiers got together and there was power sharing. What the Prime Minister said today demeans the native people. What native groups are out here supporting the Meech Lake Accord? I cannot find any. How can the Prime Minister say that this will help the native people? That statement is demeaning and wrong.
His second cheap shot was against former Prime Minister Trudeau. The Prime Minister said that the previous Government put through the Constitution in 1982 with the notwithstanding clause in it; notwithstanding the Charter of Rights, the provinces and this Parliament could overrule the Charter of Rights. I saw Trudeau the night we passed the 1982 Constitution Accord in this House. I thought he would be a happy man but he was sad. I asked him why he was sad because it was his big night. He said he was sad because the Constitution was flawed, referring to the notwithstanding clause. The present Prime Minister came into this House today and said that we have a bad Constitution because the notwithstanding clause was inserted. He bargained with the Premiers but did not remove it. How can he come back to the House and take that kind of a cheap shot at the 1982 Constitution? When he was bargaining with the Premiers at Meech Lake he should have had the notwithstanding clause removed. I cannot see anything that the federal Government gained in this matter. I suppose the gain is having Quebec included.
Perhaps we should be a little honest in this matter. I know that there are people in my Party who hold their views deeply on this matter.
And they are all wrong, I suppose?
In the executive meeting of the B.C. Party they voted against Meech Lake. When we had a provincial council meeting and an overwhelming vote of about 500 to 50 against it-
What about the caucus and the Leader?

My colleague asked me about my caucus and the Leader. The caucus and the Leader have voted for Meech Lake. I want to put on the record-and I respect their vote- that the British Columbia Party, in spite of the leadership of the Leader, the provincial Leader, the party president and the caucus, voted against Meech Lake. Why? They obviously hold their views deeply. Similarly in Nova Scotia the Party voted against it. There is a lot of division on Meech Lake.
Let me ask what will happen now. I do not agree with Sharon Carstairs. I do not think Meech Lake is dead. I think Gary Doer's Manitoba is more correct when he says Meech Lake is in trouble and it needs some changes. I think the federal Government should think about how it will make changes to it.
June 14, 1988

From this whole debate and the amendments put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), by members of the Liberal Party and by others, some amendments can be distilled. I think this thing can be changed before it finally passes. I would suggest that the Prime Minister consider sitting down with Mr. Remillard, the Interprovincial Affairs Minister from Quebec, Ian Scott from Ontario, the Attorney General of Saskatchewan, Mrs. Carstairs, Mr. Doer, a representative of the Premier of Manitoba, as well as the Premier of New Brunswick. Perhaps there may be some amendments that would be acceptable to the various groups involved so that a constitutional deal could go through in the Canadian tradition which is more by consensus than by having something rammed through. If that does not happen, I think Meech Lake will die, and the proponents of Meech Lake have to face that.
I would suggest that in the long term we have to change our method of constitutional amendment. The wheeling, dealing, last minute, back room bargaining is not the way a modern Constitution should be changed. I think there is sufficient good will to have accommodated Quebec and all the other interests, native, women, and multicultural. Some interests will clash, that is true, but other interests can be worked out and we could have an agreement that would have more support.
Meech Lake does not have the support of the people of Canada. Can Hon. Members not see that the emperor has no clothes? Some Members are reluctant to vote for it and will abstain. The whole tone of this debate is different from that of 1982. We as a country can do better. We can come up with a Constitution with which we can all live.
I want to close by saying that I do not know what the future holds for Meech Lake. I think it could be dead and we have to face up to that fact. I have said that Parliament and the Supreme Court are national institutions and the flaw in Meech Lake is that it provides that nominations to the court are to be made from a list prepared by the provinces, in effect giving them control of the appointments, and the same is true for the Senate.
The provisions relating to the creation of provinces in the North and to the Supreme Court of Canada reveal the thinking behind Meech Lake, and that is that national institutions are thought to be without legitimacy unless the provinces share in the power that the national Government used to exercise. This represents, in my view, a diminished federalism, an irresolute idea of Canada. I believe Meech Lake can be rewritten and it ought to be rewritten. It is not my idea of Canada, and I think we as a country can do better.

Madam Speaker, I would like to return to the question of the status of Quebec after the 1981 constitutional agreement was reached on November 5. The Hon. Member referred to that in his speech and mentioned the vote in the House. He said something about 75 Quebecers, and then I said
Constitution Amendment, 1987
"70". Actually the number former Prime Minister Trudeau referred to in the Senate was 71, and he was referring to some research that had been done by someone else. I have not checked the record myself, but I think we can safely assume that there were 71 Quebec MPs representing the whole province who voted for the agreement, and four against.
The National Assembly of Quebec passed a resolution on December 1 opposing the patriation package, and that resolution was adopted by a vote of 70 to 38. Thirty-eight Liberal Members of the Quebec National Assembly refused to condemn the patriation agreement. So we have a total, therefore, of 109 elected representatives from Quebec, here in Parliament or in the National Assembly, who voted for the patriation of the Constitution and 74 who voted against it.
It might be of interest to the Hon. Member that the resolution that was proposed by the Parti Quebecois at the time reads as follows:
The National Assembly of Quebec,
mindful of the right of the people of Quebec to self-determination,...
declares that it cannot accept the plan to patriate the Constitution unless it
meets the following conditions:
1. It must be recognized that the two founding peoples of Canada are fundamentally equal and that Quebec, by virtue of its language, culture and institutions, forms a distinct society within the Canadian federal system and has all the attributes of a distinct national community.
This clause was opposed by members of the Quebec Liberal Party in 1981 when it was presented in a resolution by the PQ. That same Quebec Liberal Party, several years later, under the leadership of Mr. Bourassa, proposes the same thing that his Party voted against earlier, and that is the identical language we find in the Meech Lake Accord. It makes interesting reading and I commend it to the Hon. Member.

Madam Speaker, we are coming at this from different parts of the country. People in British Columbia are asking if I can put it into the language of the street: "Why the heck are you giving Bill Vander Zalm and the likes of him power to eventually control the Senate of Canada, power to put their nominees on the Supreme Court of Canada"? They are asking: "Are you crazy, what are you doing?" This is how many of the people of British Columbia feel. I know that Premier Vander Zalm will not be there forever, but that is the feeling of the people of British Columbia.
The Hon. Member is an English-speaking Quebecer, and I realize the difficult position of English-speaking people in Quebec. There is a feeling in my part of the country that we are not opposed to recognizing Quebec as a distinct society, providing that minority rights can be protected in Quebec. We know it is a strange situation because the majority is really a minority. The French majority of Quebec is a minority in Canada, so it has to have powers to protect itself. I am not against that and I am not against Quebec signing this agreement. I want to clear this up in case I gave the opposite impression in my speech. I am damn glad that Quebec signed it. I was only saying that we should be realistic. Quebec did

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
not sign before because it was a separatist Government and it was not going to sign anything.
When we make a deal with Quebec, as we did, let us not make it at the expense of the national institutions which protect, in the long run, both French and English. I said originally, if I can use the language of the street again: "You know, Canadians don't think of Mario Lemieux as Team Quebec or Wayne Gretzky as Team Alberta; they think of both of them as Team Canada". I think that Trudeau proved that with his victories in Quebec, and so did Laurier. Canadians, both French and English, think of the whole country.
By rejecting Meech Lake, I am not rejecting Quebec or the distinct society of Quebec or Quebec in Canada. I am concerned about this wheeling and dealing that the Prime Minister has done which has fundamentally weakened the country by ignoring the legitimate aspirations of our native people, of women, and of multicultural groups, and by allowing the provincial premiers, the Vander Zalms and the Devines, into the Supreme Court and ultimately into control of the Senate. We will rue the day when that comes through. I hope I am wrong, but that is how I see it and that is how I think a lot of people in my home Province of British Columbia see it as well.

Madam Speaker, I rise tonight to speak on this amendment with mixed feelings. First,
I am pleased that we are here to debate a constitutional amendment which will serve its first purpose, that is, to bring Quebec formally back into the Constitution. This is an extremely important part of Canadian history. I, people from my constituency, and others from the North support it, in that we know that it will greatly enhance Canada as a nation. Without Quebec formally in the Constitution, without recognizing the distinct qualities of Quebec, many of the contributions Quebec has made, and the integral part of the spirit, culture, and history of Quebec, we have not been a full and whole country.
While appreciating the accomplishment of that important historic event, I want to speak about some compromises that have been made which I do not believe, if addressed, would unravel this Accord or be in any way detrimental to the fundamental purpose of having the Province of Quebec formally in the Constitution.
As a northerner, as someone from a constituency which has neither been consulted nor has been a party or signatory to this amendment, I rise with some sadness and perhaps some anger to speak about my concerns. It is sad that in so doing it may seem that I do not support the main intent of the constitutional amendment. That is certainly not true. However, it is extremely important for Canadians as a whole to realize the depth of feeling, the depth of solidarity, and the commitment which northerners have to furthering the constitutional process.
The Quebecois could probably best understand the feeling of being on the outside looking in which northerners have about this process. They could in a sense become our soul mates and, I hope, understand that what I have to say does not in any way detract from the important historical event but puts forward a problem that we are creating by rectifying a wrong.
In order for the circle of Confederation to be complete, it is essential that Members of the House also welcome northerners and accept the rights of Canada's First Nations, the aboriginal people. I will spend my time this evening addressing several main issues concerning this amendment, which concerns have been addressed by my Party through amendments that were voted down by the Government. Northerners will not forget which Party voted against the North and against aboriginal rights.
There are four main parts of the amendment which I will address, the first being the unanimity clause regarding the creation of new provinces; the second being the clause relating to the extension of provincial boundaries; the third being the failure to include the territories in appointments to the Senate and the Supreme Court; and the fourth being the failure to include aboriginal issues as a priority for First Ministers' Conferences and to redress that particular outstanding federal issue.
First, turning to the question about provincehood, since 1871 provinces came into the Confederation in negotiation with the federal Government. The purpose, one assumes, of this is that it is intended that the federal Government should have a Canadian-wide vision. Provinces, quite understandably and quite responsibly, have a priority of a provincial vision. One must wonder why we have a federal Government if the federal Government's purpose is not to provide an integrated whole and not to have a vision which rises above a parochial provincial one. It is for this reason, I assume, that new provinces historically, the last being the Province of Newfoundland in 1949, negotiated this with the federal Government.
Not only this federal Government but the former Liberal Government did not have this Canadian vision. In 1982, when the Constitution returned to Canada, there was the same issue concerning the creation of new provinces. The current Constitution states that, in order for a new province to be created, seven provinces and 50 per cent of the population must give their assent. The amendment under discussion tonight says, of course, that there must be unanimity in that consent.
I would like to give some examples supporting my assertion that neither the former federal Government nor the current federal Government had a Canadian vision which included the North. In 1981 the former Hon. Member for the Yukon moved an amendment to delete the sections on the requirements for new provincehood as well as the sections on boundary extension. The Liberal Government of the day defeated
June 14, 1988

that motion despite some very poignant pleas about why that should be deleted from the 1982 Constitution.
I quote, for example, one Member who said that should those measures, that is, the measures concerning provincehood and boundary extension, be enacted they would "virtually eliminate any hope that the two northern territories could evolve as a province, as did the rest of the country-this resolution-is offensive, repugnant and also ludicrous". That was said in reference to the provincehood resolution. That speaker went on to say that if these measures were to pass in the 1981-82 Constitution, the Territories "would be condemned to perpetual serfdom and to perpetual colonial status unless these offensive clauses are withdrawn".
The current President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) who made those statements in 1981 and six of her current cabinet colleagues obviously thought very strongly at that time that the clauses related to provincehood and boundary extension were seriously detrimental, since such terms as "serfdom" were used, to the furtherance of the northern parts of the country.
Both the Governments of the Yukon and of the Northwest Territories, for approximately the last two years, have been invited periodically to meetings of the Premiers on a number of various issues. They are signatories, for example, to a number of federal-provincial-territorial agreements. Very often Ministers from the Yukon and Northwest Territories attend joint federal-provincial-territorial meetings. In that forum the territories are regarded as a legitimate quasi-provincial Government, if not having all the provincial powers.
It is perhaps important at this point to reiterate that during the joint constitutional hearings held in the summer on the Meech Lake Accord it was clear that many people were surprised that both the Government of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Government were quasi-provincial Governments. The federal Government has devolved many powers to these Governments in the areas, for example, of justice, health, forestry, social services, and so on.
Therefore, in both the territories we have a government leader who is analogous to a premier and a functioning legislature which meets on the same parliamentary rules as this House. These government leaders are elected, as are government members, by the population of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. They are elected on the assumption that elected leaders represent the views of their constituents and will do so not only in the territorial forum but in the federal arena.
This assumption was somewhat rudely shattered when the Meech Lake Accord was under discussion. The government leaders of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon were not consulted, but they came to Ottawa to make their views known. They were not allowed to participate in the meeting to
Constitution Amendment, 1987
express those views and had to do so through the media and other means.
This is not the way for a country to reach a harmonious confederation. It simply is not at all conducive to the kind of harmony which this constitutional amendment strives to create.
Let me give another example to support my contention that the current federal Government does not seem to recognize that there are two territories in Canada. I received many letters from my constituency about a specific publication called Strengthening the Canadian Federation: The Constitution Amendment of 1987", which was put out by the Government in August, 1987. The front shows a lovely picture of all the flags of Canada. Of course, they are the flags of southern Canada and do not include either the flag of the Northwest Territories or the flag of the Yukon.
One can understand when northerners receive material like this that the message is very clear: "You can dress like us, you can come and talk to us sometimes and we will tell you it's okay, but you will not really be a member; you will be outside looking in".
I do not believe that is a principle which anyone in the House would choose to champion, nor would Canadians generally feel that this was a just and equitable way to treat 75,000 Canadian citizens. The unanimity provision in the constitutional amendment is unprecedented in our history. According to my research, it is unparalleled in other modern federations such as the United States, Australia, and India. None of them require that kind of unanimity for the creation of new states or provinces.
Should the territories become a province anyway? It is important to clarify that neither of the territories at this point are discussing becoming a province imminently. However, we recognize that constitutions lay the foundation for the future. They are not just to redress past wrongs constitutions are written to set the future path. Therefore, we are extremely concerned that we will be permanently locked out of the Confederation of Canada through this unanimity provision.
Some provinces seem to be concerned that if the territories become a province they will lose a greater portion of their federal revenues. I realize that equalization payments are entrenched in the Constitution, but I think it is important to look at what is actually happening. Both in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, at least 70 per cent of our budgets are federal funds. While we may be talking about a different formula, we are still talking about an amount of money which can be equitably divided. Therefore, I find the argument that allowing for the creation of new provinces detracts from the kind of fiscal equity for existing provinces simply specious. I believe it could easily be renegotiated.
I will use the Yukon as an example. In 1985 there was a successful negotiation of a three-year economic development agreement with the federal Government. Many aspects of that

June 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
particular agreement parallel the equalization and transfer payments that take place between the federal Government and the provinces. We are not talking about a major effect or change. Many of these mechanisms in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon are in practice now.
A second argument about the creation of new provinces has been that it will create an imbalance regarding the amending formula and so on. Surely this is a relatively easy matter to address. Is it really being suggested that a country of this size cannot have 13 provinces, considering that the Northwest Territories will be going forward with a division into the eastern Arctic Nunavik and Western Arctic in a couple of years?
Is it really being suggested that this would be totally impossible and that the country could not cope with it? Again, it is simply not a valid argument.
In 1987 the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) said:
I do not think that anyone can challenge the fact that my Party and this
Government have taken a leadership role in respect to ensuring that as quickly
as possible we move forward in this area of the territories controlling their
destiny and attaining provincial status.
Currently programs are being devolved to the territories.
I do not suggest that there is any intention of duplicity when we see programs being devolved on the one hand and, on the other hand, being given some responsibility without belonging to the club. It certainly gives a message to northerners that they will never have full self-determination, despite what is happening through devolution of powers.
Let me also deal with the issue of boundary extensions. The Accord states that provinces may extend their boundaries, again under the unanimity provision. It was never contemplated in the British North America Act, the Yukon Act, or any relevant statute that any of the existing provinces would extend their boundaries northward.
I believe the idea was first expressed in the 1930s by British Columbia and was reiterated as late as the 1970s. At various times Alberta and Saskatchewan also made the same suggestions.
When I raised this issue with various provincial members and indeed with the federal Government, I was told that no one would ever use this provision. If so, I suggest that it should be deleted.
The practical consequences are ludicrous. For example, if British Columbia suddenly decided to extend its boundaries there would be an uproar.
In the minute 1 have left, I want to quote Trevor Lloyd because what he said is quite pertinent to this argument. He said: "For many years the Canadian North was governed in a prolonged fit of absence of mind". We have an opportunity to redress this absence of mind. The New Democratic Party has proposed excellent amendments which would address these matters.
Let me finish by stating why I think this issue is important. I held a contest for some Grade 6 students in my constituency. They drew posters depicting what Canada Day meant to them. I think they show why northerners are concerned about the future. Helen Weber of Christ the King School has a poster showing Indian people and non-Indians, the gold rush, the Canadian dag, and the past. For her, the future is a question mark. I think it is time to respond to that question mark.
Let me quote Rosanna Dick from Ross River, Yukon, who said: "To me Canada means the Yukon Territory, my home". For Rosanna Dick, Stuart Dolan, Helen Weber, and all those children who feel that Canada is their home and their country, we have an opportunity, through a just amendment that will not unravel the Constitution, to show these children that they have a future that is not a question mark.

Madam Speaker, I would ask the Hon. Member for the Yukon exactly what the amendment would entail. Where does she see the opposition to the amendment coming from? Is it simply in an egregious error that perhaps the provinces have not considered it, or does she think that the provinces in fact have their own agendas, in other words, they want to grab the North for themselves? Is it true that, for example, if one is a lawyer in northern Canada, one cannot be appointed to the Supreme Court of Canada because under the Accord that is not permitted? I just wonder if the Hon. Member could tell me more precisely what the amendments would propose and where the Opposition, if any, would come from?

There are several amendments that have already been proposed which I mentioned in my speech. In 1981, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) proposed an amendment regarding the boundary extension. It was in the previous discussions in the 1982 Constitution that boundary extensions should not take place without the consent of those involved, in other words, the residents of the territories. That amendment was, of course, voted down by the then Liberal Government.
In 1987, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) made an amendment in this House stating that aboriginal rights should be addressed and that section of the constitutional amendment under debate tonight should be changed to include acknowledgement of the concerns around aboriginal issues and the concern about the unanimity provision for provincehood. That amendment was voted down by the current Government.
Also in 1987, the Hon. Member for Skeena made an amendment stating that the Joint Committee on the Meech Lake Accord should travel to the North. That amendment was voted down by the current Government. It is interesting that when one reads the report from the Senate hearings, one finds that in fact the Senate committee travelled to the North, it heard what people had to say, and as a result the kind of
June 14, 1988

amendments it proposed-I almost hesitate to say so with some of my personal feelings about the other place-first of all, are similar to the amendments proposed by my own Party and do address the issues I have raised.
I have put forward three Private Member's motions, one for the inclusion of government leaders in further constitutional talks, another for the deletion of the section on boundary extension and a third for the deletion of the unanimity provision with respect to provincial provinces. So Members, hopefully, will have an opportunity to show their solidarity with the North should these be chosen, as well as in voting for my Party's amendments when we vote on this constitutional amendment.
In terms of the question, where does the Opposition come from, it is hard to say. I was not invited to the First Ministers' conference. I probably will be next time, but I was not invited last time. From reading the joint constitutional hearings, I find there are certainly quotes from Senators that certain provinces were jealous of the trappings of provincehood the territories had. Others were concerned about equalization payments, and so on. So clearly it was not a mistake or forgetful lapse. It was deliberate.
One thing that is very important, I think, for people to recognize is that the treatment of the North in this amendment was not an oversight. It was a deliberate act. When it comes to the appointment of Senators, it is a curious thing because, yes, as I understand the amendment, the Yukon would not be able to appoint Senators. I am not sure if the one who is there gets drummed out in some sort of official ceremony-and as I understand it, it could not appoint Supreme Court Judges.
What is interesting about that particular section is that the Supreme Court Judges themselves, as you will know, backed by the Canadian Bar Association, supported a particular amendment to redress that particular issue. Therefore, it is difficult to say where the opposition comes from. I think clearly there are very few issues about which there is some unanimity in the North, and this is one.
I think I can say fairly confidently that we feel this has to be a federal territorial issue because it is the federal Government which is supposed to have the Canadian vision. We do not expect each individual province to have that kind of vision. The hope, I suppose, of First Ministers conferences is that there will be some kind of collective vision. If so, I would say it is limited because we in the territories have to be worried about the bargaining. We have been a bargaining chip before. That was certainly a point the former Member from the Yukon made in the 1981-82 debates on the constitutional Accord.
I think we have to be worried about what kind of powers, what kind of agreements, will be made if, indeed, at some point, 10 or 15 years down the road, the territories knock on the door and say: "We would like to become provinces". What will have to be traded off? I think you trade off in the national interest, not in a parochial interest.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
It is difficult to say what the particular barriers are because they were closed meetings, of course, which is another interesting point about the process. It is interesting when one of the most historic documents in Canada is a very private matter. I appreciate the negotiations being private, but we are not really privy to the kinds of reasons people had for the very serious decisions they have made.

Madam Speaker, may I join in the small but very attentive audience tonight and say what a very powerful statement our colleague has made. I do want to make two minor points that arose, I think, out of an error introduced by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). It is not a matter that a lawyer practising in the Yukon or the Northwest Territories might not become an nominee for the Supreme Court Bench, it is if a province is willing to nominate him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: Listen to the Prime Minister today and you know differently. The decision will be made by the Prime Minister of Canada.

I am sorry, I am talking about nominations. The Hon. Member has obviously not been in a state to listen. In the matter of nominations, the fact is, and I am sure the Hon. Member would agree, as I have outlined, and I just want to correct my friend, the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway.
On the matter of Senate appointments, it was the Joint Committee's understanding, under the relative section-and it slips me for the moment-of the BN A Act, the federal Government is still entirely free to appoint Senators from the two territories. That section of the BNA Act would still be paramount.
I would like to conclude my comment with a question. There is an absence of will on the part of both the previous Government and the present Government to include at all conferences, leaders of the two territories, apart from the sort of jealousy that may be involved in provinces somehow including territorial leaders at First Ministers' meetings. I agree with the Hon. Member that there is not that much difference between 10 and 13, should we divide the Northwest Territories. Is there any other reason that the Hon. Member has thought of? Does it relate, for example-and I realize this is a sensitive point- to the possibility that there will be aboriginal self-government in at least one of the territories in the foreseeable future?
Madam Speaker, I cannot-
